chapters.summary: This chapter contains 31 verses and records God creating heaven and earth in six days: light and the division of day and night; a firmament separating waters; seas and dry land; vegetation; sun, moon, and stars for signs and seasons; sea creatures and birds, blessed to multiply; land animals; and humanity, male and female, in God’s image with dominion, commands to multiply, and provision of plants for food.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records God finishing creation, resting on the seventh day, and blessing and sanctifying it. It describes God forming man from dust, planting Eden, and placing the man there to tend it. It lists Eden’s river and its four heads (Pison, Gihon, Hiddekel, Euphrates). God commands not to eat from the tree of knowledge. Animals are named, woman is made from man’s rib, and marriage is established.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the serpent tempting the woman to eat the forbidden fruit; she and Adam eat, realize their nakedness, and hide. The LORD God questions them, pronounces curses on the serpent, the woman, and Adam, and describes pain in childbirth, toil, and death. Adam names his wife Eve; God clothes them and expels them from Eden, guarding the tree of life with cherubim and a flaming sword.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the births of Cain and Abel, their occupations and offerings, and Cain’s murder of Abel. It describes God’s questioning, Cain’s curse to be a fugitive, and a protective mark set on him. Cain settles in Nod, builds a city, and his descendants are listed, including Lamech’s family. Seth and Enos are born, and people begin calling on the LORD.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the genealogy from Adam to Noah, beginning with God creating humanity male and female. It lists each patriarch’s age at fathering the next named son, additional years lived, total lifespan, and death: Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, and Lamech. It notes Enoch walks with God and is taken by God. Lamech names Noah, and Noah fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records human multiplication, “sons of God” taking wives, and the presence of giants and mighty men. God observes widespread wickedness and violence, declares a 120-year limit, and determines to destroy life by a flood. Noah is described as righteous and has Shem, Ham, and Japheth. God commands Noah to build an ark with specified dimensions, bring his family and pairs of animals, store food, and Noah obeys.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD commanding Noah to enter the ark with his family and to take clean animals and birds by sevens and unclean by twos. After seven days rain falls forty days; fountains of the deep break up. The LORD shuts them in. Floodwaters lift the ark, cover hills and mountains, and destroy all land life. Waters prevail 150 days.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records God causing the floodwaters to subside, stopping rain and closing the deep, and the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends a raven and then doves, receiving an olive leaf and later no return. God commands Noah’s family and all creatures to leave the ark and multiply. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. The LORD declares He will not again curse the ground or destroy all living things, and seasons continue.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records God blessing Noah’s family to multiply, granting animals for food, and forbidding eating blood. It requires accountability for lifeblood and states that whoever sheds human blood is to be put to death. God establishes a covenant with Noah and all living creatures never again to destroy all flesh by flood, with the rainbow as the sign. It names Shem, Ham, and Japheth, recounts Noah’s drunkenness and Ham’s act, Shem and Japheth covering Noah, Noah’s curse on Canaan, blessings on Shem and Japheth, and Noah’s lifespan and death.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the genealogies of Noah’s sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth after the flood, listing their descendants and associated nations, lands, and languages. It notes Nimrod’s rise and his kingdom’s beginnings at Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar, and mentions Asshur building Nineveh and related cities. It traces Canaanite families and borders, and Shem’s line through Arphaxad to Eber, Peleg, and Joktan.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the building of a city and tower in Shinar, the LORD confounding human language, and the scattering of people, naming the place Babel. It also lists Shem’s descendants from Arphaxad to Terah, identifies Abram’s family (Sarai, Lot, Milcah), notes Sarai’s barrenness, and recounts Terah’s migration from Ur toward Canaan, settling and dying in Haran.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records the LORD calling Abram to leave his country and promising to make him a great nation, bless him, and bless all families through him. Abram departs from Haran with Sarai and Lot to Canaan, travels to Shechem and near Bethel, and builds altars. A famine leads him to Egypt, where Sarai is taken into Pharaoh’s house after Abram calls her his sister; plagues strike Pharaoh, who returns Sarai and sends them away.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Abram’s return from Egypt to the Negev and to Beth-el, where he worships at his altar. It describes conflict between Abram’s and Lot’s herdsmen, leading to their separation. Lot chooses the Jordan plain near Sodom; Abram remains in Canaan. The LORD promises Abram the land and numerous descendants, and Abram settles by Mamre in Hebron and builds an altar.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a war between four eastern kings and five kings of the Siddim valley, the plundering of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot’s capture. Abram pursues the captors with 318 trained servants to Dan and Hobah, rescues Lot and recovers goods and people. Melchizedek king of Salem blesses Abram, who gives tithes. Abram refuses Sodom’s goods except provisions and allies’ portions.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the LORD speaking to Abram in a vision, promising protection, an heir from Abram’s own body, and descendants as numerous as stars. Abram believes. The LORD reaffirms bringing him from Ur to inherit the land, instructs a covenant sacrifice, foretells Abram’s descendants’ bondage and deliverance after 400 years, and establishes the land boundaries and listed nations.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Sarai’s barrenness and her giving Hagar, an Egyptian handmaid, to Abram after ten years in Canaan. Hagar conceives and conflicts arise, leading Sarai to treat her harshly and Hagar to flee. The angel of the LORD meets Hagar by a fountain on the way to Shur, commands her to return, promises numerous descendants, and names her son Ishmael. The well is called Beer-lahai-roi, between Kadesh and Bered. Hagar bears Ishmael when Abram is 86.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records the LORD appearing to Abram, commanding him to walk before God, and establishing an everlasting covenant promising many nations and the land of Canaan. Abram is renamed Abraham, and Sarai is renamed Sarah. Circumcision is instituted as the covenant sign for all males. God promises Sarah bears Isaac and blesses Ishmael with twelve princes. Abraham circumcises himself, Ishmael, and his household.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD appearing to Abraham in the plains of Mamre with three men, whom Abraham hosts. The LORD promises Sarah will bear a son; Sarah laughs and then denies it. The men depart toward Sodom, and the LORD speaks of judging Sodom and Gomorrah. Abraham intercedes, bargaining from fifty down to ten righteous for the city to be spared, then the LORD departs.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records two angels visiting Lot in Sodom, the city’s men surrounding his house, and the angels striking them with blindness. Lot is warned to flee; his sons-in-law refuse. Lot, his wife, and two daughters escape toward Zoar; Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed by fire and brimstone. Lot’s wife looks back and becomes salt. Abraham sees the smoke. Lot later dwells in a cave; his daughters bear Moab and Ben-ammi.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Abraham sojourning in Gerar between Kadesh and Shur, saying Sarah is his sister, and Abimelech king of Gerar taking her. God warns Abimelech in a dream to restore Sarah or die, noting Abraham is a prophet who will pray. Abimelech confronts Abraham, returns Sarah with gifts and land, and gives silver to Sarah. Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s household and reopens closed wombs.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Isaac’s birth to Sarah, Abraham’s naming and circumcising him, and a feast at his weaning. Sarah demands Hagar and Ishmael be sent away; God directs Abraham, promises to make Ishmael a nation, and provides water in the wilderness of Beer-sheba. Ishmael grows in Paran and marries an Egyptian. Abimelech and Phichol make a covenant with Abraham over a disputed well, naming Beer-sheba.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records God commanding Abraham to offer Isaac in the land of Moriah. Abraham travels, prepares an altar, and binds Isaac, but an angel stops him; Abraham sacrifices a ram instead and names the place Jehovah-jireh. The LORD reaffirms covenant blessings on Abraham’s seed. The chapter ends with Nahor’s family genealogy, including Bethuel and Rebekah.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Sarah’s death at Kirjath-arba (Hebron) in Canaan and Abraham’s mourning. Abraham negotiates with the sons of Heth to obtain a burial place, requesting Ephron son of Zohar’s cave of Machpelah near Mamre. Ephron offers the field and cave; Abraham insists on payment and weighs 400 shekels of silver. The field, cave, and trees are legally secured to Abraham, and Sarah is buried there.

This chapter contains 67 verses and records Abraham commissioning his chief servant to secure a wife for Isaac from Abraham’s kindred, not from the Canaanites. The servant travels to Mesopotamia, prays at a well, and meets Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel and kin to Nahor. Laban and Bethuel consent; gifts are given. Rebekah agrees to go, journeys to Canaan, meets Isaac near Beer-lahai-roi, and becomes his wife.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Abraham’s marriage to Keturah and the birth of their sons, his inheritance to Isaac, and gifts sending other sons eastward. It reports Abraham’s death at 175 and burial by Isaac and Ishmael at Machpelah near Mamre. It lists Ishmael’s twelve sons and his death. It covers Isaac and Rebekah, the conception and birth of twins Esau and Jacob, and Esau selling his birthright to Jacob for bread and lentil pottage.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records a famine leading Isaac to Gerar, where the LORD commands him not to go to Egypt and reaffirms covenant blessings. Isaac claims Rebekah is his sister; Abimelech discovers she is his wife and orders protection for them. Isaac prospers; Philistines stop wells and drive him away. Isaac reopens and digs wells (Esek, Sitnah, Rehoboth), goes to Beer-sheba, builds an altar, and makes a covenant with Abimelech. Esau marries two Hittite women, grieving Isaac and Rebekah.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Isaac, old and blind, planning to bless Esau after a hunt; Rebekah directs Jacob to impersonate Esau with goat skins and prepared meat, and Isaac blesses Jacob with prosperity and dominion. Esau arrives, learns the blessing is taken, and receives a secondary blessing. Esau plans to kill Jacob; Rebekah sends Jacob to Laban in Haran and cites concern about Jacob marrying daughters of Heth.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Isaac blessing Jacob and sending him to Padan-aram to marry among Laban’s family, not Canaanites. Esau takes Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael, as an additional wife. Jacob travels from Beer-sheba toward Haran, dreams of a ladder with angels, and receives promises of land, descendants, blessing, and divine protection. Jacob names the place Bethel, sets up a stone pillar, anoints it, vows loyalty, and promises a tenth.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jacob’s arrival in the land of the east, meeting shepherds from Haran at a well, and encountering Rachel. Jacob is received by Laban, agrees to serve seven years to marry Rachel, but is given Leah at the wedding; he then serves seven more years and also marries Rachel. Laban provides maidservants Zilpah and Bilhah. Leah bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, while Rachel is barren.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Rachel giving her maid Bilhah to Jacob, who fathers Dan and Naphtali; Leah gives Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher; a mandrakes bargain leads to Leah bearing Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah; Rachel bears Joseph. Jacob seeks to leave Laban, negotiates speckled-spotted livestock wages, uses rods while breeding, and increases his herds and servants.

This chapter contains 55 verses and records Jacob hearing Laban’s sons’ complaints, receiving God’s command to return to Canaan, and departing Padan-aram with his family and flocks. Rachel steals Laban’s household images. Laban pursues to Mount Gilead but is warned by God in a dream. He searches unsuccessfully; Jacob protests his service. They make a covenant with a heap and pillar called Galeed/Jegar-sahadutha and Mizpah, swear oaths, offer sacrifice, and separate.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Jacob meeting angels at Mahanaim, sending messengers to Esau in Seir/Edom, and fearing Esau’s approach with 400 men. Jacob divides his company, prays for deliverance, and prepares gifts of livestock in separate droves. He moves his family across the ford Jabbok, wrestles a man until daybreak, is injured in the thigh, receives the name Israel, and names the place Peniel/Penuel; Israel avoids the thigh sinew.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Jacob meeting Esau with four hundred men, arranging his family, bowing seven times, and reconciling through embrace and weeping. Jacob presents gifts, which Esau accepts, and declines Esau’s offer of escort while promising to travel slowly toward Seir. Esau returns to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth, then to Shalem near Shechem in Canaan, buys land from Hamor’s sons, and builds an altar named El-elohe-Israel.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Dinah going out, Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite taking and defiling her, and seeking marriage through Hamor. Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully, requiring circumcision for intermarriage and settlement. The men of Shechem’s city are circumcised; on the third day Simeon and Levi kill all males, including Hamor and Shechem, rescue Dinah, and the brothers plunder the city. Jacob rebukes them, fearing retaliation.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records God commanding Jacob to go to Beth-el and build an altar; Jacob orders his household to discard foreign gods and purify themselves. Jacob travels safely, builds an altar at Beth-el, and Deborah dies and is buried there. God appears, blesses Jacob, renames him Israel, promises fruitfulness and the land, and Jacob sets up a pillar. Rachel dies bearing Benjamin near Ephrath; Reuben lies with Bilhah; Jacob’s twelve sons are listed. Isaac dies at Hebron and is buried by Esau and Jacob.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records the generations of Esau (Edom), listing his wives, sons, and descendants. It recounts Esau moving from Canaan away from Jacob and dwelling in Mount Seir. It names Edomite chiefs (dukes), the Horite inhabitants of Seir and their chiefs, and the kings who reign in Edom before Israel has a king, concluding with additional Edomite dukes by families and places.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Jacob dwelling in Canaan, Joseph at seventeen reporting his brothers, and Israel favoring him with a coat. Joseph relates two dreams, increasing his brothers’ hatred and envy. Sent from Hebron to Shechem and then Dothan, Joseph is seized, stripped, and cast into a pit; Reuben seeks to spare him. Judah urges selling him; Midianites/Ishmaelites take Joseph to Egypt. The brothers deceive Jacob with the bloodied coat; Jacob mourns. Joseph is sold to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s captain.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Judah leaving his brothers, marrying Shuah’s daughter, and fathering Er, Onan, and Shelah. Judah gives Tamar to Er; Er dies, and Onan is slain for refusing to raise seed. Tamar waits, then disguises herself and conceives by Judah, taking his signet, bracelets, and staff. Judah acknowledges her; she bears twins, Pharez and Zarah.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Joseph being sold into Egypt to Potiphar, who makes him overseer as his household prospers. Potiphar’s wife repeatedly solicits Joseph; he refuses and flees, leaving his garment. She falsely accuses him, and Potiphar imprisons Joseph among the king’s prisoners. In prison Joseph gains favor, and the keeper entrusts prisoners and duties to him.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Pharaoh imprisoning his chief butler and chief baker where Joseph is confined; Joseph serves them and interprets their dreams. He foretells the butler’s restoration in three days and asks to be mentioned to Pharaoh, and foretells the baker’s execution. On Pharaoh’s birthday the butler is restored and the baker is hanged, but the butler forgets Joseph.

This chapter contains 57 verses and records Pharaoh’s two dreams of cows and grain, the failure of Egypt’s magicians to interpret, and the chief butler’s report of Joseph. Joseph interprets the dreams as seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine and advises storing a fifth during plenty. Pharaoh appoints Joseph over Egypt, gives him authority, the name Zaphnath-paaneah, and Asenath as wife; Manasseh and Ephraim are born. Joseph stores grain, then distributes and sells it during the famine as nations come to Egypt.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jacob sending ten sons to Egypt to buy grain during the Canaan famine, keeping Benjamin home. Joseph, governor of Egypt, recognizes them, accuses them of spying, imprisons them, and requires Benjamin’s return; Simeon is bound. Joseph returns their money in their sacks. The brothers report to Jacob, who refuses to send Benjamin despite Reuben’s pledge.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jacob’s sons returning to Egypt during famine, with Judah pledging to protect Benjamin. Israel sends gifts and double money. Joseph sees Benjamin, orders a meal prepared, and brings Simeon out. The brothers explain the returned money to Joseph’s steward. Joseph receives their present, asks about their father, weeps privately, and hosts them at a segregated meal, seating them by birth order and favoring Benjamin.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Joseph ordering his steward to return the brothers’ money and hide his silver cup in Benjamin’s sack. The steward pursues and accuses them; the cup is found with Benjamin, and they return to Joseph. Joseph declares Benjamin must remain his servant. Judah recounts their family situation and Jacob’s attachment to Benjamin, and offers himself as a bondman in Benjamin’s place.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Joseph revealing his identity to his brothers in Egypt, weeping and explaining the famine and his role under Pharaoh. He instructs them to bring Jacob and their households to dwell in Goshen, promising provision. Pharaoh approves and supplies wagons and goods. Joseph sends gifts, warns them not to quarrel, and they report to Jacob in Canaan that Joseph lives and rules Egypt; Jacob resolves to go see him.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jacob’s journey to Beer-sheba, his sacrifices, and God’s night vision telling him not to fear going to Egypt and promising to bring him up again. It lists the names and totals of Jacob’s family who come to Egypt (66 from Jacob, 70 including Joseph’s household). Judah goes ahead to Goshen; Joseph meets Jacob and weeps. Joseph instructs the family to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds to dwell in Goshen.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Joseph presenting five brothers and Jacob to Pharaoh, who grants them Goshen and assigns capable men over his cattle. Jacob states he is 130 and blesses Pharaoh; Joseph settles and feeds the family in Rameses. During famine Joseph collects money, then cattle, then land and people for Pharaoh, exempting priests, and sets a fifth-tax law. Israel prospers; Jacob lives 17 years, and makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Jacob, sick in Egypt, receiving Joseph and his sons Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob recalls God’s appearance at Luz and the promise of land to his seed, adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own heirs, and mentions Rachel’s death near Ephrath (Bethlehem). He blesses the boys, crossing his hands to place Ephraim before Manasseh, foretells Ephraim’s greater increase, promises God will return Israel to their fathers’ land, and gives Joseph an extra portion taken from the Amorite.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Jacob gathering his sons to declare what will befall them and to bless them. He pronounces sayings over Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, and Benjamin. Jacob commands his sons to bury him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre in Canaan, bought from Ephron the Hittite, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah are buried. Jacob then dies.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Joseph mourning Jacob, having Israel embalmed, and receiving Pharaoh’s permission to bury him in Canaan at Machpelah; a large Egyptian company accompanies the funeral and mourns at Atad. Joseph’s brothers fear revenge and seek forgiveness; Joseph reassures and provides for them. The chapter notes Joseph’s 110-year life, descendants through Ephraim and Manasseh, his prophecy of Israel’s return, his oath about his bones, and his death and embalming in Egypt.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the names of Jacob’s family who enter Egypt and the growth of the Israelites after Joseph’s generation dies. A new Pharaoh oppresses Israel with taskmasters and hard labor, building Pithom and Raamses. Pharaoh orders Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill male infants; they refuse and are questioned. Pharaoh then commands all Egyptians to cast every newborn Hebrew son into the river.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Moses’ birth to Levite parents, his concealment and placement in an ark on the Nile, and his adoption by Pharaoh’s daughter, with his mother hired to nurse him. It covers Moses killing an Egyptian, his flight to Midian, aid to Reuel’s daughters, marriage to Zipporah, and birth of Gershom. It ends with Israel’s cries heard as God remembers the covenant.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Moses tending Jethro’s flock at Horeb, where the LORD appears in a burning bush and commands him to remove his shoes. God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, states Israel’s affliction in Egypt, and commissions Moses to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out to serve God on the mountain. God reveals the name “I AM,” instructs Moses to gather Israel’s elders, predicts Pharaoh’s resistance, promises wonders, and Israel’s receiving Egyptian goods.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD giving Moses signs (rod to serpent, leprous hand healed, water to blood) to persuade Israel, addressing Moses’ lack of eloquence, and appointing Aaron as spokesman. Moses returns from Midian with his family, is told Pharaoh’s heart will be hardened, and is to demand Israel’s release under threat to Egypt’s firstborn. Zipporah circumcises their son. Aaron meets Moses; they speak to Israel’s elders, perform signs, and the people believe and worship.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Moses and Aaron asking Pharaoh to let Israel go to hold a feast and sacrifice in the wilderness. Pharaoh refuses and increases Israel’s labor by requiring bricks without providing straw. Israelites scatter to gather stubble, and their officers are beaten for failing quotas. The officers complain to Pharaoh, then blame Moses and Aaron. Moses prays, questioning why deliverance delays.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD assuring Moses that Pharaoh will release Israel by a strong hand, reaffirming the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give Canaan, and promising deliverance from Egyptian bondage. Israel does not listen because of hardship. The LORD commands Moses and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh. A genealogy lists heads of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, including Moses and Aaron’s lineage and descendants.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the LORD appointing Moses to speak to Pharaoh through Aaron, foretelling Pharaoh’s hardened heart and coming judgments. Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh; Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians’ serpents, yet Pharaoh resists. The LORD sends them to the Nile; Aaron strikes Egypt’s waters, turning them to blood, killing fish and fouling the river for seven days.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Moses and Aaron demanding Israel’s release from Pharaoh, followed by three plagues in Egypt: frogs, lice, and swarms of flies. Pharaoh asks Moses to pray for relief and makes temporary promises, but hardens his heart after the frogs and flies are removed. The magicians imitate the frogs but cannot produce lice and acknowledge God’s power. Goshen is spared from the flies.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records the LORD sending Moses to demand Israel’s release and bringing three plagues on Egypt: a livestock disease killing Egyptian cattle but not Israel’s, boils on people and animals that disable the magicians, and a severe hailstorm with thunder and fire that devastates crops, trees, and those in the field while sparing Goshen. Pharaoh confesses sin, asks Moses to pray, then hardens his heart and refuses.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records the LORD sending Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh, warning of locusts if Israel is not released. Locusts devastate Egypt; Pharaoh briefly confesses sin, then the LORD removes them by a west wind and hardens Pharaoh’s heart. Moses then brings three days of darkness; Israel has light. Pharaoh offers partial release, Moses demands all people and livestock, and Pharaoh expels him.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records the LORD announcing to Moses one final plague on Egypt after which Pharaoh will expel Israel. Moses tells the people to request silver and gold from Egyptians, and the LORD gives them favor. Moses warns that at midnight all Egyptian firstborn, including beasts, will die, causing great mourning, while Israel is unharmed. Pharaoh’s servants will demand Israel leave. Pharaoh refuses; Moses and Aaron perform wonders, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records the LORD’s Passover instructions to Moses and Aaron: selecting an unblemished lamb, applying blood on doorposts, eating roasted lamb with unleavened bread, and removing leaven for seven days with holy convocations. It recounts the death of Egypt’s firstborn, Pharaoh’s order to depart, Israel’s departure from Rameses to Succoth, and the 430-year sojourn. It gives Passover participation rules tied to circumcision.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD’s command to sanctify Israel’s firstborn and establish the Feast of Unleavened Bread in Abib, with instructions to teach children and keep leaven out. It commands redeeming firstborn humans and certain animals. It describes God leading Israel from Egypt by the wilderness toward the Red Sea, Moses taking Joseph’s bones, encampments at Succoth and Etham, and guidance by pillar of cloud and fire.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD directing Israel to camp by the sea near Pi-hahiroth as Pharaoh pursues with chariots. Israel fears and complains, and Moses tells them to stand firm. The LORD commands Moses to stretch out his rod; an east wind parts the sea, and Israel crosses on dry ground. Egyptians follow, are hindered, and the waters return, drowning Pharaoh’s army; Israel sees the deliverance and believes.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Moses and Israel singing a song to the LORD about Pharaoh’s chariots drowned in the Red Sea and the LORD’s reign. Miriam leads the women with timbrels and dancing. Moses brings Israel into the wilderness of Shur; after three days they reach Marah’s bitter water, murmur, and the LORD shows a tree to sweeten it. A statute and command to heed the LORD is given, and they camp at Elim.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Israel traveling from Elim to the wilderness of Sin and murmuring against Moses and Aaron for lack of food. The LORD promises bread from heaven, sends quail and manna, and gives rules for daily gathering, no storing overnight, and double gathering on the sixth day for the sabbath. Disobedience brings spoilage and rebuke. An omer of manna is preserved before the Testimony; manna lasts forty years.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Israel camping at Rephidim without water, the people quarreling with Moses, and the LORD providing water when Moses strikes the rock at Horeb; the place is named Massah and Meribah. It also covers Amalek attacking Israel, Joshua leading the battle while Moses, Aaron, and Hur support raised hands, Israel’s victory, a command to record the event, an altar named Jehovah-nissi, and a declaration of ongoing war with Amalek.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jethro, priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, bringing Zipporah and Moses’ sons Gershom and Eliezer to Moses at the mount of God. Moses recounts Israel’s deliverance; Jethro blesses the LORD, offers sacrifices, and eats with Aaron and Israel’s elders. Jethro observes Moses judging alone and advises appointing qualified rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Moses implements this system; Jethro returns home.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Israel arriving in the wilderness of Sinai and camping before Mount Sinai. The LORD calls Moses up, recounts deliverance from Egypt, and offers a covenant requiring obedience; the people agree. The LORD commands sanctification, washing, and boundaries around the mountain with death penalties for violation. On the third day thunder, lightning, trumpet, smoke, and quaking accompany the LORD’s descent; Moses speaks with God, is warned to restrain the people, and is told to return with Aaron.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records God speaking from Sinai, declaring he brought Israel from Egypt, and giving commandments: no other gods, no images, reverence his name, keep the Sabbath, honor parents, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting. The people fear the thunder and trumpet and ask Moses to mediate. God forbids silver and gold gods and gives altar instructions.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records legal judgments on Hebrew servitude and release, treatment of a maidservant, and penalties for homicide, manslaughter refuge, assault on parents, kidnapping, and cursing parents. It sets compensation for injuries, including harm to a pregnant woman and “eye for eye” restitution, and rules for harming servants. It also covers liability for goring oxen, ransom payments, pits left uncovered, and livestock damage.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records laws on restitution for theft, burglary, and damage by animals or fire; disputes over entrusted property, lost items, and borrowing or hiring animals. It covers seduction and marriage payment, and penalties for witchcraft, bestiality, and idolatrous sacrifice. It commands fair treatment of strangers, widows, and orphans, forbids usury and retaining a poor man’s pledge overnight, and prohibits cursing rulers. It requires firstfruits and firstborn offerings and forbids eating torn flesh.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records laws on truthful testimony, impartial justice, aiding an enemy’s livestock, rejecting bribery, and not oppressing strangers. It commands sabbath rest, a sabbatical year for fields, and forbids naming other gods. It institutes three annual feasts and offerings. God promises an Angel to lead Israel, defeat Canaanite nations, set borders, and forbids covenants or idol worship.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Moses being called up with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to worship, while Moses alone approaches the LORD. Moses reports the LORD’s words, writes them, builds an altar and twelve pillars, and sacrifices offerings. Blood is sprinkled on the altar and people as covenant confirmation. The leaders see God and eat. Moses ascends Sinai with Joshua to receive stone tablets; Aaron and Hur oversee the people. A cloud and glory cover the mountain; Moses remains forty days and nights.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses to collect willing offerings from Israel for a sanctuary. It lists required materials and commands construction according to the revealed pattern. It gives specifications for the ark of the testimony, its rings, staves, mercy seat, and cherubim. It details the table for shewbread and its vessels, and the golden lampstand with seven lamps and utensils.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records instructions for constructing the tabernacle: ten linen curtains with cherubim joined by loops and gold clasps; eleven goats’ hair curtains joined with brass clasps; coverings of dyed rams’ skins and badgers’ skins. It specifies shittim-wood boards, silver sockets, bars overlaid with gold, and assembly pattern. It commands making the veil and door hanging, placing the ark and mercy seat, and arranging the table and candlestick.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records instructions to make the brass-covered burnt offering altar with horns, grate, rings, staves, and utensils. It specifies the tabernacle court hangings, pillars, sockets, hooks, gate curtain, and dimensions, and requires brass for vessels and pins. Israel is commanded to bring pure beaten olive oil for the lamp, and Aaron and his sons tend it evening to morning as a perpetual statute.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records instructions to appoint Aaron and his sons as priests and to make holy garments. It details the ephod with onyx shoulder stones engraved with Israel’s tribes, and the breastplate with twelve named stones, rings, chains, and the Urim and Thummim. It describes the blue robe with bells and pomegranates, the gold plate “HOLINESS TO THE LORD,” linen coat, mitre, girdle, sons’ garments, anointing and consecration, and linen breeches required when serving to avoid death.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records instructions to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests at the tabernacle door through washing, priestly garments, anointing oil, and sacrifices: a bull for a sin offering, a ram for a burnt offering, and a ram of consecration with blood applied to ear, thumb, and toe. It assigns wave/heave portions, regulates eating holy meat, commands seven-day consecration and altar cleansing, institutes daily morning/evening lamb offerings, and states God meets and dwells with Israel.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records instructions to Moses for the gold-covered incense altar, its placement, and Aaron’s daily incense and annual atonement rite. It requires a half-shekel ransom from men twenty and older at a census for tabernacle service. It commands a bronze laver for priestly washing. It gives recipes and restrictions for holy anointing oil and sacred incense, with penalties for imitation.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the LORD appointing Bezaleel of Judah and Aholiab of Dan, giving skill to craft the tabernacle, ark, furnishings, priestly garments, anointing oil, and incense. It commands Israel to keep the sabbath as a perpetual covenant sign, prescribing death for sabbath profanation. It ends with Moses receiving two stone tablets of testimony on Sinai.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Israel asking Aaron for gods while Moses delays on Sinai; Aaron collects gold and makes a molten calf, an altar, and a feast with offerings and revelry. The LORD tells Moses and threatens judgment; Moses intercedes citing the patriarch promises. Moses descends with the tablets, breaks them, destroys the calf, confronts Aaron, and orders the Levites to slay about 3,000. Moses seeks forgiveness; the LORD sends an Angel and plagues the people.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD directing Moses to lead Israel from Horeb toward the promised land with an angel, not God’s presence among them; the people mourn and remove ornaments. Moses pitches the tabernacle outside the camp, where the cloudy pillar descends and the LORD speaks with Moses; Joshua remains there. Moses asks for guidance and God’s presence; the LORD promises to go with him. Moses requests to see God’s glory; God allows only a partial view from a rock cleft.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records the LORD instructing Moses to hew new stone tablets and meet Him on Sinai, where the LORD proclaims His name and renews covenant terms. Commands include rejecting covenants and intermarriage with Canaanites, destroying idols, keeping feasts, redeeming firstborn, Sabbath rest, and bringing firstfruits. Moses fasts forty days, receives the commandments, and returns with a shining face, using a veil before Israel.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Moses gathering Israel, restating Sabbath laws (six days work, seventh-day rest; no fire; death for violation), and commanding a freewill offering for constructing the tabernacle and its furnishings, priestly garments, and service items. The people bring metals, fabrics, skins, wood, oil, spices, and stones; women spin yarn; rulers supply gems. Moses appoints Bezaleel and Aholiab as skilled craftsmen and teachers.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Bezaleel, Aholiab, and other skilled workers receiving Israel’s offerings for the sanctuary until Moses commands the people to stop because it is sufficient. It covers construction of the tabernacle: linen curtains with cherubim, goat-hair tent curtains, loop-and-tache fastenings, coverings of rams’ skins and badgers’ skins, shittim-wood boards with silver sockets, gold-overlaid bars and rings, the veil with four pillars, and the doorway hanging with five pillars and brass sockets.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Bezaleel making tabernacle furnishings: the ark of shittim wood overlaid with gold, its rings, staves, mercy seat, and gold cherubim; the table of shewbread with its crown, border, rings, staves, and gold vessels; the pure-gold candlestick with six branches, bowls, knops, flowers, seven lamps, and tools; the incense altar overlaid with gold with rings and staves; and preparation of holy anointing oil and sweet incense.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records construction of the bronze altar with its vessels, grate, rings, and staves, and the bronze laver. It describes making the tabernacle court hangings, pillars, sockets, gate curtain, and pins. It lists an inventory of gold, silver, and brass offerings and their uses, under Moses’ command, overseen by Ithamar, with work done by Bezaleel and Aholiab.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records the making of priestly garments for Aaron and his sons, including the ephod, breastplate with twelve named stones, robe with pomegranates and bells, coats, mitre, girdle, and gold plate inscribed “HOLINESS TO THE LORD.” It also lists the completed tabernacle and furnishings brought to Moses, who inspects the work, finds it done as commanded, and blesses Israel.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records the LORD commanding Moses to set up and anoint the tabernacle and its furnishings, wash and clothe Aaron and his sons, and establish their priesthood. Moses erects the tabernacle, places the ark, table, lampstand, altars, laver, and court, and offers sacrifices. A cloud covers the tent and the LORD’s glory fills it; Israel travels only when the cloud lifts, with fire by night.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the LORD speaking to Moses from the tabernacle to instruct Israel on burnt offerings. It specifies acceptable animals from herd, flock, or birds, requiring males without blemish. It outlines laying hands on the offering, killing it, priestly handling and sprinkling of blood, washing parts, arranging on wood and fire, and burning the whole offering on the altar.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records instructions for the grain (meat) offering: fine flour with oil and frankincense, presented to Aaron’s sons; a memorial portion is burned on the altar and the remainder belongs to the priests as most holy. It specifies baked, pan, and fryingpan unleavened forms, prohibits leaven and honey, requires salt with all offerings, and describes firstfruits grain offerings.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records regulations for peace offerings from the herd, flock, or goats, requiring unblemished male or female animals. The offerer lays a hand on the animal and kills it at the tabernacle entrance, while Aaron’s sons sprinkle the blood around the altar. Specified fat portions, kidneys, and the caul above the liver are removed and burned on the altar. It states all fat belongs to the LORD and forbids eating fat or blood permanently.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses on sin offerings for unintentional sins. It specifies required animals and procedures for an anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler, and a common person. It details laying on hands, slaughter at the tabernacle, blood application to the veil and altar horns, pouring blood at the altar base, burning fat, and burning the bull outside the camp for priest and congregation offerings.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records laws for guilt and trespass offerings. It lists offenses requiring confession: withholding testimony, touching unclean things, and making rash oaths. It prescribes offerings by ability: a lamb or kid, or two turtledoves/pigeons, or fine flour without oil or frankincense. It details priestly procedures and atonement. It also covers unintentional trespass in holy things, requiring a ram, restitution plus one-fifth, and forgiveness.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses on trespass involving deceit or theft, requiring restitution plus one-fifth and a ram offering for atonement. It commands Aaron and his sons regarding burnt offerings, maintaining perpetual altar fire, and ash removal. It details grain offerings, including priest portions, and the anointed priest’s daily flour offering wholly burned. It gives rules for sin offerings, priest consumption, blood and vessel handling, and burning offerings brought into the tabernacle.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records laws for the trespass offering, including slaughter location, blood sprinkling, burning specified fat parts, and priestly portions. It assigns priests the hide of burnt offerings and portions of grain offerings. It details peace offerings (thanksgiving, vow, voluntary), required breads, eating time limits, and rules about uncleanness. It forbids eating fat and blood and defines wave breast and heave shoulder portions for Aaron’s line, concluding the offering laws given at Sinai.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Moses consecrating Aaron and his sons at the tabernacle entrance before the congregation. Moses washes them, clothes them with priestly garments, and anoints the tabernacle, altar, and Aaron. He offers a bull for a sin offering and two rams for burnt offering and consecration, applying blood to ear, thumb, and toe, waving portions, and burning remains. Aaron’s family stays seven days.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Moses directing Aaron on the eighth day to present prescribed sin, burnt, grain, and peace offerings for himself and the people at the tabernacle. Aaron performs the sacrifices, applies and sprinkles blood on the altar, burns specified fat portions, and burns remaining flesh outside the camp. Aaron and Moses bless the people; the LORD’s glory appears, and fire consumes the offering.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Nadab and Abihu offering unauthorized fire and being consumed by fire from the LORD. Moses orders Mishael and Elzaphan to remove their bodies and instructs Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar not to mourn or leave the tabernacle. The LORD commands priests not to drink wine when serving and to distinguish holy from common and teach Israel. Moses gives rules for eating offerings, questions the burned sin offering goat, and accepts Aaron’s explanation.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses and Aaron on clean and unclean animals for Israel. It lists permitted land animals (cloven hoof and chewing cud) and forbidden ones, rules for fish (fins and scales), and prohibited birds and most creeping things, allowing certain locusts. It gives impurity rules for touching carcasses and contaminated vessels, food, ovens, water sources, and seed, and commands holiness by avoiding defilement.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses on purification after childbirth. A mother is unclean 7 days after a son’s birth (with circumcision on day 8) and remains in purification 33 more days; after a daughter, unclean 14 days and purification 66 more days. Afterward she brings offerings to the tabernacle for cleansing, with alternate birds if poor.

This chapter contains 59 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses and Aaron for priestly examination of suspected leprosy in skin eruptions, boils, burns, scalp or beard sores, baldness sores, and bright spots. It sets quarantine periods, signs for declaring clean or unclean, and procedures for cleansing. It commands diagnosed lepers to display uncleanness and live outside the camp, and gives rules for inspecting, washing, tearing, or burning infected garments and skins.

This chapter contains 57 verses and records laws for cleansing a person healed of leprosy, including priestly inspection outside the camp, two birds with cedar, scarlet, and hyssop, washing and shaving, and eighth-day offerings with blood and oil applied to ear, thumb, and toe, with provisions for the poor. It also covers house “leprosy” in Canaan: inspection, quarantine, removing stones, scraping and replastering, demolition if persistent, and a bird-based cleansing rite, defining clean and unclean.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses and Aaron on ceremonial uncleanness from bodily discharges. It details impurity from a man’s running issue, contact contamination of beds, seats, saddles, and vessels, required washing, and offerings after seven days and on the eighth day. It also covers emission of seed, a woman’s menstruation and prolonged bleeding, associated cleansing, required sacrifices, and separating Israel to prevent defiling the tabernacle.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses for Aaron’s entry into the Holy Place after Nadab and Abihu’s death. It details the yearly Day of Atonement ritual: priestly washing and linen garments, sin and burnt offerings, incense and blood sprinkling in the sanctuary, atonement for tabernacle and altar, casting lots over two goats, sending the scapegoat into the wilderness, disposal and washing rules, and a seventh-month fast and sabbath statute.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records the LORD’s commands through Moses to Aaron, his sons, and Israel that slaughtered ox, lamb, or goat must be brought to the tabernacle for offerings, with offenders cut off, ending sacrifices in the open field. It forbids eating blood for Israelites and resident strangers, requires draining and covering blood from hunted animals, and prescribes washing after eating animals that died naturally or were torn.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD speaking to Moses with instructions for Israel to avoid Egyptian and Canaanite practices and keep God’s statutes. It lists prohibitions on uncovering nakedness of close relatives, relations with in-laws, and certain unions. It forbids intercourse during menstruation, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, male same-sex intercourse, and bestiality. It warns these acts defile people and land, leading to expulsion and offenders being cut off.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records the LORD’s commands through Moses for Israel to be holy, honor parents, keep Sabbaths, avoid idols, and regulate peace offerings. It forbids theft, lying, false oaths, oppression, injustice, slander, hatred, vengeance, and mixed breeding/seed/fabric. It orders gleaning for the poor, fair wages, honest measures, respect for the disabled and elderly, love for neighbor and stranger, sexual penalties, fruit-tree rules, and bans blood-eating, divination, necromancy, and body markings.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records the LORD’s commands through Moses on penalties for giving offspring to Molech, consulting familiar spirits or wizards, cursing parents, adultery, incest, male homosexual acts, taking a woman and her mother, bestiality, sex during menstruation, and other forbidden kinship unions. It commands Israel to be holy, keep statutes, avoid pagan customs, distinguish clean and unclean animals, and warns the land may expel them.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD’s commands to Moses for Aaronic priests: limits on defilement for the dead, bans on pagan mourning marks, marriage restrictions, and punishment for a priest’s daughter who commits whoredom. It adds stricter rules for the high priest regarding contact with the dead and choosing a virgin wife. It bars priests with physical blemishes from altar service, though they may eat holy food. Moses relays these instructions to Israel.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses for Aaron’s family on handling holy offerings: priests must avoid holy food while unclean and avoid defiling foods; only priestly household members may eat. It requires restitution plus a fifth for accidental eating. It sets rules for acceptable sacrifices: unblemished males, no defective animals, age limits, mother and young not killed same day, and thanksgiving offerings eaten same day.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses for Israel’s appointed feasts and holy convocations: the weekly Sabbath, Passover, and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread; firstfruits and the wave sheaf with required offerings; counting fifty days to the feast of weeks with wave loaves and sacrifices; gleaning for poor and stranger; memorial of trumpets; Day of Atonement with fasting and work prohibitions; and the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles with an eighth-day assembly, booths, and specified branches.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records commands for Israel to provide pure olive oil so Aaron keeps the tabernacle lamps burning continually, and instructions for baking and setting twelve cakes of showbread with frankincense each Sabbath for Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place. It recounts a blasphemy case, the offender’s stoning, and laws on blasphemy, murder, restitution for killing animals, and proportional injury penalties applied equally to native and stranger.

This chapter contains 55 verses and records the LORD’s commands to Moses at Sinai on the sabbatical year and the Jubilee: resting the land, sounding the trumpet, proclaiming liberty, and returning property and families. It sets rules for fair pricing by years to Jubilee, land redemption, and exceptions for houses in walled cities and Levite property. It commands aid to the poor, forbids usury, and regulates servitude and redemption of Israelites and foreigners.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records commands to reject idols, keep Sabbaths, and reverence the sanctuary. It outlines blessings for obedience: rain, abundant harvests, safety, peace, victory, fruitfulness, and God’s tabernacle among Israel. It lists escalating curses for disobedience: disease, famine, drought, defeat, wild beasts, sword, pestilence, siege, cannibalism, destruction of high places, desolation, scattering, and land enjoying sabbaths. It provides restoration terms through confession and covenant remembrance with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob at Sinai by Moses.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses on vows and dedications: valuation of persons by age and sex, and priestly adjustment for the poor. It covers rules for dedicating animals, houses, and fields, including redemption with an added fifth and Jubilee-related land return. It forbids altering offerings, treats firstlings and devoted things as non-redeemable, and sets tithes of produce and livestock.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records the LORD commanding Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai to census Israel’s males age twenty and upward by tribes for military service, naming tribal leaders who assist. It lists each tribe’s count and gives the total of 603,550. Levi is excluded and appointed to care for, transport, and guard the tabernacle, camping around it; strangers approaching are put to death.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses and Aaron for Israel’s camp arrangement around the tabernacle by tribal standards and family ensigns. It lists the tribes positioned east, south, west, and north with their captains and numbered hosts, and gives the marching order with Levites and the tabernacle in the center. It totals 603,550 men, excluding Levites, and notes Israel obeys.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records Aaron’s sons and the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, then assigns the Levites to assist Aaron and guard the tabernacle, warning that unauthorized persons approaching are put to death. It numbers Levite males by clan (Gershon, Kohath, Merari), gives their camp positions and duties, totals 22,000 Levites, counts 22,273 Israelite firstborn, and commands redemption of the excess firstborn at five shekels each paid to Aaron.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records the census of Levite clans aged 30–50 for tabernacle service. It details Kohathites’ duties carrying the most holy objects after Aaron’s sons cover them, with warnings not to touch or see holy things uncovered. It assigns Gershonites to transport curtains and hangings and Merarites to transport frames, bars, pillars, and sockets, under Ithamar. It lists totals: Kohath 2,750; Gershon 2,630; Merari 3,200; overall 8,580.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records commands to remove from the camp those with leprosy, bodily issues, or corpse defilement. It requires confession and restitution for trespass, adding one-fifth, paid to the injured party or to the priest if none. It assigns certain holy offerings to the priest. It gives the jealousy test: a suspected wife is brought with a barley offering; the priest administers holy water with tabernacle dust and an oath, with outcomes for guilt or innocence.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records laws for the Nazirite vow, including abstaining from grape products, not cutting hair, and avoiding contact with the dead, with procedures and offerings if defiled and at vow completion at the tabernacle. It also gives Aaron and his sons the prescribed blessing for Israel and states the LORD puts his name on the people and blesses them.

This chapter contains 89 verses and records the tabernacle’s anointing and the tribal leaders’ offerings. Six wagons and twelve oxen are given to the Levites: Gershon receives two wagons and four oxen, Merari four wagons and eight oxen, and Kohath none. Over twelve days each prince presents identical altar-dedication offerings. Totals of silver, gold, and animal sacrifices are listed. Moses hears the LORD’s voice from the mercy seat between the cherubim.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the LORD’s instructions for Aaron to light the seven lamps of the golden candlestick. It covers the cleansing and dedication of the Levites: sprinkling purifying water, shaving, washing clothes, presenting bullocks for sin and burnt offerings, and Israel laying hands on them. It states Levites replace Israel’s firstborn and are given to Aaron. It sets service ages 25–50, then lighter duties.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD commanding Moses in the Sinai wilderness to keep Passover on the fourteenth day, with a provision for those unclean by a dead body or traveling to observe it in the second month. It sets penalties for neglect and one ordinance for natives and strangers. It also covers the cloud and fire over the tabernacle guiding Israel’s camping and journeys by the LORD’s command.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records God commanding Moses to make two silver trumpets for assembling Israel, directing camp movements, war alarms, and festival offerings, blown by Aaron’s sons. It then narrates Israel’s departure from Sinai to Paran, listing the marching order of tribes and Levites. Moses invites Hobab to guide them; the ark and cloud lead, and Moses speaks set prayers at departure and rest.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Israel’s complaints and God’s fire at Taberah, quenched after Moses prays. The people crave meat and despise manna; Moses protests the burden of leadership. God appoints seventy elders, places Moses’ spirit on them, and they prophesy; Eldad and Medad prophesy in camp. Quail arrive by wind, but a plague strikes; the place is named Kibroth-hattaavah, then they travel to Hazeroth.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Miriam and Aaron speaking against Moses over his Ethiopian wife and claiming prophetic authority. The LORD summons them to the tabernacle, appears in a cloud, and declares Moses uniquely faithful, spoken to directly. God’s anger follows; Miriam becomes leprous. Aaron confesses, Moses intercedes, and Miriam is shut outside the camp seven days. Israel delays, then departs Hazeroth for Paran.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD commanding Moses to send one ruler from each tribe to spy Canaan from Paran. It lists the spies, including Caleb and Hoshea renamed Joshua. They search from Zin to Rehob, visit Hebron, and bring grapes, pomegranates, and figs from Eshcol after forty days. They report fertile land but strong peoples and walled cities; Caleb urges entry while others discourage, citing Anak giants.

This chapter contains 45 verses and records Israel weeping and murmuring against Moses and Aaron, proposing to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urge trust in the LORD; the congregation seeks to stone them, and the LORD’s glory appears. Moses intercedes; the LORD pardons yet decrees the unbelieving generation will die in the wilderness, with 40 years of wandering; only Joshua and Caleb enter. The evil-report spies die by plague. A presumptuous attack fails; Amalekites and Canaanites defeat Israel to Hormah.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses on grain, oil, and drink offerings accompanying burnt and peace offerings for lambs, rams, and bullocks, applying to Israelites and sojourners. It commands a first-dough heave offering when entering the land, outlines sacrifices for unintentional sins, and states presumptuous sin brings being cut off. It recounts a Sabbath stick-gatherer stoned outside the camp, and commands blue-fringed garments to remember commandments.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records Korah with Dathan and Abiram leading 250 leaders to challenge Moses and Aaron’s authority and priesthood. Moses orders a censer test at the tabernacle; the LORD appears and the rebels gather. The congregation separates; the earth swallows Dathan and Abiram and their households, and fire consumes the 250 offering incense. Eleazar plates the censers for the altar as a memorial. The next day a plague begins; Aaron makes atonement, and 14,700 die.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the LORD instructing Moses to collect twelve rods from Israel’s princes, with Aaron’s name on Levi’s rod, and place them before the testimony in the tabernacle. Aaron’s rod buds, blossoms, and yields almonds, identifying the chosen priesthood. The LORD commands it be kept as a sign against rebels to stop murmuring. Israel fears approaching the tabernacle will bring death.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Aaron about priestly responsibility for sanctuary and altar, the Levites’ assigned tabernacle service, and restrictions on outsiders. It lists priests’ portions from offerings, firstfruits, devoted things, and firstborn redemption. It states priests and Levites receive no land inheritance, assigns Israel’s tithes to Levites, and requires Levites to offer a tithe of the tithe to Aaron.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the ordinance of the red heifer: Israel provides an unblemished heifer, Eleazar oversees its slaughter outside the camp, blood is sprinkled toward the tabernacle, and the heifer is burned with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet. The ashes are stored for “water of separation” to purify those defiled by contact with the dead, tents, vessels, bones, graves, or corpses, with washing and time limits.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Israel arriving at the wilderness of Zin and staying at Kadesh, where Miriam dies. The people complain for lack of water; Moses strikes the rock and water flows, and the LORD declares Moses and Aaron will not bring Israel into the land. Moses requests passage through Edom, but Edom refuses. Israel travels to Mount Hor, where Aaron dies and Eleazar receives his garments; Israel mourns thirty days.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Israel’s defeat of Arad the Canaanite and the naming of Hormah. It covers the journey around Edom, complaints against God and Moses, fiery serpents, and the bronze serpent on a pole for healing. It lists camps from Oboth to Pisgah and the well at Beer with a song. Israel requests passage from Sihon, fights at Jahaz, captures Heshbon and Amorite cities, takes Jaazer, and defeats Og of Bashan at Edrei, possessing their lands.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Israel camping in the plains of Moab near Jericho, while Balak king of Moab fears Israel and hires Balaam from Pethor to curse them. God forbids Balaam, then permits him to go but only speak God’s word. The angel opposes Balaam on the road; his donkey sees the angel, turns aside, speaks, and Balaam then sees the angel and is warned. Balaam meets Balak at Arnon, goes to Kirjath-huzoth, receives sacrifices, and is taken to Baal’s high places to view Israel.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Balaam directing Balak to build seven altars and offer bullocks and rams in multiple locations. The LORD meets Balaam and puts words in his mouth, resulting in oracles that refuse to curse Israel and instead bless Jacob, describing Israel’s separation, numbers, and deliverance from Egypt. Balak moves Balaam from Pisgah to Peor seeking a curse.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Balaam, moved by the Spirit of God, blessing Israel while viewing their tents by tribes. He declares Israel’s prosperity, strength, and a king exalted above Agag, and pronounces blessing on those who bless Israel. Balak becomes angry and dismisses him. Balaam delivers further oracles about future dominion from Jacob and judgments on Moab, Edom/Seir, Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur, and Eber, then Balaam and Balak depart.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Israel at Shittim committing sexual immorality with Moabite women and worshiping Baal-peor. The LORD orders Moses to execute leaders and offenders; a plague breaks out. Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman in a tent, and the plague stops after 24,000 die. The LORD grants Phinehas a covenant of peace and lasting priesthood, names Zimri and Cozbi, and commands Israel to attack Midian.

This chapter contains 65 verses and records a second census after the plague, commanded to Moses and Eleazar in the plains of Moab near Jericho, numbering men twenty years and older by tribe and family, with totals for each and for Israel. It notes Korah’s rebellion deaths, Er and Onan’s deaths, Zelophehad’s daughters, and counts Levites separately. It commands land inheritance by number and by lot, and states only Caleb and Joshua remain from the Sinai census.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the daughters of Zelophehad requesting inheritance rights; the LORD grants them land and establishes inheritance laws when no son exists. It then has Moses view Canaan from Mount Abarim and hear he will die for the Meribah rebellion. Moses asks for a successor, and the LORD appoints Joshua; Moses publicly commissions him before Eleazar and the congregation, with guidance by Urim.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD’s instructions to Moses for Israel’s required offerings: the continual daily burnt offering of two year-old lambs with grain and drink offerings; additional Sabbath offerings; monthly new-moon offerings of bullocks, a ram, lambs, and a goat for a sin offering; Passover on the fourteenth day and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread with holy convocations and daily sacrifices; and the day of firstfruits with prescribed burnt, grain, drink, and sin offerings.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records the required seventh-month offerings: the first-day trumpet convocation with no servile work; the tenth-day holy convocation with soul-affliction and no work; and the fifteenth-day seven-day feast with daily burnt, grain, drink, and sin offerings, decreasing bullocks each day, plus an eighth-day solemn assembly. It lists animals and measures and says Moses tells Israel these commands.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Moses giving statutes on vows and oaths. A man must keep his vow. A daughter’s vow stands unless her father annuls it when first hearing. A wife’s vow stands unless her husband annuls it that day; silence confirms it. Widows’ and divorced women’s vows stand. If a husband later voids a vow, he bears iniquity.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records the LORD commanding Moses to avenge Israel on Midian. Twelve thousand Israelites with Phinehas fight, kill Midianite males, five kings, and Balaam, and take captives and spoil, burning cities. Moses orders execution of certain captives and seven-day purification. Eleazar gives rules for cleansing metals. The prey is counted, divided, and tribute given to Eleazar and Levites; officers present gold for the tabernacle.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Gad and Reuben requesting Gilead and Jazer east of the Jordan for their cattle. Moses warns them not to discourage Israel, recalling Kadesh-barnea, and conditions their inheritance on armed participation in conquering Canaan. They agree; Moses assigns lands of Sihon and Og to Gad, Reuben, and half Manasseh. Cities are built/renamed; Machir, Jair, and Nobah capture and settle Gilead, Havoth-jair, and Kenath.

This chapter contains 56 verses and records Israel’s travel stages from Rameses in Egypt to the plains of Moab by the Jordan near Jericho, as written by Moses by the LORD’s command. It notes the sea crossing, encampments including Sinai, Kadesh, and Mount Hor, and Aaron’s death there. The LORD commands driving out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroying images and high places, dividing the land by lot, and warns of consequences for failure.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records the LORD instructing Moses to define Israel’s inheritance boundaries in Canaan, listing the south, west, north, and east borders using landmarks such as Zin, Kadesh-barnea, the river of Egypt, the Great Sea, mount Hor, Hamath, Chinnereth, Jordan, and the Salt Sea. It notes Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh already receive land east of Jordan, and appoints Eleazar, Joshua, and named tribal princes to divide Canaan.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD commanding Israel to give the Levites 48 cities with measured suburbs, including six cities of refuge. It sets procedures for accidental manslayers to flee, stand judgment, and remain until the high priest’s death. It defines murder by intent and weapons, assigns the avenger of blood, requires multiple witnesses, forbids ransom for murderers or refugees, and prohibits polluting the land with bloodshed.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the Gileadite family heads of Manasseh petitioning Moses about Zelophehad’s daughters marrying outside their tribe and transferring land at jubilee. Moses commands that female heirs marry within their father’s tribal clan so inheritances do not move between tribes. Zelophehad’s daughters marry their cousins in Manasseh, and the chapter closes with these laws given in Moab near Jericho.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Moses speaking to Israel in Moab in the fortieth year after defeating Sihon and Og. He recalls the command to leave Horeb and possess Canaan, appointing tribal leaders and judges with instructions for impartial judgment. He recounts sending twelve spies from Kadesh-barnea, Israel’s refusal and murmuring, and the LORD’s oath that the adult generation will not enter except Caleb, with Joshua appointed to lead. Israel’s unauthorized attack fails; they remain at Kadesh.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Israel’s journey from the Red Sea area around Mount Seir, with commands not to fight Esau in Seir, Moab in Ar, or Ammon, but to buy food and water. It notes the passing of 38 years until the fighting men die off, and the crossing of Zered and Arnon. Moses requests passage from Sihon; Sihon refuses, fights at Jahaz, and Israel captures Heshbon’s cities and spoils, stopping short of Ammon and Jabbok.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Israel’s march to Bashan, the defeat of Og at Edrei, and the capture of sixty fortified cities in Argob, with spoil taken. It lists conquered territory from Arnon to Hermon and assigns lands to Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh, including Jair’s settlements. Moses commands the eastern tribes to aid conquest, encourages Joshua, and is denied entry, viewing Canaan from Pisgah near Beth-peor.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records Moses exhorting Israel to obey statutes without adding or diminishing, recalling Baal-peor and Horeb where the Ten Commandments are given. He warns against idolatry and worship of heavenly bodies, foretells exile for corruption, and promises mercy if they seek and obey God. Moses appoints three cities of refuge east of Jordan: Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan, and notes the law’s setting near Beth-peor.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Moses gathering Israel to hear and keep the covenant made at Horeb. It restates the Ten Commandments, including exclusive worship, no idols, honoring God’s name, Sabbath observance, honoring parents, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting. Israel fears the fire and asks Moses to mediate; the LORD instructs obedience and promises life in the land.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Moses commanding Israel to keep God’s statutes in the promised land, affirming the LORD as one and commanding love for Him with all heart, soul, and might. It instructs teaching these words to children and displaying them on hand, forehead, doorposts, and gates. It warns against forgetting God after prosperity, following other gods, and tempting Him at Massah, and directs explaining the exodus and commandments to future children.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records commands for Israel on entering Canaan to defeat and destroy seven nations, make no covenants or intermarriage, and demolish altars, images, groves, and idols. It states Israel is chosen by the LORD, recalls deliverance from Egypt, and urges obedience. It promises blessings, health, and multiplication for obedience, warns against fear, and forbids taking idol gold or bringing abominations home.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Moses exhorting Israel to keep God’s commandments to live and possess the land. It recalls the forty years in the wilderness, including testing, chastening, manna, preserved clothing and feet, and water from rock amid serpents and drought. It describes the promised land’s resources and commands blessing God after eating. It warns against forgetting God, crediting wealth to oneself, idolatry, and disobedience, with perishing like displaced nations.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Moses warning Israel before crossing the Jordan that conquest is not due to their righteousness but the nations’ wickedness and God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He recounts Israel’s rebellion, especially at Horeb: Moses receives the covenant tablets after forty days, descends to the molten calf, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and intercedes forty days; he prays for Aaron and recalls provocations at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and rebellion at Kadesh-barnea.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Moses hewing new stone tablets, making a wooden ark, and receiving again the ten commandments. It notes Israel’s journeys, Aaron’s death at Mosera, and Eleazar succeeding him. The LORD separates Levi to carry the ark and minister without land inheritance. Moses recounts forty days on the mount, then commands Israel to fear, love, serve, obey, and love the stranger.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Moses urging Israel to love the LORD and keep his commandments, recalling God’s acts in Egypt, at the Red Sea, in the wilderness, and against Dathan and Abiram. It contrasts Canaan with Egypt, promises rain and produce for obedience, warns against idolatry and drought, commands teaching and inscribing the words, defines borders, and sets blessing and curse on Gerizim and Ebal.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records commands to destroy Canaanite worship sites and images, and to worship only at the place the LORD chooses. It requires bringing sacrifices, tithes, vows, and offerings there, rejoicing with households and Levites, and not offering burnt offerings elsewhere. It permits eating meat in towns but forbids eating blood. It warns against adopting pagan practices and commands not to add to or diminish the statutes.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records laws against apostasy and idolatry. It commands Israel not to heed prophets or dreamers whose signs lead to other gods, but to fear and obey the LORD. It requires execution of close relatives or friends who entice to idolatry. It orders investigation of an apostate city and, if confirmed, its destruction, burning of spoil, and prohibition of rebuilding.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records commands for Israel not to cut themselves for the dead and to remain a holy people. It lists clean and unclean animals, fish, birds, and flying creeping things, and forbids eating carcasses and boiling a kid in its mother’s milk. It commands annual tithing, eating the tithe at the chosen place, converting it to money for travel, and supporting Levites; every third year a stored tithe feeds Levites and the needy.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records laws for a seven-year debt release among Israelites, allowing collection from foreigners. It commands generosity to the poor and forbids withholding loans because the release year approaches. It mandates freeing Hebrew servants in the seventh year with liberal provisions, with an ear-piercing rite for lifelong service. It also requires dedicating firstborn male herd and flock, eating them at the chosen place, rejecting blemished animals, and forbidding blood consumption.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records instructions to keep Passover in Abib at the place the LORD chooses, eating unleavened bread seven days and holding a solemn assembly. It covers counting seven weeks to the Feast of Weeks with freewill offerings and rejoicing with Levites and the needy. It commands the Feast of Tabernacles, male appearances three times yearly, appointing just judges, and forbids groves near the altar and images.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records laws forbidding blemished sacrifices and requiring investigation and stoning for idolatry on testimony of two or three witnesses. It directs difficult cases to the chosen place for priests and the judge, mandates obedience to their rulings, and prescribes death for presumptuous refusal. It regulates Israel’s king: chosen by God, Israelite, not multiplying horses, wives, or wealth, and writing and reading the law daily.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records regulations for Levite priests having no land inheritance, receiving portions of sacrifices, firstfruits, and equal support when serving at the chosen sanctuary. It forbids adopting Canaanite practices such as child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, and consulting spirits. It promises a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen, sets penalties for false prophets, and gives a test: unfulfilled words are not from the LORD.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records commands to set apart three cities of refuge, with roads prepared, for unintentional killers to flee from the avenger of blood; it distinguishes accidental killing from murder and orders elders to deliver a murderer to execution. It forbids removing a neighbor’s landmark, requires two or three witnesses to establish a matter, prescribes inquiry and punishment for false witnesses, and states proportional justice (life for life, eye for eye).

This chapter contains 20 verses and records laws for Israel’s warfare: the priest encourages troops not to fear; officers exempt men with an undedicated house, uneaten vineyard, unconsummated betrothal, or fearfulness, then appoint captains. It commands offering peace to distant cities and terms for siege and spoil, but mandates total destruction of specified Canaanite nations. It forbids cutting edible trees during sieges.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records laws for dealing with an unsolved murder through measuring to the nearest city, sacrificing an unyoked heifer in an uncultivated valley, priestly involvement, and elders’ handwashing and prayer. It covers regulations for marrying a female captive and releasing her if rejected, inheritance rights of the firstborn of an unloved wife, punishment of a stubborn son, and same-day burial of an executed man hanged on a tree.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records laws requiring returning lost animals or property and helping a neighbor’s fallen beast; prohibiting cross-dressing; regulating taking birds from a nest; requiring a roof parapet; forbidding mixed seeds, unequal plowing, and mixed fabrics; commanding fringes on garments. It sets procedures and penalties for false accusations of non-virginity, adultery, betrothed relations in city or field, intercourse with an unbetrothed virgin, and forbids taking a father’s wife.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records laws on admission to the congregation, excluding certain men and Ammonites/Moabites, recalling their hostility and Balaam.
