It commands not seeking their peace, allows Edomites and Egyptians in the third generation, and gives camp holiness and sanitation rules. It forbids returning escaped servants, prohibits prostitution and related offerings, restricts usury, requires prompt payment of vows, and permits eating from a neighbor’s field without taking goods.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records laws on divorce certificates and forbidding remarriage to a former husband, exemption of a newly married man from war for one year, limits on pledges (not taking millstones, returning a poor man’s cloak, not entering a house for security), punishment for kidnapping Israelites, leprosy procedures under priests, prompt payment of hired workers, individual responsibility for sin, just treatment of foreigners, orphans, and widows, and gleaning leftovers for them.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records laws for judges to acquit the righteous and condemn the wicked, limiting flogging to forty stripes, and forbidding muzzling an ox while threshing. It covers levirate marriage duties and the public shame rite for refusal. It commands punishment for a woman who seizes a man’s genitals in a fight, requires honest weights and measures, and orders Israel to remember Amalek’s attack and later blot out Amalek’s remembrance.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records instructions for offering firstfruits at the chosen sanctuary with a confession recounting Israel’s descent to Egypt, oppression, and deliverance into a fruitful land. It commands rejoicing with the Levite and resident foreigner, and the third-year tithe for Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows with a declaration of obedience and a request for blessing. It affirms Israel’s covenant commitment to keep God’s commandments.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Moses, the elders, priests, and Levites commanding Israel to keep the law after crossing the Jordan. They instruct setting up plastered stones on Mount Ebal, writing the law on them, building an uncut-stone altar, and offering burnt and peace offerings. Tribes stand on Gerizim and Ebal for blessings and curses, and Levites pronounce curses for idolatry, dishonoring parents, injustice, sexual sins, violence, bribery, and failing to keep the law.

This chapter contains 68 verses and records blessings promised for diligent obedience to the LORD’s commandments—prosperity in city and field, fruitful families and herds, victory over enemies, rain, abundance, and prominence among nations. It then lists curses for disobedience: disease, drought, crop failure, defeat, oppression, loss of family and property, foreign invasion and siege, cannibalism, plagues, reduced numbers, scattering among nations, and return to Egypt in captivity.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Moses renewing the LORD’s covenant with Israel in Moab, recalling Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, and victory over Sihon and Og with land given to Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh. All Israel, including families and foreigners, stands to enter the oath. Moses warns against idolatry and self-assured disobedience, listing curses, land devastation, exile, and nations’ questions; revealed law is to be obeyed.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Moses promising Israel’s restoration if they repent and obey: God gathers them from exile, returns them to their land, prospers them, and “circumcises” their heart; curses fall on enemies. It states the commandment is accessible and near. Moses sets before them life and death, blessing and curse, urges choosing life by loving and obeying the LORD, warning against idolatry and perishing.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Moses, aged 120, telling Israel he will not cross the Jordan, commissioning Joshua, and urging courage. Moses writes the law, gives it to priests and elders, and commands its public reading every seventh year at Tabernacles. The LORD appears in a cloud, foretells Israel’s future apostasy and troubles, and commands a song as a witness. Moses writes the song, stores the law by the ark, summons leaders, and calls heaven and earth to witness.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records the Song of Moses: a summons to heaven and earth, recounting the LORD’s care for Israel, Israel’s corruption and idolatry, and announced judgments by famine, sword, and scattering. It affirms the LORD’s vengeance and mercy, calls Israel to teach and obey the law, and commands Moses to ascend Mount Nebo in Abarim to view Canaan and die for the Meribah-Kadesh trespass.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Moses’ final blessing of Israel before his death. It recalls the LORD’s appearing from Sinai, Seir, and Paran, and the giving of the law. Moses blesses the tribes: Reuben, Judah, Levi (Urim and Thummim; priestly teaching and sacrifice), Benjamin, Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh), Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher. It concludes with Israel’s safety, provision, and victory over enemies under God’s protection.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Moses ascending from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo at Pisgah, where the LORD shows him the land from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah, the valley of Jericho, and Zoar. The LORD recalls the promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and states Moses will not enter. Moses dies in Moab and is buried near Beth-peor; Israel mourns thirty days. Joshua receives wisdom through Moses’ laying on of hands and leads Israel. Moses’ unmatched prophetic role and signs in Egypt are noted.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the LORD commissioning Joshua after Moses’ death to lead Israel across the Jordan into the promised land, defining its boundaries and promising divine presence. Joshua is commanded to be strong, obey and meditate on the law, and prepare provisions for crossing in three days. He instructs Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh to send armed men; they pledge obedience and punish rebellion.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Joshua sending two spies from Shittim to Jericho, where Rahab hides them from the king’s search. Rahab reports fear in Canaan due to Israel’s deeds at the Red Sea and against Sihon and Og, and requests protection for her family. The spies swear an oath, instruct her to display a scarlet cord, and set terms of safety and secrecy. The spies escape, hide three days, return to Joshua, and report Jericho’s fear.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Israel’s departure from Shittim to the Jordan River, officers’ instructions to follow the ark at a distance, and Joshua’s command to sanctify. The LORD directs priests bearing the ark to stand in the Jordan, selects twelve men from the tribes, and causes the Jordan’s waters to heap up near Adam by Zaretan. Israel crosses on dry ground opposite Jericho while priests stand in the riverbed.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Israel’s complete crossing of the Jordan, God’s command to select twelve men to take twelve stones from where the priests stand, and Joshua’s setting up memorial stones in the river and at Gilgal. It notes the armed men of Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh crossing, the priests carrying the ark exiting, the river returning, the camp at Gilgal, and instructions to explain the sign to future children.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Canaanite and Amorite kings fearing after the Jordan crossing, the LORD commanding Joshua to circumcise Israel at Gilgal, and the reason the wilderness-born males are uncircumcised. Israel heals, keeps Passover on the plains of Jericho, eats produce of Canaan, and manna ceases. Near Jericho Joshua meets the captain of the LORD’s host and removes his shoe on holy ground.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Israel’s siege of Jericho. The LORD instructs Joshua to march around the city for six days, then seven times on the seventh day with priests, the ark, and ram’s-horn trumpets, keeping silent until the shout. The walls fall, Jericho is taken and destroyed; valuables go to the LORD’s treasury. Rahab and her family are spared. Joshua curses rebuilding Jericho; Joshua’s fame spreads.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Israel’s trespass through Achan taking the accursed spoil, leading to defeat at Ai and the death of thirty-six men. Joshua mourns before the ark, and the LORD says Israel has sinned and must remove the accursed thing. Israel is examined by tribe and household; Achan confesses hiding a garment, silver, and gold. The items are retrieved, and Achan and his household are judged in the valley of Achor.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records the LORD directing Joshua to take Ai by ambush, allowing Israel to keep spoil and cattle. Joshua deploys forces between Beth-el and Ai, feigns retreat, and signals with a spear as the ambush burns and captures the city. Israel kills Ai’s inhabitants, hangs the king, and makes Ai a desolation. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law, and reads blessings and cursings to all Israel.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Canaanite kings uniting to fight Israel, while Gibeon deceives Joshua at Gilgal with worn provisions to obtain a peace treaty. Israel accepts their terms without seeking the LORD’s counsel. Three days later Israel learns Gibeon and nearby towns are neighbors but keeps the oath. Joshua spares them and assigns them as hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the LORD’s altar.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records five Amorite kings (Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon) attacking Gibeon, Joshua marching from Gilgal, defeating them at Gibeon and Beth-horon, and hailstones killing many. Joshua commands the sun and moon to stand still and pursues the enemy to Makkedah. The five kings are captured, executed, and buried. Israel captures Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir, subduing southern Canaan and returning to Gilgal.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Jabin of Hazor forming a northern coalition that gathers at the waters of Merom to fight Israel. The LORD tells Joshua to hough their horses and burn their chariots; Israel defeats the coalition, pursues them, and destroys their cities, burning Hazor. Joshua captures extensive territory, cuts off the Anakim from key mountain regions, and apportions the land to Israel; the land rests from war.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a list of defeated kings and territories taken by Israel. It names Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan east of the Jordan, smitten by Moses and allotted to Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh. It also lists kings conquered west of the Jordan by Joshua, from Baal-gad to Mount Halak, totaling thirty-one kings.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD telling aged Joshua that much land remains, listing unconquered areas (Philistine borders, Geshuri, Sidonian and Lebanon regions) and commanding division by lot for nine and a half tribes. It reviews Moses’s eastern allotments to Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh, naming borders and cities, notes Geshurites and Maachathites remain, and states Levi receives no land inheritance.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records the division of Canaan by lot under Eleazar, Joshua, and tribal leaders, following commands given through Moses, with Levites receiving cities but no land inheritance. Caleb approaches Joshua at Gilgal, recalls Moses’ promise from Kadesh-barnea, and requests the mountain region with Anakim strongholds. Joshua blesses Caleb and grants him Hebron (formerly Kirjath-arba), and the land has rest from war.

This chapter contains 63 verses and records Judah’s tribal allotment, detailing its borders from Edom and the wilderness of Zin to the Salt Sea, Jordan, and the Great Sea, naming boundary landmarks and cities. It assigns Hebron to Caleb, who drives out Anak’s sons, captures Debir through Othniel, and gives Achsah upper and lower springs. It lists Judah’s cities by regions and notes Judah cannot drive out the Jebusites in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records the allotment for the children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, giving boundary descriptions from Jordan near Jericho through Beth-el, Luz, Ataroth, Beth-horon, and Gezer to the sea. It details Ephraim’s border lines and notes separate Ephraimite cities within Manasseh’s inheritance. Ephraim does not drive out Canaanites in Gezer, who remain and pay tribute.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the land allotment for Manasseh, naming Machir’s portion in Gilead and Bashan and listing Manasseh’s clans. Zelophehad’s daughters (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah) request and receive an inheritance. It defines Manasseh’s borders and towns in Issachar and Asher, notes remaining Canaanites put to tribute, and recounts Joseph’s complaint and Joshua’s instruction to clear hill country despite iron chariots.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Israel assembling at Shiloh and setting up the tabernacle, with seven tribes still lacking inheritance. Joshua appoints three men per tribe to survey and divide the land into seven parts, then casts lots at Shiloh. Benjamin receives territory between Judah and Joseph; the chapter details its borders and lists its cities, including Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records the allotment of land by lot to Simeon (within Judah), Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, listing their borders and cities. Dan’s territory proves too small, so they take Leshem and rename it Dan. Israel gives Joshua Timnath-serah in Mount Ephraim. Eleazar, Joshua, and tribal leaders finalize the division at Shiloh before the tabernacle.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records the LORD instructing Joshua to appoint cities of refuge for unintentional killers to escape the avenger of blood. It outlines procedures at the city gate with the elders and protection until judgment and the high priest’s death. It lists the cities: Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan, for Israelites and resident strangers.

This chapter contains 45 verses and records the Levites requesting cities at Shiloh as commanded through Moses. Israel assigns by lot 48 Levitical cities with suburbs from the tribal inheritances: 13 for Aaron’s priests, 10 for remaining Kohathites, 13 for Gershonites, and 12 for Merarites, naming cities including refuge cities. It concludes that Israel possesses the land and has rest from enemies.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Joshua dismissing Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh to their lands east of Jordan with a charge to keep Moses’ law. They build a large altar by the Jordan; Israel gathers at Shiloh to war. Phinehas and ten princes investigate. The tribes explain the altar is a witness, not for sacrifice. The delegation reports peace; the altar is named Ed.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Joshua, aged, assembling Israel’s leaders to recount the LORD’s victories and the land allotments, promising remaining nations will be expelled. He commands courage to keep Moses’ law, avoid pagan nations, gods, and intermarriage, and cleave to and love the LORD. He warns covenant-breaking and idolatry bring loss of divine help, affliction, and destruction from the land.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Joshua gathering Israel at Shechem, recounting God’s acts from Terah and Abraham through the exodus, wilderness, and conquest. Joshua commands the people to fear and serve the LORD, put away foreign gods, and choose whom to serve. Israel pledges obedience; Joshua makes a covenant, writes it, and sets a stone witness. It records Joshua’s death and burial, Israel’s continued service, Joseph’s bones buried at Shechem, and Eleazar’s death.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Israel’s early campaigns after Joshua’s death. The LORD directs Judah to lead; Judah and Simeon defeat Canaanites at Bezek, capture Adoni-bezek, and take Jerusalem. Judah captures Hebron and Debir; Caleb gives Achsah to Othniel and grants her springs. Kenites settle in Judah; Judah defeats Zephath and takes Gaza, Askelon, and Ekron, but iron chariots hinder valley conquest. Joseph takes Bethel. Several tribes fail to expel Canaanites and impose tribute; Dan is pressed into the hill country; Amorite borders are noted.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the angel of the LORD coming from Gilgal to Bochim to rebuke Israel for making leagues and not destroying altars, warning remaining nations will be thorns and snares. The people weep and sacrifice at Bochim. It notes Joshua’s death and burial, Israel’s later idolatry, oppression by enemies, the LORD raising judges for deliverance, repeated relapse after each judge, and nations left to test Israel.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records nations left to test Israel’s obedience; Israel intermarrying and serving other gods; oppression by Chushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years; deliverance by Othniel and forty years’ rest; later oppression by Eglon of Moab with Ammon and Amalek for eighteen years; Ehud assassinating Eglon, rallying Ephraim, killing about ten thousand Moabites, and eighty years’ rest; Shamgar killing six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Israel again doing evil after Ehud dies, and the LORD selling them to Jabin king of Canaan in Hazor, with Sisera oppressing Israel twenty years. Deborah judges Israel and summons Barak to gather men from Naphtali and Zebulun to Mount Tabor. Sisera fights near the Kishon; his army is routed. Sisera flees to Jael, who kills him. Israel then subdues and destroys Jabin.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the song of Deborah and Barak praising the LORD for Israel’s deliverance from Canaan. It recounts divine intervention, conditions in Israel, and the tribes that join or refrain from battle. It describes the fight at Taanach near the waters of Megiddo and the river Kishon overwhelming Sisera’s forces. Meroz is cursed for not helping, Jael is praised for killing Sisera, and the land has rest forty years.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Israel’s oppression by Midian for seven years and their cry to the LORD. A prophet rebukes Israel for idolatry. The angel of the LORD calls Gideon at Ophrah and confirms the call by consuming his offering with fire. Gideon builds an altar and destroys Baal’s altar and grove, gaining the name Jerubbaal. Midianite allies camp in Jezreel; Gideon summons tribes and receives two fleece signs.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Gideon (Jerubbaal) encamping at the well of Harod near Midian by Moreh, the LORD reducing his army first by fear and then by a water test to 300 men. Gideon hears a Midianite dream about his victory, divides the 300 into three companies, and attacks with trumpets, pitchers, and lamps, causing Midian to flee. Israelites pursue; Ephraim seizes Jordan crossings and kills Oreb and Zeeb.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Gideon appeasing Ephraim’s complaint, pursuing Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna beyond Jordan, and punishing Succoth and Penuel for refusing aid. He captures and executes the kings, declines Israel’s offer of hereditary rule, and collects gold to make an ephod at Ophrah. Midian is subdued and Israel has forty years of quiet. Gideon’s family, death, and Israel’s return to Baal-berith are noted.

This chapter contains 57 verses and records Abimelech gaining support in Shechem, receiving silver from Baal-berith, hiring followers, and killing Jerubbaal’s seventy sons except Jotham. Shechem and the house of Millo make Abimelech king. Jotham delivers the trees-and-bramble parable and pronounces a curse. After three years, conflict arises with Shechem; Gaal opposes Abimelech, who defeats him, destroys Shechem, burns its tower, attacks Thebez, and dies by a millstone.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Tola of Issachar judging Israel 23 years in Shamir, followed by Jair the Gileadite judging 22 years, with thirty sons and thirty cities in Gilead. Israel again serves multiple foreign gods; the LORD gives them to the Philistines and Ammonites, who oppress Israel 18 years and attack across Jordan. Israel confesses, removes idols, and gathers at Mizpeh as Gilead seeks a leader against Ammon.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Jephthah’s rejection by his half-brothers, his residence in Tob, and his recall by Gilead’s elders to lead against Ammon. Jephthah negotiates with the Ammonite king, recounting Israel’s earlier movements and land claims from Arnon to Jabbok. The Spirit comes on Jephthah; he vows to offer what greets him. He defeats Ammon, then fulfills the vow involving his only daughter; Israelite women lament yearly.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Ephraim confronting Jephthah for not summoning them against Ammon, leading to war between Gilead and Ephraim. Gilead seizes Jordan fords and identifies Ephraimites by the “Shibboleth” test, killing 42,000. It notes Jephthah’s six-year judgeship and death, then summarizes judges Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon of Zebulun, and Abdon of Pirathon with their families, years served, and burial places.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Israel’s renewed evil and forty years under Philistine rule. It describes the angel of the LORD announcing to Manoah’s barren wife that she will bear Samson, to be a lifelong Nazirite, with prohibitions on wine, vine products, and unclean food, and no razor on his head. Manoah meets the angel, offers sacrifice, and the angel ascends in the flame. Samson is born, grows, and the Spirit moves him near Zorah and Eshtaol.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Samson seeking a Philistine wife in Timnath despite his parents’ protest, as the Philistines rule Israel. He kills a lion by the LORD’s Spirit and later takes honey from its carcass. At his wedding feast he poses a riddle to thirty companions; they threaten his wife, who persuades him to reveal it. Samson kills thirty men in Ashkelon for garments, returns home angry, and his wife is given to his companion.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Samson being denied access to his wife at Timnah, burning Philistine crops with 300 foxes, and the Philistines burning his wife and her father. Samson retaliates and dwells at the rock Etam. Philistines encamp at Lehi; 3,000 men of Judah bind Samson and deliver him. The Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break cords, kill 1,000 with a jawbone, name Ramath-lehi, receive water at En-hakkore, and judge Israel 20 years.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Samson in Gaza escaping a Philistine ambush by carrying off the city gate. It describes his relationship with Delilah in the valley of Sorek, her bribery by Philistine lords, and her discovery that his Nazirite hair relates to his strength. Philistines capture and blind Samson, imprison him in Gaza, and display him at a Dagon feast; he pulls down the temple pillars, killing many and himself. His family buries him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Micah of mount Ephraim confessing to stealing 1,100 shekels of silver from his mother and returning it. His mother dedicates silver to make a graven and molten image; 200 shekels are given to a founder, and the images are placed in Micah’s house. Micah establishes a household shrine with an ephod and teraphim, first appointing his son as priest. A Levite from Beth-lehem-judah arrives, is hired and consecrated as Micah’s priest; Micah expects prosperity.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the Danites sending five spies from Zorah and Eshtaol, lodging at Micah’s house in Ephraim, and receiving counsel from his Levite priest. They scout Laish, then six hundred Danites march, seize Micah’s graven image, ephod, teraphim, molten image, and the priest. Micah pursues but retreats. Dan attacks and burns Laish, rebuilds it as Dan, and sets up the image with Jonathan’s line as priests.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records a Levite from mount Ephraim retrieving his concubine from Beth-lehem-judah, then traveling past Jebus to Gibeah in Benjamin. An Ephraimite old man hosts them. Men of Gibeah surround the house demanding the Levite; the concubine is given to them and abused through the night, then collapses at the door and dies. The Levite dismembers her into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Israel assembling at Mizpeh to hear the Levite’s report of the crime at Gibeah. Israel demands Benjamin surrender the offenders; Benjamin refuses and musters for war. Israel inquires of the LORD at the house of God; Judah leads. After two defeats, Israel fasts and offers sacrifices; the LORD promises victory. Israel uses an ambush, burns Gibeah, routs Benjamin, kills about 25,000, and 600 flee to Rimmon; Israel devastates Benjamin’s cities.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Israel’s oath at Mizpeh not to give daughters to Benjamin, followed by mourning and offerings at the house of God. Israel seeks survivors for Benjamin, attacks Jabesh-gilead for not assembling, and brings 400 virgins to Shiloh as wives. Elders direct Benjamin to seize wives at Shiloh’s feast; Benjamin repopulates and rebuilds. Israel disperses; there is no king.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a famine in Judah that leads Elimelech, Naomi, and their sons to Moab. Elimelech dies; the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, then both sons die. Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem after hearing food is restored, urges her daughters-in-law to return, and Orpah leaves. Ruth commits to Naomi and her God. Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem at barley harvest; Naomi asks to be called Mara.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Ruth seeking permission to glean in fields near Bethlehem, happening upon Boaz’s field, a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech. Boaz learns her identity, acknowledges her care for Naomi, and instructs workers to protect and assist her, inviting her to eat. Ruth gathers about an ephah of barley, reports to Naomi, and Naomi identifies Boaz as a near kinsman; Ruth continues gleaning through harvests.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Naomi instructing Ruth to visit Boaz at the threshing floor after he eats and sleeps. Ruth uncovers Boaz’s feet and asks him to act as near kinsman. Boaz agrees but notes a nearer kinsman has prior right, promising to resolve it. He sends Ruth away early with six measures of barley, and Naomi tells Ruth to wait for the outcome.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Boaz meeting the nearer kinsman at Bethlehem’s gate with ten elders to settle Naomi’s land redemption. The kinsman declines after learning Ruth must be taken as wife to preserve Mahlon’s line; he confirms by removing his shoe. Boaz redeems the property, marries Ruth, and she bears Obed. Naomi nurses the child; Obed is father of Jesse and grandfather of David, followed by a genealogy from Pharez to David.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim with wives Hannah and Peninnah, yearly worship at Shiloh where Eli, Hophni, and Phinehas serve. Hannah, barren and provoked, prays and vows to dedicate a son to the LORD with no razor on his head. Eli mistakes her for drunk, then blesses her. Hannah bears Samuel, later brings him to Shiloh with offerings, and dedicates him to lifelong service.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Hannah’s prayer praising the LORD’s sovereignty and reversal of fortunes, then describes Samuel ministering before Eli at Shiloh. It details the corrupt practices of Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas with sacrifices and women, Eli’s rebuke, and Samuel’s growth. A man of God pronounces judgment on Eli’s house, foretells both sons’ death, and promises a faithful priest.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the LORD calling Samuel at night in the temple at Shiloh near the ark while Eli’s sight is dim. After three misunderstandings, Eli instructs Samuel to answer, and the LORD announces judgment on Eli’s house for his sons’ iniquity. Samuel reports the message to Eli. Samuel grows, is established as a prophet from Dan to Beer-sheba, and the LORD continues revealing himself at Shiloh.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Israel’s battles with the Philistines near Eben-ezer and Aphek, including initial defeat and the elders bringing the ark from Shiloh with Hophni and Phinehas. Israel suffers a greater defeat, thirty thousand die, the ark is captured, and Eli’s sons are killed. A messenger reports to Eli in Shiloh; Eli dies. Phinehas’s wife bears a son, names him Ichabod, and dies.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records the Philistines taking the ark from Eben-ezer to Ashdod and placing it in Dagon’s temple. Dagon falls before the ark twice, and the second time his head and hands break off, leading to a taboo about the threshold. The LORD afflicts Ashdod with destruction and emerods, so the Philistine lords move the ark to Gath, then to Ekron, where similar plagues and deaths cause cries and demands to return the ark.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the Philistines keeping the ark seven months, consulting priests and diviners, and returning it with trespass offerings of five golden emerods and five golden mice on a new cart drawn by two milch kine. The ark comes to Beth-shemesh; Levites place it on a stone and sacrifices are offered. God strikes men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the ark, and messengers call Kirjath-jearim to take it.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the ark being kept at Kirjath-jearim in Abinadab’s house under Eleazar. After twenty years, Samuel calls Israel to put away Baalim and Ashtaroth and gather at Mizpeh for fasting, confession, and prayer. The Philistines attack, but the LORD thunders as Samuel offers a lamb, and Israel pursues them to Beth-car. Samuel sets up Eben-ezer, Philistine-held cities are restored, and Samuel judges Israel, traveling to Beth-el, Gilgal, and Mizpeh, returning to Ramah and building an altar.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Samuel appointing Joel and Abiah as judges in Beer-sheba, their corruption, and Israel’s elders requesting a king at Ramah. Samuel prays, and the LORD says the people reject Him and tells Samuel to warn them. Samuel lists royal demands: conscription, forced labor, taking daughters, land, servants, livestock, and tithes, and future unanswered cries. The people insist; the LORD instructs Samuel to appoint a king.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Saul son of Kish of Benjamin searching for lost asses with a servant, traveling through Ephraim, Shalisha, Shalim, and Zuph. They seek a seer in a city and meet Samuel. The LORD tells Samuel to anoint a Benjamite as leader to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Samuel honors Saul at a high-place sacrifice, speaks with him, and prepares to reveal God’s word.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Samuel anointing Saul with oil and giving signs that occur as Saul travels, including receiving bread and prophesying when the Spirit comes upon him. Saul speaks with his uncle but hides the matter of the kingdom. At Mizpeh Samuel assembles Israel, rebukes them for seeking a king, and Saul is chosen by lot and presented. Samuel records the manner of the kingdom; Saul returns to Gibeah amid mixed support.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Nahash the Ammonite besieging Jabesh-gilead and demanding the right eyes of its men. Jabesh requests seven days to seek help. Messengers reach Gibeah; Saul musters Israel at Bezek, sends assurance, and attacks in three companies, defeating and scattering the Ammonites. Saul forbids executing dissenters, and Samuel leads Israel to Gilgal to renew the kingdom and confirm Saul as king with peace offerings.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Samuel’s address to Israel after appointing a king. Samuel asks the people to testify that he has not defrauded or oppressed them, and they affirm it. He recounts the LORD’s deliverances from Egypt and through judges, notes Israel’s request for a king when Nahash threatens, and warns obedience brings favor while rebellion brings judgment. Samuel calls thunder and rain at wheat harvest; the people fear and ask prayer. Samuel urges wholehearted service and warns both people and king face destruction if they persist in wickedness.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Saul’s early reign, his selection of troops at Michmash and Gibeah, and Jonathan’s attack on a Philistine garrison at Geba. The Philistines muster at Michmash, and Israelites hide or flee across the Jordan. Saul offers burnt and peace offerings at Gilgal before Samuel arrives; Samuel rebukes him and says his kingdom will not continue. Philistine raids and disarmament leave Israel without weapons except Saul and Jonathan.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records Jonathan and his armourbearer secretly attacking the Philistine garrison near Michmash between Bozez and Seneh, causing panic and Israel’s pursuit to Beth-aven and Aijalon. Saul consults Ahiah and the ark, then swears a fasting oath; Jonathan unknowingly eats honey. The people eat meat with blood; Saul stops it and builds an altar. Lots identify Jonathan, but the people spare him. It also summarizes Saul’s wars, family, and commanders.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Samuel commanding Saul to destroy Amalek completely. Saul musters Israel at Telaim, warns the Kenites to depart, defeats Amalek from Havilah to Shur, but spares King Agag and the best livestock. God tells Samuel he rejects Saul for disobedience. Samuel confronts Saul at Gilgal, declares obedience above sacrifice, and announces the kingdom is torn from Saul. Samuel executes Agag, returns to Ramah, and no longer visits Saul.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD sending Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from Jesse’s sons, choosing David after rejecting the older brothers. Samuel anoints David, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. The Spirit departs from Saul and an evil spirit troubles him. Saul’s servants seek a harp player; David is brought to Saul, becomes his armourbearer, and his playing relieves Saul.

This chapter contains 58 verses and records the Philistines and Israel encamped at Shochoh and the valley of Elah, where Goliath of Gath challenges Israel for forty days. David, sent by Jesse to his brothers, volunteers to fight, declines Saul’s armor, and meets Goliath with sling and stones. David kills him, beheads him, Israel pursues the Philistines toward Gath and Ekron, and Saul inquires David’s lineage through Abner.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Jonathan’s covenant with David and his gifts to him, while Saul keeps David in his service and promotes him over soldiers. Women praise David after victory, provoking Saul’s jealousy and attempts to kill him with a javelin. Saul plots to endanger David through marriage offers; Merab is given to Adriel, and David marries Michal after killing Philistines. Saul becomes David’s continual enemy as David prospers in battle.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Saul ordering Jonathan and his servants to kill David, Jonathan warning David and persuading Saul to spare him temporarily, and David defeating Philistines. Saul later throws a javelin at David and sends messengers to kill him; Michal helps David escape and deceives the messengers with an image. David flees to Samuel at Ramah; Saul’s messengers and Saul prophesy under God’s Spirit at Naioth.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records David fleeing to Jonathan, questioning Saul’s intent to kill him. David and Jonathan plan a new-moon test and agree on arrow signals; Jonathan renews a covenant with David and his house. At Saul’s table David is absent; Jonathan explains Bethlehem, Saul rages, and throws a javelin at Jonathan. Jonathan signals danger, meets David to weep and part, and sends him away in peace.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records David coming to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, requesting food and receiving the hallowed shewbread, with Doeg the Edomite present. David also asks for a weapon and takes Goliath’s sword. He then flees from Saul to Achish king of Gath; recognized by Achish’s servants, David feigns madness, and Achish dismisses him.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records David fleeing to the cave of Adullam, gathering about four hundred distressed men, and placing his parents with the king of Moab before moving to the forest of Hareth at Gad’s direction. Saul in Gibeah accuses his servants of conspiracy; Doeg reports David aided at Nob by priest Ahimelech. Saul summons the priests, orders their execution; Doeg kills eighty-five and Nob is destroyed. Abiathar escapes to David.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records David inquiring of the LORD and rescuing Keilah from the Philistines, then learning Saul will come and that Keilah’s men will deliver him, so he departs with about six hundred men. Abiathar joins David with an ephod. David hides in Ziph and Maon; Jonathan meets him and makes a covenant. Ziphites inform Saul; Saul nearly captures David but withdraws due to a Philistine invasion. David goes to En-gedi.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Saul pursuing David in the wilderness of En-gedi with three thousand men. Saul enters a cave where David hides; David cuts off the skirt of Saul’s robe but refuses to harm him and restrains his men. David confronts Saul and claims innocence. Saul weeps, acknowledges David’s righteousness and future kingship, and asks David to spare his descendants; David swears, and they depart.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Samuel’s death and burial at Ramah, and David going to the wilderness of Paran. David requests provisions from Nabal of Maon during sheep-shearing at Carmel; Nabal refuses, and David prepares to attack. Abigail brings gifts, meets David, and persuades him to refrain. Nabal later dies; David marries Abigail and also Ahinoam, while Saul gives Michal to Phalti.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the Ziphites informing Saul of David at Hachilah, Saul pursuing with 3,000 men, and David spying the camp. David and Abishai enter at night, take Saul’s spear and water cruse, and David refuses to kill the LORD’s anointed. David rebukes Abner from a distance, speaks with Saul, returns the spear, and Saul confesses sin, blesses David, and they part.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records David fleeing Saul to Gath with six hundred men and his wives Ahinoam and Abigail. Achish gives David Ziklag, and David lives among the Philistines a year and four months. David raids the Geshurites, Gezrites, and Amalekites, taking livestock and goods and leaving no survivors. He reports raids against Judah’s south, and Achish believes him and trusts him.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Philistine forces assembling at Shunem as Saul camps at Gilboa and fears. Saul receives no answer from the LORD by dreams, Urim, or prophets, so he seeks a medium at En-dor in disguise. The woman summons Samuel, who tells Saul the kingdom is given to David, cites Saul’s disobedience regarding Amalek, and foretells defeat and Saul and his sons’ death. Saul collapses, then eats and departs.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the Philistines assembling at Aphek while Israel camps near Jezreel. David and his men march with Achish, but Philistine princes object to Hebrews in the army, fearing David may turn against them. Achish defends David yet orders him to return peacefully. David departs early with his men; the Philistines advance to Jezreel.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Amalekites burning Ziklag and taking captive the families of David and his men. David inquires of the LORD through Abiathar and pursues to the brook Besor, leaving two hundred behind. An abandoned Egyptian guides them to the raiders; David defeats them and recovers all captives and spoil. He establishes equal sharing of spoil and sends portions to elders of Judah in multiple towns.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the Philistines’ battle against Israel at Mount Gilboa, where Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua are slain and Saul, wounded by archers, falls on his sword; his armourbearer also dies. Israelites flee and abandon cities. Philistines behead Saul, display his body at Beth-shan, and place his armour in Ashtaroth’s house. Men of Jabesh-gilead recover and burn the bodies, bury the bones, and fast seven days.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records David in Ziklag receiving news of Saul and Jonathan’s deaths from an Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul on Mount Gilboa and brings Saul’s crown and bracelet. David and his men mourn, weep, and fast. David orders the Amalekite executed for slaying the LORD’s anointed and recites a lament over Saul and Jonathan, including instructions to teach Judah the bow.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records David inquiring of the LORD and going to Hebron, where Judah anoints him king. David blesses Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul. Abner installs Ish-bosheth as king over Israel from Mahanaim. Abner and Joab’s forces meet at Gibeon; a contest leads to battle, Asahel pursues Abner and is killed. Joab halts pursuit; casualties and Asahel’s burial at Bethlehem are noted.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records the ongoing war between Saul’s house and David as David strengthens in Hebron and fathers six sons. Abner quarrels with Ish-bosheth over Rizpah, then offers to transfer Israel’s allegiance to David. David requires Michal’s return. Abner negotiates with Israel’s elders and Benjamin and meets David, but Joab recalls and kills Abner at Hebron. David publicly mourns, curses Joab’s house, fasts, and denies involvement.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Ish-bosheth’s fear after Abner dies. It identifies Rechab and Baanah, captains from Beeroth in Benjamin, and notes Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth. Rechab and Baanah assassinate and behead Ish-bosheth at noon, carry the head to David in Hebron, and claim reward. David condemns the killing, orders their execution, displays their bodies, and buries Ish-bosheth’s head in Abner’s tomb.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the tribes and elders anointing David king at Hebron, his reign length, and his move from Hebron to Jerusalem. David captures the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites, builds the city of David, and receives materials from Hiram of Tyre for a house. It lists David’s children born in Jerusalem and records two victories over the Philistines in the valley of Rephaim after David inquires of the LORD.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records David gathering 30,000 men to bring the ark from Baale of Judah; Uzzah touches the ark at Nachon’s threshingfloor and dies, and the place is named Perez-uzzah. The ark stays three months with Obed-edom, who is blessed. David brings the ark to the city of David with sacrifices, dancing, shouting, and offerings, blesses and feeds the people, and Michal despises him; she remains childless.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records David’s desire to build a house for the ark, Nathan’s initial approval, and the LORD’s message that David will not build it. The LORD recalls bringing Israel from Egypt, promises Israel a secure place, and covenants to establish David’s house, seed, and throne, with discipline but not rejection. David prays in thanksgiving and asks for the promised blessing.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records David’s victories over the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah, and the Syrians of Damascus, taking spoil and establishing garrisons. It notes Toi of Hamath sending his son Joram with gifts, which David dedicates along with tribute from subdued nations. David defeats Edom and places garrisons there. It lists David’s administration: Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, Ahimelech, Seraiah, Benaiah, and David’s sons.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records David seeking a remaining member of Saul’s house to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba identifies Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth in Lo-debar, and David brings him to Jerusalem. David restores Saul’s lands to Mephibosheth, appoints Ziba and his household to work the fields, and commands Mephibosheth to eat continually at the king’s table.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Hanun succeeding the Ammonite king, humiliating David’s envoys, and provoking conflict. The Ammonites hire Syrian forces from Beth-rehob, Zoba, Maacah, and Ish-tob. Joab and Abishai divide Israel’s army and rout the Syrians and Ammonites. The Syrians regroup under Hadarezer at Helam; David crosses the Jordan, defeats them, kills Shobach, and receives their submission.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records David staying in Jerusalem while Joab besieges Rabbah, David taking Bath-sheba (Uriah’s wife) and she conceives, and David summoning Uriah but failing to have him visit his home. David sends Uriah back with a letter ordering Joab to place him in deadly combat; Uriah dies. Bath-sheba mourns, David marries her, and the LORD is displeased.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Nathan confronting David with a parable and accusing him of killing Uriah and taking his wife; the LORD announces judgments on David’s house, and David confesses. The child becomes sick and dies after David fasts and prays. David comforts Bath-sheba; Solomon is born and also named Jedidiah. Joab captures Rabbah; David takes the city, crown, spoil, and returns to Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Amnon’s desire for Tamar, Jonadab’s counsel, David sending Tamar to Amnon, and Amnon forcing her and then casting her out. Tamar mourns and stays with Absalom, who hates Amnon. After two years Absalom arranges Amnon’s killing at Baal-hazor; the king’s sons flee. David mourns; Absalom flees to Talmai king of Geshur for three years.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Joab arranging for a wise woman of Tekoah to present David a case about a threatened heir, leading her to appeal for restoring a banished person. David perceives Joab’s involvement and orders Absalom brought back from Geshur to Jerusalem but not to see the king. Absalom lives two years, burns Joab’s field to gain an audience, then is summoned; he bows and David kisses him.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Absalom gaining public favor at the gate, then going to Hebron under a vow and proclaiming himself king with spies and supporters, including Ahithophel. David flees Jerusalem with his household and troops, crosses the Kidron toward the wilderness, and sends Zadok and Abiathar back with the ark. David prays against Ahithophel’s counsel and instructs Hushai to return to Jerusalem as an informant.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records David meeting Ziba, who brings provisions and accuses Mephibosheth of staying in Jerusalem; David grants Ziba Mephibosheth’s estate. At Bahurim Shimei curses David and throws stones; Abishai offers to kill him, but David restrains his men. Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel; Hushai greets Absalom and claims loyalty. Ahithophel advises Absalom to go in to David’s concubines publicly, and Absalom does so.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Ahithophel advising Absalom to pursue and kill David, and Hushai countering with counsel to gather all Israel, which Absalom accepts. Hushai warns Zadok and Abiathar; Jonathan and Ahimaaz relay the message while hiding at En-rogel and Bahurim. David crosses the Jordan to Mahanaim. Ahithophel hangs himself. Absalom crosses Jordan, appoints Amasa, camps in Gilead, and supporters bring provisions to David.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records David organizing his forces under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, commanding them to deal gently with Absalom. It covers the battle in the wood of Ephraim, heavy Israelite casualties, and Absalom caught in an oak and killed by Joab and his men. Absalom is buried in a pit. Ahimaaz and Cushi run with news; David learns Absalom is dead and mourns.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Joab rebuking David for mourning Absalom, prompting David to sit in the gate and address the troops. Israel and Judah debate restoring David; David sends to Zadok and Abiathar and promises Amasa command in Joab’s place. David returns to the Jordan; Shimei seeks pardon and is spared. Mephibosheth explains Ziba’s deceit and the land is divided. Barzillai declines reward; Chimham goes with David. Judah and Israel quarrel over escorting the king.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Sheba son of Bichri leading a revolt against David as Israel follows Sheba and Judah stays with the king. David confines his ten concubines in Jerusalem and orders Amasa to muster Judah, but Joab kills Amasa at Gibeon and pursues Sheba. Joab besieges Abel of Beth-maachah; a wise woman negotiates Sheba’s execution, his head is thrown out, and the siege ends. It lists David’s chief officials.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a three-year famine in David’s reign traced to Saul’s killing of Gibeonites. David negotiates restitution; seven of Saul’s descendants are handed over and hanged, while Mephibosheth is spared. Rizpah guards the bodies; David gathers and buries the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and the executed men at Zelah, and the famine ends. It also covers battles with Philistines where Abishai saves David and other warriors kill four giant-descended men.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records David’s song to the LORD after deliverance from Saul and other enemies. David calls the LORD his rock, fortress, and savior, describing God’s dramatic intervention with thunder, earthquake, and rescue from “many waters.” He states that the LORD rewards righteousness and shows mercy or opposition accordingly. He recounts victories in battle, subduing enemies and foreign peoples, and promises public thanksgiving, noting mercy to David and his descendants.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records David’s last words, stating the LORD speaks through him and describing just rule, an everlasting covenant, and judgment on the sons of Belial. It lists David’s mighty men and their exploits against Philistines, including Adino, Eleazar, and Shammah, and the three who bring water from Bethlehem. It notes Abishai and Benaiah’s feats and names the thirty-seven, including Uriah.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records David ordering Joab to number Israel and Judah, the census route from Dan to Beer-sheba, and the totals reported. David confesses sin, and the prophet Gad offers three judgments; David chooses three days of pestilence, killing seventy thousand. The destroying angel stops at Araunah’s threshingfloor; David buys it, builds an altar, offers sacrifices, and the plague ceases.

This chapter contains 53 verses and records David’s old age and Abishag the Shunammite ministering to him. Adonijah proclaims himself king with support from Joab and Abiathar, holds a feast at Zoheleth by En-rogel, and excludes Solomon and key leaders. Nathan and Bath-sheba inform David, who orders Solomon anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan. Public acclamation disrupts Adonijah’s party; Adonijah seeks asylum at the altar, and Solomon spares him conditionally.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records David’s final charge to Solomon to keep the law of Moses and deal with Joab, Shimei, and the sons of Barzillai. David dies and is buried; Solomon’s reign is established. Adonijah seeks Abishag through Bathsheba and is executed by Benaiah. Abiathar is exiled and removed as priest; Joab is killed at the altar; Benaiah and Zadok are appointed. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem, breaks the oath by going to Gath, and is executed.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Solomon’s marriage alliance with Pharaoh’s daughter and continued sacrifice at high places before the temple is built. At Gibeon Solomon offers many sacrifices, and the LORD appears in a dream, granting him wisdom, plus riches and honor, and promising long life if he keeps God’s commandments. Solomon worships at Jerusalem before the ark. He judges the dispute of two prostitutes over a child, and Israel hears of his judgment.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Solomon’s rule over all Israel, naming his chief officials and twelve district officers who supply provisions by monthly rotation. It lists their territories and notes marriages to Solomon’s daughters. It describes the size and daily provisions of Solomon’s court, his dominion from the River to Philistia and Egypt, peace and security in Israel, and his horses and chariots. It reports God-given wisdom, proverbs and songs, natural knowledge, and foreign visitors seeking his wisdom.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Hiram king of Tyre congratulating Solomon and making a league with him. Solomon declares his plan to build a house for the LORD and requests cedar and fir from Lebanon with Sidonian cutters. Hiram supplies timber by sea; Solomon pays wheat and oil yearly. Solomon raises labor levies, appoints Adoniram, organizes workers and overseers, and gathers prepared stones and timber for the temple foundation.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Solomon beginning and completing the LORD’s temple, giving dates, dimensions, and construction details, including stone prepared offsite, surrounding chambers, and cedar and fir interior work. It reports the LORD’s word to Solomon about obedience and dwelling with Israel. It describes the oracle for the ark, gold overlaying, carved cherubim and palm motifs, doors, inner court, and the seven-year building timeline.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records Solomon’s thirteen-year construction of his palace complex, including the House of the Forest of Lebanon, porches, courts, and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter, built with costly stone and cedar. It describes Hiram of Tyre casting temple furnishings: bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea on twelve oxen, ten bases with lavers, and other bronze vessels cast near the Jordan. It lists gold altar, table, lampstands, utensils, and David’s dedicated treasures placed in the temple.

This chapter contains 66 verses and records Solomon assembling Israel’s elders in Jerusalem to bring the ark into the temple and dedicate it with extensive sacrifices. The ark is placed in the most holy place, and a cloud fills the house. Solomon blesses the people and prays toward the temple for forgiveness, justice, deliverance in war, relief from drought and plagues, and restoration from captivity, including for foreigners who pray there. He blesses Israel to keep commandments, holds a fourteen-day feast, then dismisses the people.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records the LORD’s second appearance to Solomon, promising an enduring throne for obedience and warning of Israel’s removal and the temple’s rejection for idolatry. It covers Solomon giving Hiram twenty Galilean cities, Hiram’s displeasure, and a gold payment. It lists Solomon’s building projects, forced labor from remaining Canaanite peoples, Israelite roles, offerings, and a Red Sea fleet to Ophir for gold.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records the queen of Sheba visiting Solomon in Jerusalem to test him with questions, observing his wisdom, house, and court, and giving gold, spices, and stones. It covers imports from Ophir and Tharshish, use of almug wood, Solomon’s annual gold revenue, golden shields and ivory throne, global gifts, chariots and horsemen, and trade in horses and chariots from Egypt.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Solomon’s foreign wives turning his heart to other gods, leading him to build high places near Jerusalem. The LORD pronounces judgment to divide the kingdom after Solomon, leaving one tribe for David and Jerusalem. It introduces adversaries Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus. Ahijah prophesies ten tribes to Jeroboam; Solomon seeks to kill him, and Jeroboam flees to Egypt. Solomon dies; Rehoboam succeeds.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Rehoboam’s coronation at Shechem, Israel’s request for lighter burdens, and Rehoboam’s harsh reply following young men’s counsel. Israel rebels, Adoram is stoned, and Jeroboam is made king over Israel while Rehoboam rules Judah and Benjamin. Shemaiah tells Rehoboam not to fight. Jeroboam builds Shechem and Penuel, sets golden calves at Bethel and Dan, appoints non-Levite priests, and institutes a feast and sacrifices at Bethel.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records a man of God from Judah prophesying at Bethel against Jeroboam’s altar, giving signs as the altar splits and Jeroboam’s hand withers then is healed. The man refuses food, is deceived by an old prophet, disobeys, and is killed by a lion. The old prophet buries him. Jeroboam continues appointing high-place priests.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Abijah son of Jeroboam falling sick, Jeroboam sending his disguised wife to Ahijah at Shiloh, and Ahijah prophesying judgment on Jeroboam’s house, Abijah’s death, and Israel’s scattering. Abijah dies at Tirzah and Nadab succeeds Jeroboam. It also covers Rehoboam’s reign in Judah, Judah’s idolatry, Shishak of Egypt taking Jerusalem’s treasures, continual war with Jeroboam, and Abijam succeeding Rehoboam.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Abijam’s three-year reign in Judah and ongoing war with Jeroboam. It covers Asa’s forty-one-year reign, his removal of idols and sodomites, deposing Maachah, and dedicating treasures to the temple. It describes Asa bribing Ben-hadad of Syria to break with Baasha, Baasha halting Ramah’s fortification, and Asa building Geba and Mizpah. It records Nadab’s reign, Baasha’s coup at Gibbethon, destruction of Jeroboam’s house, and Baasha’s reign in Tirzah.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jehu’s prophecy of judgment against Baasha’s house, Baasha’s death, and Elah’s brief reign in Tirzah. Zimri assassinates Elah, exterminates Baasha’s lineage, reigns seven days, and dies by burning the palace. Israel divides between Tibni and Omri; Omri prevails, reigns twelve years, buys and builds Samaria, and is succeeded by Ahab, who marries Jezebel, promotes Baal worship, and Hiel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of his sons.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Elijah the Tishbite declaring to Ahab that no dew or rain will fall except by his word. The LORD directs Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, where ravens feed him until the brook dries. Elijah goes to Zarephath, is sustained by a widow whose meal and oil do not fail, and later prays for her dead son, who revives.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Elijah being sent to Ahab during famine in Samaria, with Obadiah hiding prophets from Jezebel. Elijah summons Israel and Baal’s prophets to Mount Carmel for a fire test. Baal’s prophets fail; the LORD answers by fire on Elijah’s water-soaked altar of twelve stones. The people confess the LORD, Baal’s prophets are slain at Kishon, and rain returns as Ahab goes to Jezreel and Elijah runs before him.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Jezebel threatening Elijah, Elijah fleeing to Beer-sheba and into the wilderness, and an angel providing food and water. Elijah travels forty days to Horeb, stays in a cave, and hears the LORD in a still small voice after wind, earthquake, and fire. The LORD commands anointing Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, notes seven thousand faithful, and Elijah calls Elisha, who sacrifices oxen and follows him.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Ben-hadad of Syria besieging Samaria and demanding Ahab’s wealth and family. Israel’s elders advise refusal. A prophet tells Ahab the LORD will deliver Syria; Israel defeats Ben-hadad and his allies. Another warning predicts renewed attack; Ben-hadad fights at Aphek and is again defeated. Ahab spares Ben-hadad by covenant. A disguised prophet condemns Ahab for releasing one appointed for destruction.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Ahab seeking Naboth’s vineyard in Jezreel, Naboth refusing to give his ancestral inheritance, and Jezebel arranging false accusations and Naboth’s stoning so Ahab takes the vineyard. The LORD sends Elijah to confront Ahab and announce judgment on Ahab’s house and Jezebel. Ahab humbles himself with fasting, and the LORD delays the disaster to his son’s days.

This chapter contains 53 verses and records Jehoshaphat visiting Ahab, consultation about war for Ramoth-gilead, and Micaiah prophesying Ahab’s defeat and a lying spirit in the prophets. Ahab imprisons Micaiah, disguises himself, and is killed by an arrow; Israel retreats and Ahab is buried in Samaria. It notes Jehoshaphat’s reign and reforms, broken ships at Ezion-geber, and Ahaziah succeeding Ahab and serving Baal.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Moab’s rebellion after Ahab’s death, Ahaziah’s injury in Samaria, and his sending messengers to consult Baal-zebub of Ekron. An angel directs Elijah to intercept them and pronounce Ahaziah’s death. Ahaziah sends two captains with fifties who are consumed by fire from heaven; a third pleads and Elijah goes to the king, repeats the oracle, and Ahaziah dies. Jehoram succeeds him.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Elijah traveling with Elisha from Gilgal to Beth-el, Jericho, and the Jordan, dividing the river with his mantle, and being taken into heaven by a whirlwind with chariot and horses of fire. Elisha receives Elijah’s mantle, parts the Jordan, is acknowledged by the sons of the prophets, and they search unsuccessfully for Elijah. Elisha heals Jericho’s water with salt, curses mocking youths at Beth-el, and two she-bears maul forty-two; he goes to Carmel and Samaria.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jehoram’s reign in Israel and Moab’s rebellion under Mesha. Jehoram allies with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom and marches through Edom’s wilderness, lacking water. Elisha prophesies ditches filled with water and victory over Moab. Water comes, Moab mistakes it for blood, attacks, and is defeated as Israel devastates the land and besieges Kir-haraseth. Mesha sacrifices his firstborn; Israel withdraws.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Elisha multiplying a widow’s oil so she can pay her debt and save her sons from bondage. It describes a Shunammite woman housing Elisha; he promises and she bears a son, who later dies and is restored to life by Elisha at Shunem. It covers Elisha purifying poisonous pottage at Gilgal and feeding a hundred men with twenty barley loaves from Baal-shalisha.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Naaman, Syrian army captain with leprosy, being directed by an Israelite maid to Elisha in Samaria. Naaman brings a letter and gifts to Israel’s king; Elisha instructs him to wash seven times in the Jordan, and he is healed. Naaman acknowledges Israel’s God, requests earth, and seeks pardon regarding Rimmon. Gehazi deceives Naaman for silver and garments; Elisha rebukes him and pronounces Naaman’s leprosy on Gehazi.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Elisha aiding the prophets by recovering a borrowed axe head in the Jordan, warning Israel’s king of Syrian ambushes, and blinding a Syrian force at Dothan before leading it to Samaria and sparing it with food and release. It also covers Ben-hadad’s siege and famine in Samaria, a woman’s complaint to the king, and the king’s threat against Elisha and sending a messenger to him.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Elisha prophesying that food prices in besieged Samaria drop within a day, while a royal officer doubts and is told he will see it but not eat. Four lepers find the Syrian camp deserted after the Syrians flee, report it, and scouts confirm the flight to the Jordan. The people plunder the camp, prices fall as foretold, and the officer is trampled at the gate and dies.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Elisha warning the Shunammite woman of a seven-year famine; she sojourns among the Philistines and later receives restoration of her land and its produce by the king. Elisha visits Damascus, foretells Ben-hadad’s death and Hazael’s future kingship and violence against Israel; Hazael kills Ben-hadad and reigns. Jehoram of Judah reigns, Edom and Libnah revolt, and Ahaziah succeeds; Ahaziah joins Joram of Israel against Hazael, and Joram is wounded and retreats to Jezreel.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Elisha sending a prophet to anoint Jehu king over Israel at Ramoth-gilead, charging him to destroy Ahab’s house and foretelling Jezebel’s death. Jehu is proclaimed by the captains, rides to Jezreel, kills Joram in Naboth’s field, and has the body cast there. Jehu pursues and kills Ahaziah of Judah. At Jezreel, eunuchs throw down Jezebel; dogs consume her remains, fulfilling Elijah’s word.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Jehu ordering the rulers of Samaria to kill Ahab’s seventy sons and sending their heads to Jezreel. Jehu kills remaining members of Ahab’s house and slays forty-two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah near the shearing house. He allies with Jehonadab, gathers Baal worshipers, massacres them, destroys Baal’s temple and images, yet continues Jeroboam’s calf worship. The LORD promises Jehu four generations on Israel’s throne; Hazael attacks Israel; Jehu dies and Jehoahaz succeeds.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Athaliah killing the royal heirs after Ahaziah’s death, while Jehosheba hides Joash in the LORD’s house for six years. In the seventh year Jehoiada organizes guards, makes a covenant, arms them with temple weapons, and crowns and anoints Joash king. Athaliah is seized and executed outside the temple; a covenant is renewed, Baal’s house is destroyed, Mattan is killed, and Joash is enthroned at age seven.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Jehoash (Joash) beginning to reign in Jerusalem for forty years, doing right under Jehoiada’s instruction while high places remain. It covers temple repair funding: collection of dedicated money, a chest set by the altar, counting and paying workmen, and limits on making vessels; trespass and sin money belongs to priests. It records Hazael of Syria taking Gath, Jehoash sending temple and palace treasures as tribute, and Joash’s assassination at Millo; Amaziah succeeds him.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jehoahaz reigning in Samaria, doing evil, Israel’s oppression by Hazael and Ben-hadad of Syria, Jehoahaz’s plea, and partial deliverance though idolatry continues. It notes Jehoahaz’s death and Jehoash’s reign. Elisha, dying, instructs Jehoash with arrows and foretells three victories at Aphek. Elisha dies; a dead man revives on his bones. Hazael dies; Jehoash retakes cities from Ben-hadad three times.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Amaziah of Judah’s reign, his execution of his father’s assassins, sparing their children per the Law, victory over Edom, and defeat by Jehoash of Israel at Beth-shemesh, followed by Jerusalem’s wall being broken and temple and royal treasures taken. It reports Amaziah’s assassination, Azariah’s accession and rebuilding Elath, and Jeroboam II’s reign, territorial restorations per Jonah, and succession by Zechariah.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records the reigns of Azariah (Uzziah) in Judah and multiple kings in Israel. Azariah reigns in Jerusalem, leaves high places, is struck with leprosy, and Jotham governs. Israel’s kings Zachariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah reign amid conspiracies and assassinations. Menahem pays tribute to Pul of Assyria. Tiglath-pileser captures northern cities and exiles captives. Jotham reigns in Judah, builds a temple gate, faces threats from Rezin and Pekah, and Ahaz succeeds him.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Ahaz beginning to reign in Judah, practicing idolatry and child sacrifice, and worshiping at high places. Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem; Rezin recovers Elath. Ahaz sends temple and royal treasures to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for help; Assyria captures Damascus, kills Rezin, and exiles captives to Kir. Ahaz copies a Damascus altar, directs Urijah to build it, moves the bronze altar, alters temple furnishings, and dies; Hezekiah succeeds.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Hoshea’s reign in Samaria, Assyria’s siege and capture of Samaria, and Israel’s deportation to Halah, Habor by the Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. It recounts Israel’s sins, rejected covenant, and prophetic warnings. Assyria resettles Samaria with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim; lions strike them, a priest teaches at Beth-el, and mixed worship continues.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Hezekiah beginning to reign in Judah, his reforms removing high places, idols, and the bronze serpent, and his revolt against Assyria and victories over Philistines. It notes Assyria’s siege and capture of Samaria and Israel’s deportation. Sennacherib invades Judah; Hezekiah pays tribute from temple treasures. Assyrian envoys confront Jerusalem; Rab-shakeh delivers threats; officials report to Hezekiah.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Hezekiah mourning and seeking the LORD in the temple, sending Eliakim, Shebna, and priests to Isaiah. Isaiah delivers assurance that Assyria will withdraw and its king die at home. Sennacherib sends a threatening letter; Hezekiah prays for deliverance. Isaiah prophesies Jerusalem’s preservation, a sign for Judah, and Assyria’s retreat. An angel kills 185,000 Assyrians; Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and is slain by sons; Esarhaddon succeeds.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Hezekiah’s mortal illness, Isaiah’s message to set his house in order, Hezekiah’s prayer, and God’s promise to heal him and add fifteen years, with deliverance from Assyria. Isaiah applies a fig lump and gives a sign as the shadow on Ahaz’s dial goes back ten degrees. Babylon’s king sends envoys; Hezekiah shows his treasures. Isaiah foretells Babylonian exile and captivity of Hezekiah’s sons. Hezekiah’s works and Manasseh’s succession are noted.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Manasseh’s 55-year reign in Jerusalem, his restoration of high places, Baal worship, astral worship, sorcery, child sacrifice, and placing an image in the LORD’s house. Prophets announce judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for these abominations and bloodshed. Manasseh dies and Amon reigns two years, follows the same idolatry, is assassinated by servants, and Josiah succeeds him.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Josiah’s reign in Jerusalem, including his temple repair project funded by collected silver. Hilkiah finds the book of the law, Shaphan reads it to the king, and Josiah mourns and seeks counsel. Hilkiah and others consult Huldah, who foretells judgment on Judah for idolatry but promises Josiah dies in peace.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records King Josiah gathering Judah and Jerusalem, reading the book of the covenant, and renewing a covenant to keep the LORD’s commandments. Josiah removes Baal and Asherah items, deposes idolatrous priests, defiles high places (including Topheth), destroys altars, and purges practices in Judah and Samaria, including at Beth-el. He commands a Passover in Jerusalem. The chapter reports coming judgment on Judah, Josiah’s death at Megiddo, Jehoahaz’s brief reign and removal by Pharaoh-nechoh, and Jehoiakim’s accession and tribute.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar’s invasion, Jehoiakim’s three-year vassalage and later rebellion, and raids on Judah by Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites. Jehoiakim dies and Jehoiachin reigns three months before Jerusalem is besieged and he surrenders. Babylon removes temple and palace treasures, deports leaders, warriors, craftsmen, and the royal household, and appoints Mattaniah as King Zedekiah, who later rebels.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar’s siege of Jerusalem, famine, breach of the city, Zedekiah’s flight, capture near Jericho, judgment at Riblah, and his blinding and exile. Nebuzar-adan burns the temple and city, breaks walls, carries captives, and seizes temple vessels. Priests and officials are executed at Riblah. Gedaliah governs at Mizpah and is assassinated; people flee to Egypt. Jehoiachin is released and provided for in Babylon.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records genealogies from Adam through Noah’s sons and their descendants, listing the lines of Japheth, Ham (including Nimrod and Philistine origins), and Shem to Abraham. It names Abraham’s descendants through Isaac, Ishmael, and Keturah, then traces Esau’s line, Seir’s families, and lists Edom’s kings before Israel’s monarchy and the chiefs (dukes) of Edom.

This chapter contains 55 verses and records genealogies of Israel, focusing on Judah and Hezron’s lines. It lists Judah’s sons, Tamar’s sons Pharez and Zerah, and descendants leading to Jesse and David, including David’s brothers and sisters and Zeruiah’s sons. It traces Caleb’s descendants, Hezron’s marriage into Machir’s house, Jerahmeel’s family, Sheshan’s line through his servant Jarha, and clan origins tied to places like Tekoa, Gilead, Kirjath-jearim, Bethlehem, and Jabez.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records genealogies of David’s descendants. It lists David’s sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem, notes his reign lengths there, and mentions Tamar. It traces the royal line from Solomon through Judah’s kings to Josiah, names Josiah’s sons, and continues through Jehoiakim and Jeconiah to Salathiel, Pedaiah, Zerubbabel, and later descendants down to Elioenai’s seven sons.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records genealogies of Judah and Simeon, listing descendants, clans, and associated towns. It notes Jabez’s prayer for blessing and protection. It mentions craftsmen, linen workers, and potters serving the king. It lists Simeonite settlements through David’s reign, then princes who seek pasture near Gedor. In Hezekiah’s days Simeonites displace Hamites and later strike remaining Amalekites at mount Seir.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records genealogies of Reuben and Gad, noting Reuben’s lost birthright, and settlements from Aroer to Nebo, Baal-meon, Gilead, Bashan, and Sharon. It recounts wars in Saul’s days against Hagarites, Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab, listing a force of 44,760 and captured livestock. It lists half-Manasseh leaders and territory, then reports idolatry and Assyrian exile by Pul and Tilgath-pilneser to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan.

This chapter contains 81 verses and records Levite genealogies from Levi through Gershom, Kohath, and Merari, including Aaron’s priestly line to Jehozadak and the exile. It lists David’s appointed temple singers Heman, Asaph, and Ethan and notes Levite tabernacle duties. It details priestly functions of Aaron’s descendants and enumerates Levitical towns and cities of refuge assigned by lot across Israel, including Hebron, Shechem, Golan, and Ramoth.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records genealogies of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher, listing clan leaders and military totals. It notes Ephraim’s sons are killed by men of Gath, his mourning, and the birth of Beriah; it mentions Sherah building Beth-horon and Uzzen-sherah. It also lists Joseph’s settlements, including Beth-el, Gezer, Shechem, Beth-shean, Megiddo, and Dor.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin, listing descendants of Benjamin through Bela and other family heads, including Ehud, Shaharaim in Moab, and Elpaal. It notes Shamed building Ono and Lod, and Beriah and Shema driving out inhabitants of Gath. It identifies chief men dwelling in Jerusalem and Gibeon, and traces Saul’s line through Kish to Jonathan, Merib-baal, and later descendants, including Ulam’s archer sons.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Israel’s genealogical registration and the return of inhabitants to their cities after the Babylonian captivity. It lists families dwelling in Jerusalem from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, and names priests, Levites, Nethinim, porters, singers, and their temple duties over gates, chambers, vessels, offerings, and supplies. It also gives the genealogy from Jehiel of Gibeon through Ner, Kish, Saul, Jonathan, and Azel.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the Philistines’ battle against Israel at Mount Gilboa, where Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua are killed and Saul, wounded by archers, dies by falling on his sword; his armourbearer also dies. Philistines occupy Israelite cities, remove Saul’s head and armor, and place them in pagan temples. Men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve and bury the bodies and fast seven days. Saul’s death is linked to disobedience and consulting a familiar spirit, and the kingdom transfers to David.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Israel gathering at Hebron to anoint David king by covenant with the elders. David captures Jebus (Jerusalem), takes the stronghold of Zion, and builds the city while Joab becomes chief after first attacking the Jebusites. It lists David’s mighty men, their exploits at Pas-dammim and Bethlehem, and names the valiant men of the armies.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records warriors from Benjamin, Gad, Judah, and other tribes joining David at Ziklag and in the wilderness, including named captains and their skills. David tests their intentions, receives Amasai’s pledge, and appoints captains. It lists troop numbers from each tribe coming to Hebron to make David king, and describes three days of provisions and rejoicing in Israel.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records David consulting Israel’s leaders to gather the people, priests, and Levites to bring the ark from Kirjath-jearim. David assembles Israel from Shihor of Egypt to Hemath, transports the ark on a new cart from Abinadab’s house with Uzza and Ahio, and leads music and rejoicing. At Chidon, Uzza touches the ark and dies. David names Perez-uzza, fears God, and leaves the ark with Obed-edom, whose house is blessed.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Hiram king of Tyre sending cedar timber, masons, and carpenters to build David a house. David recognizes his kingdom is established and takes more wives in Jerusalem, listing sons born there. Philistines attack in the valley of Rephaim; David inquires of God, defeats them at Baal-perazim, and burns their abandoned idols. A second Philistine advance is met by God’s strategy near mulberry trees; David routs them from Gibeon to Gezer, and his fame spreads.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records David preparing a place and tent for the ark in Jerusalem, declaring that Levites must carry it, and assembling Israel, priests, and Levite clans. He commands sanctification after a prior breach, and the Levites bear the ark on staves as Moses commanded. Musicians and doorkeepers are appointed, trumpets are blown, sacrifices are offered, and the ark is brought from Obed-edom with shouting; Michal sees David dancing and despises him.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records the ark being set in David’s tent with burnt and peace offerings, David blessing the people and distributing food and drink, and Levites (including Asaph) appointed to minister with instruments and trumpets.
