It includes a psalm of thanksgiving recalling God’s covenant with the patriarchs and urging worship. David assigns ongoing service before the ark and at Gibeon, then the people and David return home.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records David telling Nathan he wants to build a house for the ark; God tells Nathan David will not build it. God recounts raising David from shepherd to ruler, promises to plant Israel and subdue enemies, and promises to build David a lasting dynasty through his son who will build the house. David prays thanksgiving and asks God to establish and bless his house and Israel forever.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records David’s victories over the Philistines (taking Gath), Moab, and Hadarezer of Zobah near Hamath and the Euphrates, including defeat of Syrians of Damascus and establishment of garrisons. David takes chariots, gold shields, and brass from Tibhath and Chun; Tou of Hamath sends Hadoram with gifts. David dedicates spoils from several nations. Abishai defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt; garrisons are set. Officials are listed.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Nahash of Ammon dying and Hanun succeeding him. David sends messengers to comfort Hanun, but Ammonite princes suspect spying; Hanun humiliates the envoys. David shelters them at Jericho. Ammon hires Syrian forces from Mesopotamia, Maachah, and Zobah and camps at Medeba. Joab and Abishai battle Syrians and Ammonites; both retreat. David later defeats reinforcements, kills Shophach, and Hadarezer’s servants make peace and cease aiding Ammon.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Joab besieging and destroying Rabbah of the Ammonites while David remains in Jerusalem. David takes the Ammonite king’s crown and much spoil, and the captives are punished; the army returns to Jerusalem. It also covers wars with the Philistines at Gezer and Gath, where Sibbechai kills Sippai, Elhanan kills Lahmi (Goliath’s brother), and Jonathan kills another giant.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Satan provoking David to number Israel; Joab conducts the census from Beer-sheba to Dan and reports totals. God is displeased, and through Gad offers David three judgments; David chooses pestilence, and 70,000 die. An angel threatens Jerusalem but stops at Ornan’s threshingfloor; David buys the site, builds an altar, offers sacrifices, fire answers, and the angel sheathes his sword.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records David identifying the temple site and altar, gathering resident foreigners as laborers, and preparing stone, iron, bronze, cedar, gold, and silver for building. David charges Solomon to build the LORD’s house, recounting that he is forbidden due to warfare and bloodshed, and that Solomon will have rest. He urges obedience to the law and commands Israel’s princes to help and seek the LORD.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records David, in old age, making Solomon king and assembling Israel’s leaders, priests, and Levites. It numbers 38,000 Levites and assigns 24,000 to temple work, 6,000 as officers and judges, 4,000 as gatekeepers, and 4,000 as musicians. David organizes Levites by Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, listing key families, and sets duties from age twenty, assisting Aaron’s sons in temple service, offerings, and daily praise.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the divisions of Aaron’s sons, noting Nadab and Abihu die childless and Eleazar and Ithamar serve as priests. David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, assigns priestly courses by lot, listing 24 orders from Jehoiarib to Maaziah. It also lists Levitical family heads and notes they likewise cast lots before David and priestly leaders.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records David and the captains appointing temple musicians from the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with harps, psalteries, and cymbals. It lists their families, notes 288 trained singers, and describes casting lots for 24 divisions, each led by a named leader with twelve associates for orderly service in the house of the LORD.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Levitical divisions of temple gatekeepers from Korahites and Merarites, listing families of Meshelemiah, Obed-edom, and Hosah. It assigns gate duties by casting lots for east, north, south, west, Asuppim, Shallecheth, and Parbar, with daily numbers. It names officials over temple and dedicated treasures, and Levite officers and judges for Israel, including Jerijah’s appointment over Transjordan tribes.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records David’s military courses of 24,000 men rotating monthly under named commanders, and princes appointed over Israel’s tribes. It notes David does not count those under twenty, and Joab’s unfinished census brings wrath. It lists officials over royal treasuries, storehouses, agriculture, vineyards, oil, herds, camels, asses, and flocks, and names key counselors and commanders.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records David assembling Israel’s leaders in Jerusalem, stating he intended to build a house for the ark but is forbidden because of warfare. He declares Solomon chosen to reign and build the temple, urges obedience and wholehearted service, and charges Solomon to be strong. David gives Solomon temple plans, priest and Levite courses, and weight specifications for gold and silver vessels, assuring support from officials and skilled workers.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records David presenting Solomon as God’s chosen successor and urging offerings for the temple. David contributes gold, silver, and materials; Israel’s leaders and people give willingly, with jewels placed under Jehiel. David blesses and thanks the LORD, prays for Israel’s loyalty and Solomon’s obedience. The congregation worships, offers large sacrifices, eats before the LORD, anoints Solomon and Zadok, and submits to Solomon. It notes David’s 40-year reign, death, and sources for his acts.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Solomon being strengthened as king, assembling Israel, and going to Gibeon where the tabernacle and bronze altar stand. Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, and God appears, inviting a request. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to judge the people; God grants these and also promises riches and honor. Solomon returns to Jerusalem, gathers chariots and horsemen, increases silver, gold, and cedar, and imports horses and chariots from Egypt for regional kings.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Solomon’s plans to build a temple for the LORD and a royal house, including worship purposes and required offerings. He assigns 70,000 burden bearers, 80,000 mountain hewers, and 3,600 overseers. Solomon requests timber from Lebanon and a skilled craftsman from Huram king of Tyre, offering wheat, barley, wine, and oil. Huram agrees, sends a craftsman, and ships logs to Joppa for transport to Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Solomon beginning the LORD’s temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, at the site prepared by David at Ornan’s threshing floor, in Solomon’s fourth year. It gives measurements and materials for the porch, main hall, and most holy place, including gold overlay, carvings, veil, and two gold-covered cherubim. It also describes two front pillars with chains and pomegranates, named Jachin and Boaz.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the making of temple furnishings for Solomon: a bronze altar, the molten sea on twelve oxen with oxen figures, ten lavers, ten gold lampstands, ten tables, and gold basins. It describes priestly courts and brass-overlaid doors. Huram makes pillars with chapiters, wreaths, and 400 pomegranates, plus utensils, cast in the Jordan plain near Succoth and Zeredathah, and lists additional gold vessels and doors.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Solomon finishing the LORD’s house and depositing David’s dedicated treasures. Solomon assembles Israel’s elders and tribal heads in Jerusalem in the seventh month to bring the ark from Zion. Priests and Levites carry the ark, tabernacle, and holy vessels, and sacrifices are offered. The ark is placed in the most holy place under cherubim; it contains the two tables from Horeb. Singers and trumpeters praise, a cloud fills the temple, and priests cannot minister.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Solomon blessing Israel at the temple dedication, recounting God’s choice of Jerusalem and promise to David, and placing the ark in the house. Solomon prays with hands spread, asking God to hear prayers toward the temple, forgive sins, judge oaths, restore after defeat, send rain, relieve famine and plague, hear foreigners, grant victory, and show mercy in captivity. He closes with petitions for priests and the anointed.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records fire from heaven consuming Solomon’s offerings as the LORD’s glory fills the temple, preventing priestly entry. Israel worships, and Solomon dedicates the house with vast sacrifices, priestly service, and a seven-day feast with an eighth-day assembly, then dismisses the people. The LORD appears to Solomon, accepts the temple, calls for repentance in calamity, promises to hear prayers there, and warns of exile and temple desolation if Israel serves other gods.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Solomon’s building projects after twenty years, including rebuilding cities from Huram, fortifying Tadmor, Hamath store cities, Beth-horon, Baalath, and chariot and horsemen cities. It notes his campaign at Hamath-zobah, tribute labor from remaining Canaanites, and Israelite military roles. Solomon relocates Pharaoh’s daughter, organizes temple offerings and priestly/Levitical courses, and sends ships from Ezion-geber/Eloth to Ophir for gold.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the queen of Sheba visiting Solomon in Jerusalem to test him, exchanging gifts, and praising his wisdom and prosperity. It lists Solomon’s annual gold income, imports from Ophir and Tarshish, and items made from gold and algum wood, including shields, vessels, and an ivory throne. It notes foreign rulers seeking Solomon, his horses and chariots, his forty-year reign, death, burial, and Rehoboam succeeding him.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Rehoboam going to Shechem to be made king, with Jeroboam returning from Egypt and leading Israel to request lighter labor burdens. Rehoboam consults elders and then young men, rejects the elders’ advice, and answers harshly with increased discipline. Israel renounces the house of David, stones Hadoram over tribute, and Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem as the kingdom divides.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Rehoboam assembling 180,000 men to fight Israel, then obeying the LORD’s word through Shemaiah to stop. It covers Rehoboam fortifying Jerusalem and building defense cities in Judah and Benjamin with supplies and weapons. Priests, Levites, and other Israelites migrate to Judah after Jeroboam rejects them. It lists Rehoboam’s wives, children, appointing Abijah as chief, and dispersing sons to fortified cities.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Rehoboam forsaking the LORD’s law, prompting Shishak king of Egypt to invade Judah in Rehoboam’s fifth year, seize fortified cities, and come to Jerusalem. Shemaiah warns Judah’s leaders, who humble themselves, leading to limited deliverance but continued servitude. Shishak takes temple and palace treasures, including Solomon’s gold shields, replaced with bronze. Rehoboam’s reign details, wars with Jeroboam, death, and Abijah’s succession are noted.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Abijah beginning to reign over Judah in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year and warring with Jeroboam of Israel. Abijah addresses Israel from mount Zemaraim, citing the Davidic covenant and condemning golden calves and unauthorized priests, while affirming temple worship and Aaronic priests. Jeroboam sets an ambush; Judah cries to the LORD, priests sound trumpets, and Israel is defeated with heavy losses. Abijah captures Beth-el, Jeshanah, and Ephrain; Jeroboam later dies. Abijah’s family and Iddo’s record are noted.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Abijah’s death, Asa’s reign, and ten years of peace in Judah. Asa removes foreign altars, high places, images, and groves, and commands Judah to seek the LORD and obey the law. He fortifies cities and organizes forces from Judah and Benjamin. Zerah the Ethiopian invades at Mareshah; Asa prays, Judah routs the Ethiopians, pursues to Gerar, takes spoil, smites nearby cities, and returns to Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Azariah son of Oded prophesying to King Asa that seeking the LORD brings help and forsaking brings abandonment, recalling past lack of true worship and peace. Asa removes idols in Judah, Benjamin, and captured Ephraim cities, renews the LORD’s altar, and gathers people at Jerusalem to sacrifice and covenant to seek the LORD, with death for refusal. Asa deposes Maachah, destroys her idol at Kidron, dedicates treasures, and the land has rest until Asa’s thirty-fifth year.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Baasha of Israel fortifying Ramah to restrict Judah, Asa of Judah sending temple and royal treasures to Ben-hadad of Syria for aid, and Syrian attacks on Israelite cities prompting Baasha to stop. Asa repurposes Ramah’s materials to build Geba and Mizpah. Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on Syria; Asa imprisons him and oppresses people. Asa later suffers a severe foot disease, seeks physicians, dies, and is buried in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Jehoshaphat succeeding Asa as king of Judah, fortifying cities and placing garrisons, including in Ephraim. It states he seeks the LORD, removes high places and groves, and sends princes, Levites, and priests to teach from the book of the law throughout Judah. Surrounding kingdoms fear and do not war; Philistines and Arabians bring tribute. It lists military divisions and commanders stationed in Jerusalem and fenced cities.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jehoshaphat allying with Ahab and traveling to Samaria, where Ahab urges war at Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat requests inquiry of the LORD; Ahab consults 400 prophets, then summons Micaiah, who foretells Israel scattered and describes a lying spirit deceiving Ahab’s prophets. Micaiah is struck and imprisoned. Ahab disguises himself in battle; Jehoshaphat is spared; Ahab is mortally wounded and dies.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records Jehoshaphat returning safely to Jerusalem, where Jehu son of Hanani rebukes him for aiding the ungodly and warns of divine wrath while noting his removal of groves and seeking God. Jehoshaphat travels from Beer-sheba to Mount Ephraim to restore worship, appoints judges in Judah, and instructs them to judge in the fear of the LORD without partiality or bribes, establishing a Jerusalem court led by Amariah and Zebadiah.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir invading Judah, with their host at En-gedi. Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast, prays in the temple, and Jahaziel prophesies Judah need not fight. Judah marches from Tekoa with singers; the enemy armies destroy each other. Judah gathers spoil three days, blesses God in the valley of Berachah, and returns to Jerusalem. Jehoshaphat’s reign is summarized; he allies with Ahaziah to build Tarshish ships at Ezion-geber, and the ships are broken after Eliezer’s prophecy.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Jehoshaphat’s death and Jehoram’s eight-year reign in Jerusalem. Jehoram kills his brothers and some princes, marries Ahab’s daughter, and promotes high places, leading Judah astray. Edom and Libnah revolt. Elijah sends a letter warning of plagues and disease. Philistines and Arabians raid Judah, taking Jehoram’s goods, wives, and sons, leaving only Jehoahaz. Jehoram dies of bowel disease and is buried without royal honors.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Ahaziah’s accession in Jerusalem after his brothers are slain, his one-year reign influenced by Athaliah and Ahab’s house, and his alliance with Israel’s Jehoram against Hazael at Ramoth-gilead. It describes Jehu killing Judah’s princes and Ahaziah, Athaliah destroying the royal seed, and Jehoshabeath hiding Joash in God’s house six years while Athaliah rules.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Jehoiada’s seventh-year covenant with captains, Levites, and leaders in Judah to enthrone the king’s son in Jerusalem. It details Sabbath guard assignments at the temple and palace, arming men with David’s weapons, crowning and anointing the young king, and Athaliah’s removal and death at the horse gate. It covers a covenant to be the LORD’s people, destruction of Baal’s temple, restoration of priestly duties and gatekeeping, and the king’s placement on the throne.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Joash reigning 40 years in Jerusalem, doing right under Jehoiada, taking wives, and organizing collections to repair the temple, hiring craftsmen and making vessels for worship. After Jehoiada dies, Joash follows Judah’s princes into idol service, ignores prophets, and orders Zechariah stoned. Syria invades Judah, Joash is diseased, assassinated by servants, and Amaziah succeeds him.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Amaziah’s reign in Jerusalem, his execution of his father’s assassins while sparing their children per the Law, and his mustering of Judah and Benjamin. He hires but dismisses Israelite troops after a warning, defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt, then adopts Edomite gods and rejects prophetic rebuke. He challenges Joash of Israel, is defeated at Beth-shemesh, Jerusalem’s wall is breached, treasures are taken, and Amaziah is later assassinated at Lachish and buried.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Uzziah becoming king of Judah at sixteen and reigning 52 years in Jerusalem. It covers his building of Eloth, towers, wells, and fortifications, his wars against Philistines, Arabians, and Mehunims, and gifts from Ammon. It lists his organized army and weapons. It records his unlawful incense offering, confrontation by Azariah and priests, leprosy, isolation, Jotham governing, Uzziah’s death and burial, and Isaiah’s record.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records Jotham beginning to reign in Jerusalem at age 25 for 16 years, son of Jerushah daughter of Zadok. He does what is right yet does not enter the LORD’s temple, while the people act corruptly. He builds the high gate of the LORD’s house, fortifies Ophel, and builds cities, castles, and towers in Judah. He defeats Ammon and receives annual tribute of silver, wheat, and barley for three years. Jotham dies and Ahaz succeeds him.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Ahaz’s reign in Jerusalem, his idolatry, child sacrifices, and high-place worship. Judah is defeated by Syria and Israel; Pekah kills 120,000 and captives are taken to Samaria. Prophet Oded and Ephraimite leaders require the captives’ return to Jericho. Edomites and Philistines invade; Ahaz seeks Assyrian help, gives temple treasures, but gains no aid. He sacrifices to Damascus gods, shuts the temple, builds altars, dies, and Hezekiah succeeds him.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Hezekiah’s early reign in Jerusalem, his opening and repairing of the temple doors, and his command to priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and cleanse the house of the LORD, removing uncleanness to the brook Kidron. It lists chief Levites involved, describes eight days of cleansing, restoration of vessels cast away by Ahaz, city rulers assembling, sin and burnt offerings for all Israel, Levite music with David’s instruments, abundant sacrifices and thank offerings, Levites aiding priests, and the temple service being set in order.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Hezekiah’s letters to Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, to keep Passover at Jerusalem in the second month. Proclamation goes from Beer-sheba to Dan; some mock, others come. The people remove altars, priests and Levites sanctify, and the Passover is kept though many are unclean; Hezekiah prays and the people are healed. Unleavened Bread is celebrated fourteen days with offerings, royal gifts, rejoicing, and priestly blessing.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Israel destroying idols, groves, high places, and altars in Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Hezekiah organizes priestly and Levitical courses, assigns royal offerings for daily and festival sacrifices, and commands Jerusalem to support clergy. The people bring firstfruits and tithes; heaps accumulate. Store chambers are prepared, and officials oversee collection and distribution by genealogies. Hezekiah’s reforms prosper.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Sennacherib’s invasion of Judah and siege threats against Jerusalem. Hezekiah blocks outside water sources, strengthens walls, arms forces, and encourages the people. Assyrian envoys and letters mock Hezekiah and God; Hezekiah and Isaiah pray. An angel strikes the Assyrian camp; Sennacherib returns and is killed. Hezekiah’s sickness, pride, humbling, wealth, waterworks, Babylonian envoys, death, and Manasseh’s succession are noted.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Manasseh’s 55-year reign in Jerusalem, his idolatry, altars in the LORD’s house, child sacrifice in Hinnom, and occult practices, followed by Assyrian capture and exile to Babylon. Manasseh humbles himself, prays, returns, fortifies Jerusalem, removes idols, restores worship, and commands Judah to serve the LORD. It also covers Amon’s 2-year reign, continued idolatry, his assassination, and Josiah’s accession.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Josiah’s reign in Jerusalem, his early pursuit of God, and his purge of high places, idols, and Baal altars across Judah, Jerusalem, and former northern territories. It covers temple repairs funded by collected money, Hilkiah’s discovery of the book of the law, and Shaphan’s reading to the king. Josiah consults Huldah, receives judgment and personal peace, gathers the people, reads the covenant, renews obedience, and removes abominations.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Josiah’s Passover in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the first month, including organization of priests, Levites, singers, and porters, and large offerings provided by the king and leaders. Israel keeps the feast of unleavened bread seven days. It then covers Pharaoh Necho’s march toward Carchemish, Josiah’s battle at Megiddo, his wounding and death in Jerusalem, national mourning, and Jeremiah’s lament.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Judah’s final kings: Jehoahaz is deposed by Egypt; Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah reign and do evil. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon takes captives and temple vessels. Judah’s leaders reject prophets, and Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed; survivors serve in Babylon for seventy years. Cyrus of Persia proclaims return and rebuilding in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records Cyrus king of Persia issuing a written proclamation allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem in Judah and build the LORD’s house, urging neighbors to support them with gifts and offerings. Chiefs of Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, and others prepare to go. Cyrus returns temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar, delivered through Mithredath to Sheshbazzar, with an inventory totaling 5,400 items brought from Babylon to Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 70 verses and records the list and numbers of Israelites returning from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and other leaders. It enumerates families, towns, priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinim, and Solomon’s servants, notes some without genealogies, and restricts certain priests from holy food pending Urim and Thummim. It totals people, servants, singers, livestock, and freewill offerings, and describes their resettlement in their cities.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Israel gathering in Jerusalem in the seventh month, Jeshua and Zerubbabel building an altar and offering morning and evening burnt offerings, and keeping the Feast of Tabernacles with daily, new moon, and freewill offerings. It notes temple foundations are not yet laid, supplies are obtained from Sidon and Tyre by Cyrus’s grant, Levites are appointed to oversee work, and the temple foundation is laid with praise, mixed shouting and weeping.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records opposition to Judah’s temple work. Adversaries offer to help, but Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and leaders refuse, citing Cyrus’s command. Opponents discourage builders and hire counselors from Cyrus’s reign to Darius’s. Letters accuse Jerusalem to Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes; Rehum and Shimshai request a records search. Artaxerxes orders the work stopped, and it ceases by force until Darius’s second year.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Haggai and Zechariah prophesying in Judah and Jerusalem, leading Zerubbabel and Jeshua to resume building the house of God in Jerusalem. Tatnai and Shethar-boznai question the builders’ authority and send a report to King Darius. The Jews cite Cyrus’s decree, Sheshbazzar’s return of temple vessels, and the laying of the foundation, and request a search of Babylon’s records.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Darius ordering a search for Cyrus’s decree, found at Achmetha, authorizing rebuilding the Jerusalem temple and restoring its vessels. Darius commands Tatnai to cease interference, funds the work from tribute, and supplies offerings, with penalties for مخالters. The Jews finish the temple in Darius’s sixth year, dedicate it with sacrifices, appoint priests and Levites, and keep Passover and Unleavened Bread.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Ezra’s priestly genealogy and his journey from Babylon to Jerusalem in Artaxerxes’ seventh year. It includes the king’s letter authorizing volunteers to return, providing gold, silver, vessels, and supplies for temple sacrifices, and ordering regional treasurers to assist. Priests and temple servants receive tax exemption. Ezra is commanded to appoint judges and enforce God’s law and the king’s law; he gathers chief men to go with him.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records the genealogy and numbers of families returning with Ezra from Babylon under Artaxerxes. Ezra gathers the group at the river Ahava, finds no Levites, and sends leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites and Nethinims. He proclaims a fast for safe travel, entrusts priests with weighed temple offerings, travels to Jerusalem, weighs the gifts, offers sacrifices, and delivers the king’s commissions to regional governors.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records leaders reporting that Israelites, including priests and Levites, intermarry with surrounding peoples and adopt their practices. Ezra mourns publicly, gathers those who fear God’s words, and prays at the evening sacrifice, confessing national sin and past judgments. He recalls Persian favor in restoring the temple and Judah, cites prophetic commands against such unions, and fears renewed judgment.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Ezra praying and mourning at the house of God as a large assembly in Jerusalem confesses taking foreign wives. Shechaniah proposes a covenant to put away these wives and children; leaders and people swear and a proclamation compels attendance within three days. Ezra appoints officials to investigate city by city, completes the review, and lists priests, Levites, singers, porters, and Israelites who had foreign wives and offer trespass sacrifices.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records Nehemiah in Shushan hearing from Hanani about Jerusalem’s distressed remnant, broken walls, and burned gates. Nehemiah weeps, fasts, and prays to the God of heaven, confessing Israel’s and his family’s sins and disobedience to Moses’ commandments. He appeals to promises of scattering and gathering upon repentance and asks for success and mercy before the king, noting he is the cupbearer.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Nehemiah in Nisan of Artaxerxes’ twentieth year requesting leave to go to Judah to rebuild Jerusalem. The king grants permission, letters for regional governors, and timber from Asaph, and provides an escort. Nehemiah arrives, secretly inspects Jerusalem’s broken walls and burned gates at night, then urges Jews and leaders to rebuild. Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock; Nehemiah rejects their claim in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall and gates, listing workers and assigned sections. Eliashib and priests rebuild and sanctify the sheep gate to the towers of Meah and Hananeel. Groups repair the fish, old, valley, dung, fountain, water, horse, east, and Miphkad gates, plus towers and wall segments by Siloah, David’s sepulchres, Ophel, and the broad wall. The Tekoite nobles refuse to work.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records opposition to Jerusalem’s wall-building by Sanballat, Tobiah, and allied groups who mock, threaten, and conspire to attack. Nehemiah prays, sets watches, stations families with swords, spears, and bows, and urges the people not to fear. The work continues with half laboring and half guarding; builders carry weapons, a trumpeter coordinates gathering, and workers lodge in Jerusalem and stay ready day and night.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records the people’s complaint about famine, debt, mortgages, and children being sold into bondage. Nehemiah rebukes nobles and rulers for usury, calls an assembly, and commands restoration of lands and repayment of interest; the offenders swear an oath before priests. Nehemiah describes his twelve-year governorship in Judah, refusing the governor’s allowance, continuing wall work, feeding many at his table, and praying to be remembered.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem repeatedly inviting Nehemiah to the plain of Ono and sending an open letter accusing him of planning rebellion and kingship. Nehemiah refuses, denies the charges, and prays for strength. Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple, but Nehemiah discerns the plot as hired by Tobiah and Sanballat. The wall is finished in 52 days on the 25th of Elul, and Judah’s nobles exchange letters with Tobiah, who continues intimidation.

This chapter contains 73 verses and records the wall’s completion, appointment of porters, singers, and Levites, and Nehemiah’s assignment of Hanani and Hananiah over Jerusalem with gate and watch rules. It covers Nehemiah’s gathering for genealogical registration and a detailed census list of returnees with Zerubbabel, including families, towns, priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, and Solomon’s servants, totals, animals, offerings, and settlement in cities by the seventh month.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the people assembling at the Water Gate in Jerusalem as Ezra reads the Law on the first day of the seventh month, with Levites explaining it. Nehemiah and Ezra command the people not to mourn but to celebrate and share portions. Leaders learn of the Feast of Booths; the people gather branches and build booths throughout the city. Ezra reads daily, they keep the feast seven days, and hold a solemn assembly on the eighth day.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Israel assembling with fasting, sackcloth, and separation from foreigners, confessing sins, reading the Law, and worshipping. Levites lead a prayer recounting God’s creation, Abraham’s call and covenant, the exodus, Sinai laws and Sabbath, wilderness provision, conquest, and repeated rebellions and deliverances. The prayer acknowledges present distress under foreign kings and concludes with leaders sealing a written covenant.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records the names of priests, Levites, and leaders who seal a covenant. The people swear an oath to keep the law of Moses, avoid intermarriage with surrounding peoples, and not buy or sell on the Sabbath, while observing the seventh-year release of debts. It sets temple support rules: annual shekel, offerings, wood allotments, firstfruits, firstborn, tithes, and treasury administration.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records how rulers live in Jerusalem and the people cast lots to settle one-tenth in Jerusalem, blessing volunteers. It lists chiefs and numbers from Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, gatekeepers, Nethinims, and overseers for temple business, singers, and royal matters. It also names towns and villages in Judah and Benjamin where others dwell, noting Levitical divisions.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records lists of priests and Levites returning with Zerubbabel, genealogies of high priests, and leading families to the reign of Darius. It describes the dedication of Jerusalem’s wall, including purification, two thanksgiving processions on the wall, music, sacrifices, and public rejoicing. It also covers appointing officials over temple storerooms for offerings, firstfruits, and tithes, and organizing singers and gatekeepers.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the public reading of the Law and separation from the mixed multitude; Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem, expels Tobiah from a temple chamber, and restores storage for offerings. He corrects failure to provide Levites’ portions, reestablishes tithes, and appoints treasurers. He enforces Sabbath observance by shutting Jerusalem’s gates. He rebukes intermarriage with Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, expels a priestly relative allied to Sanballat, and organizes priestly duties, wood offerings, and firstfruits.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records King Ahasuerus reigning from India to Ethiopia and holding a 180-day feast for officials and a seven-day feast in Shushan. Queen Vashti holds a women’s feast and refuses the king’s command to appear. Ahasuerus consults Persian and Median princes, and Memucan advises deposing Vashti and issuing an unalterable decree that husbands rule their households; letters go to all provinces in each language.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Ahasuerus seeking virgins to replace Vashti, with officers gathering them to Shushan under Hegai’s custody. It introduces Mordecai the Jew and his adopted cousin Esther, who conceals her identity. Esther gains favor, is taken to the king, and is crowned queen; the king holds Esther’s feast. Mordecai uncovers Bigthan and Teresh’s plot; they are executed and recorded.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records King Ahasuerus promoting Haman and commanding servants to bow to him, while Mordecai refuses. Haman, angered, plans to destroy all Jews in the empire and casts Pur (lots) to set the date. He persuades the king, receives the royal ring, and issues sealed letters to all provinces ordering all Jews killed on the thirteenth day of Adar and their spoil taken; Shushan is perplexed.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Mordecai mourning in sackcloth at the king’s gate after the decree against the Jews, with fasting and lamentation throughout the provinces. Esther sends clothing and then Hatach to learn the cause; Mordecai reports Haman’s payment offer and gives a copy of the decree, urging Esther to plead with the king. Esther cites the law about approaching uncalled. Mordecai warns she will not escape. Esther orders a three-day fast in Shushan and resolves to go to the king; Mordecai complies.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Esther approaching the king in the inner court, receiving favor, and inviting the king and Haman to a banquet, then requesting a second banquet the next day. Haman rejoices at the honor but becomes angry at Mordecai’s refusal to rise. He boasts to friends and Zeresh, who advise building a fifty-cubit gallows to hang Mordecai, and Haman orders it made.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records King Ahasuerus reading the chronicles during sleeplessness and discovering Mordecai’s unrewarded report of Bigthana and Teresh’s plot. Haman enters intending to request Mordecai’s hanging, but is asked how to honor someone the king delights to honor. Haman proposes royal clothing and a public procession; the king orders him to honor Mordecai. Haman obeys, mourns, consults Zeresh and friends, and is summoned to Esther’s banquet.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records Esther hosting Ahasuerus and Haman at a banquet where the king again offers to grant her petition. Esther asks for her life and her people’s, stating they are sold to be destroyed. She identifies Haman as the adversary. The king, enraged, leaves and returns to find Haman fallen on Esther’s bed. Harbonah mentions Haman’s gallows for Mordecai; the king orders Haman hanged there, and his wrath is pacified.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Ahasuerus giving Haman’s estate to Esther and transferring the signet ring to Mordecai, whom Esther appoints over Haman’s house. Esther petitions to counter Haman’s plot, and the king authorizes a new decree. Mordecai drafts letters across 127 provinces (India to Ethiopia) allowing Jews to assemble and defend themselves on Adar 13. Couriers publish the decree from Shushan; Mordecai is honored, Jews rejoice, and many people become Jews.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the Jews defending themselves in Ahasuerus’s provinces on Adar 13–14, killing enemies in Shushan and elsewhere, including Haman’s ten sons, without taking spoil. Esther requests a second day of action in Shushan and the sons’ hanging. The chapter establishes Purim on Adar 14–15 with feasting, sending portions, and gifts to the poor; Mordecai and Esther send confirming letters.

This chapter contains 3 verses and records King Ahasuerus imposing tribute on the land and sea isles, and notes that his deeds and Mordecai’s advancement are written in the chronicles of Media and Persia. It states Mordecai the Jew is second to the king, is esteemed among the Jews, is accepted by his brethren, seeks his people’s welfare, and speaks peace to his descendants.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes Job in Uz as upright and prosperous, with ten children and great livestock, who offers continual burnt offerings for his family. It records a heavenly assembly where the LORD permits Satan to test Job’s possessions. Job then loses oxen, asses, sheep, camels, servants, and his children through raids, fire, and a windstorm. Job mourns, worships, and does not sin or accuse God.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a heavenly council where Satan receives permission to afflict Job’s body but not take his life. Satan strikes Job with sore boils; Job sits in ashes and scrapes himself. Job’s wife urges him to curse God, but Job refuses to sin with his lips. Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar arrive, mourn, and sit silent with him seven days.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Job cursing the day of his birth and wishing that day and night be dark and removed from the calendar. He asks why he did not die at birth, describes death as rest shared by kings, princes, prisoners, and servants, and questions why life is given to the miserable. Job reports continual sighing, fears realized, and unrelieved trouble.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Eliphaz the Temanite’s first reply to Job. He recalls Job’s former encouragement of others, then questions Job’s distress. Eliphaz asserts that the innocent do not perish and that those who sow iniquity reap trouble by God’s breath. He describes a fearful night vision in which a spirit’s voice asks whether any mortal can be more just or pure than God, and states that God mistrusts servants and angels and that fragile humans quickly die.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Eliphaz urging Job to seek God rather than appeal to saints, warning that wrath and envy destroy the foolish and their households. He states trouble is part of human life, describes God’s works in nature and his overthrow of the crafty while helping the poor. Eliphaz says God’s correction should not be despised and promises deliverance, peace, safety, prosperity, and long life to the corrected.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Job’s reply, asking that his grief be weighed and describing God’s arrows and terrors against him. He compares his anguish to unsavory food, wishes God would destroy him, and questions his strength to endure. Job rebukes his friends for failing to show pity, likening them to unreliable brooks sought by Tema and Sheba, and asks them to teach him his error, asserting his integrity.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Job lamenting life’s brief, appointed toil and his months of vanity, sleepless nights, and diseased body. He says his days pass swiftly without hope and that death ends return to home. He resolves to speak and complain to God, describing terrifying dreams, desiring death, and asking why God watches, tests, and targets him, and why his sin is not pardoned.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Bildad rebuking Job’s speech, affirming that God does not pervert justice, and suggesting Job’s children suffered for sin. Bildad urges Job to seek God and be pure so his prosperity increases. He appeals to the wisdom of former generations and uses plant imagery to describe the swift downfall of those who forget God. He states God supports the upright, brings joy, shames enemies, and destroys the wicked.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Job’s reply about humanity’s inability to be just before God or contend with him. Job describes God’s power over creation and wonders beyond understanding. He says God is unseen and unstoppable, and Job cannot answer or plead his case. Job laments suffering, the fate of righteous and wicked, life’s brevity, and seeks a mediator and removal of God’s rod.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Job’s complaint to God, asking not to be condemned and to know why God contends with him. Job questions whether God treats him as a man, searches for sin, and oppresses the work of His hands. He describes God’s forming of his body and granting life, yet now hunting and afflicting him. Job wishes he had died at birth and asks for brief relief before going to darkness and the shadow of death.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Zophar the Naamathite answering Job, rebuking his many words and claim of purity, and wishing God would reveal wisdom and expose his guilt. Zophar states God’s wisdom and power are unsearchable and that God sees wickedness. He urges Job to prepare his heart, pray, and put away iniquity, promising renewed security and peace, while warning the wicked lose hope and escape.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Job’s reply to his friends, rejecting their claims to superior wisdom and describing how the upright can be mocked while robbers prosper. Job points to animals, earth, and sea as witnesses that the LORD controls life and breath. He lists God’s sovereign acts: destroying and rebuilding, withholding and flooding waters, exposing hidden things, and overturning counselors, judges, kings, princes, and nations, causing leaders to wander in darkness.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Job asserting he understands as much as his friends, calling their counsel false, and asking them to be silent. He seeks to speak directly with God, questions speaking deceitfully for God, and says God will reprove partiality. Job maintains his integrity, asks God to withdraw affliction and fear, invites God to answer, and requests knowledge of his sins while describing his suffering.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Job’s speech about human life being brief and troubled, like a flower or shadow. He asks why God judges humans and notes no one brings clean from unclean. He says God sets human limits and pleads for rest. He contrasts a tree’s regrowth with man’s death, questions life after death, asks to be hidden in the grave, and describes God numbering steps, sealing sin, and humans departing unaware of their children, ending in pain and mourning.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Eliphaz’s second speech to Job, accusing him of vain words, casting off fear, and speaking against God. Eliphaz questions Job’s claim to wisdom and asserts human impurity before God. He recounts traditional sayings about the wicked: continual pain, terror, darkness, poverty, and destruction. He describes judgment on those who oppose God, trust vanity, practice bribery, and produce deceit.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Job’s reply to his friends, calling them miserable comforters and challenging their words. Job says he could speak similarly but would instead strengthen them. He describes God as afflicting and targeting him, and people as mocking and attacking him. He laments physical decline, mourns in sackcloth, claims innocence and pure prayer, appeals for his blood and cry to be heard, looks to a heavenly witness, desires an advocate before God, and expects impending death.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Job lamenting his failing strength, nearness to the grave, and being mocked and made a byword. He asks God to provide surety for him and says others lack understanding. He warns against flattering friends, describes sorrow and dim eyes, notes the righteous persist, rebukes his companions as unwise, and speaks of broken purposes, darkness, corruption, worms, lost hope, and descent to the pit.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Bildad the Shuhite replying to Job, challenging his words and protesting being treated as vile. Bildad describes the fate of the wicked: their light is extinguished, strength fails, and they are ensnared by traps and terrors. He lists loss of home, roots, descendants, and remembrance, ending with the dwelling of one who does not know God.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Job’s reply to his friends, accusing them of reproaching and tormenting him. Job says God has overthrown him, blocked his path, removed his honor and hope, and treated him as an enemy. He describes estrangement from relatives, servants, wife, and friends, and his severe physical wasting. Job pleads for pity, asks that his words be permanently recorded, affirms that his redeemer lives and he will see God, and warns of judgment by the sword.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Zophar the Naamathite’s reply to Job. He states that the triumph of the wicked and hypocrite is brief and that they perish and are forgotten. He describes the wicked suffering inward torment, losing ill-gotten riches, and facing poison, weapons, terrors, darkness, and consuming fire. He says heaven and earth expose their iniquity, their children make restitution, and their household increase departs as God’s appointed portion.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Job’s reply urging his friends to listen, then questioning why the wicked often live long, prosper, and reject God while enjoying security and wealth. He challenges claims of swift judgment, notes that people die in differing circumstances yet share the same grave, cites travelers’ observations about delayed reckoning, and concludes his friends’ consolations are false.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Eliphaz’s third speech to Job, arguing that God gains nothing from human righteousness and accusing Job of oppression, withholding aid, and wronging widows and orphans. He links Job’s troubles to sin and cites past wicked people destroyed. Eliphaz urges Job to return to God, receive God’s words, put away iniquity, and promises restored prosperity, answered prayer, and deliverance for the humble and innocent.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Job’s reply that his suffering feels heavier than his groaning. He longs to find God and present his case, expecting an answer. Job searches in every direction but cannot perceive God’s presence. He affirms God knows his path and will try him, and he claims obedience to God’s commandments. Job states God’s purposes stand and He performs what is appointed, which troubles and frightens him amid darkness.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Job questioning why the Almighty’s times and judgments are not seen by those who know him. Job lists injustices by the wicked: removing landmarks, stealing flocks, oppressing widows and orphans, forcing the poor to hunger, thirst, and exposure, and committing murder, adultery, and theft in darkness. He notes their temporary security and eventual death and removal.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records Bildad the Shuhite asserting God’s dominion and fearfulness, and that God makes peace in his high places. He refers to God’s innumerable armies and universal light, questions how a human can be justified or clean before God, and states that even moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Job answering, questioning how his friend has helped the powerless or given true counsel. Job then lists God’s acts of power over creation: forming things under waters, seeing Sheol and destruction, stretching out the heavens and suspending earth, binding waters in clouds, setting bounds for seas and day and night, shaking heaven’s pillars, dividing the sea, and forming the heavens and the crooked serpent.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Job continuing his discourse, swearing by God to maintain integrity and speak no deceit. He refuses to justify his friends’ accusations and holds fast to righteousness. Job questions the hope of the hypocrite when God takes his soul and whether God hears him in trouble. He then describes the portion of the wicked and oppressors: their children face the sword, wealth passes to the just, and sudden terrors, storms, and God’s judgment overtake them.

This chapter contains 28 verses and describes mining for silver, gold, iron, and precious stones, noting human skill in searching hidden places. It asks where wisdom and understanding are found, stating they cannot be bought with gold or jewels and are hidden from living creatures. It records that God alone knows wisdom’s place, having ordered creation, and tells man to fear the Lord and depart from evil.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Job’s lament as he recalls earlier months when God preserved him and his household prospered. He recounts his former public honor at the city gate, where young men and leaders showed deference and listened to his counsel. Job lists past deeds of justice and mercy toward the poor, fatherless, widows, blind, and lame, and opposition to the wicked, describing his former security and leadership.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Job’s lament that younger, outcast men now mock and mistreat him, describing their former destitute life in wilderness caves and rocks. Job reports public scorn, spitting, and attacks, and attributes his affliction to God loosening his cord. He details terror, disease, pain, and mourning, says God does not answer his cries, expects death, recalls pity for the poor, and ends with instruments turned to lamentation.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Job’s oath of integrity. He claims restraint from lust and adultery, honesty over deceit, and fairness to servants. He states he aids the poor, widows, and fatherless, provides clothing, and practices hospitality. He denies trusting wealth, worshiping sun or moon, or rejoicing in enemies’ ruin. He rejects hiding sin, invites God’s judgment, and asserts just treatment of his land and workers.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the three friends ceasing to answer Job, and introduces Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite becoming angry at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer. Elihu explains he waited because of their age, affirms understanding comes from God’s spirit, and resolves to speak impartially without flattery.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Elihu urging Job to listen, claiming to speak uprightly and without terror. Elihu repeats Job’s statements of innocence and complaint that God treats him as an enemy, and replies that God is greater and need not explain. He says God warns through dreams and through pain to restrain pride and save from death, and may send an interpreter to declare uprightness, provide deliverance, restore health, and accept prayer and confession.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Elihu addressing wise men, challenging Job’s claims of righteousness and profitlessness in delighting in God. Elihu asserts God does no wickedness, repays each person according to deeds, shows no partiality, and sees all human ways. He describes God’s power over life, judgment on rulers and evildoers, and hearing the poor. He urges confession and correction, and charges Job with speaking without knowledge and adding rebellion.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Elihu challenging Job’s claim that his righteousness exceeds God’s and that purity brings no profit. Elihu points to the heavens to show God is unaffected by human sin or righteousness, which chiefly impacts other people. He notes oppressed cries and unanswered prayers caused by pride and vanity, states God does not hear empty speech, urges trust in God’s judgment, and says Job speaks vainly without knowledge.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Elihu continuing his speech, claiming to speak for God and affirming God’s might, wisdom, and justice. He says God disciplines the righteous through affliction, calls them to turn from iniquity, and warns that disobedience brings destruction. Elihu cautions Job against relying on riches and urges him to magnify God’s works, describing God’s control of rain, clouds, lightning, the sea, and thunder.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Elihu describing God’s voice and control over lightning, thunder, snow, rain, wind, frost, clouds, and fair weather. He states these events occur by God’s counsel for correction, for the land, or for mercy, and he urges Job to consider God’s works. He asks rhetorical questions about human ignorance and affirms God’s power, justice, and majesty, calling people to fear him.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records the LORD answering Job from a whirlwind, questioning him about creation and governance of the world. God asks about laying earth’s foundations, setting bounds for the sea, commanding morning, and knowledge of death’s gates. It covers light and darkness, snow, hail, rain, ice, and lightning, the stars and constellations, ordinances of heaven, and God’s provision for lions and ravens.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD questioning Job about knowledge and control of animals and nature: the birthing of wild goats and hinds; the freedom and habitat of the wild ass; the strength and untamable service of the unicorn; the wings and nesting of the ostrich; the warhorse’s power and fearlessness in battle; and the flight, nesting, and hunting of the hawk and eagle.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD answering Job, challenging him to contend with the Almighty and uphold judgment. Job responds with humility and silence. The LORD speaks from the whirlwind, questioning Job’s ability to humble the proud and save himself. The chapter describes behemoth’s creation, strength, habits, and dwelling near rivers, including reference to Jordan.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD’s questions to Job about Leviathan, asking whether he can capture, tame, bargain with, or pierce it. It describes Leviathan’s fearsome strength, armor-like scales, teeth, and invulnerability to weapons. It depicts its snorting, fiery breath, and power in sea and deep waters, concluding it has no equal on earth and rules over the proud.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Job answering the LORD, acknowledging God’s power and repenting in dust and ashes. The LORD rebukes Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, commands them to offer seven bullocks and seven rams, and directs Job to pray for them. God restores Job’s fortunes, gives him double possessions, relatives visit with gifts, and Job receives seven sons and three daughters (Jemima, Kezia, Keren-happuch), lives 140 years, and dies old.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes the contrast between the righteous and the ungodly. It states that the blessed person avoids ungodly counsel and delights in the LORD’s law, meditating on it continually. The righteous are compared to a fruitful tree by waters and prosper. The ungodly are compared to chaff, will not stand in judgment or among the righteous, and their way perishes.

This chapter contains 12 verses and describes nations and rulers opposing the LORD and his anointed and seeking to cast off restraint. The LORD in heaven responds with derision and wrath and declares his king set on Zion. A decree addresses the king as God’s Son, promises the nations as inheritance, and authority to shatter opposition. Kings and judges are urged to be wise, serve the LORD, and honor the Son to avoid perishing.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a psalmist’s cry to the LORD amid many adversaries who claim there is no help in God. The psalmist declares the LORD as shield and sustainer, reports being heard from God’s holy hill, sleeps and awakens sustained, refuses fear of surrounding multitudes, asks God to arise and save, describes enemies struck, and affirms salvation and blessing belong to the LORD.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a prayer to God for mercy and an answer in distress, a rebuke to men who pursue vanity and lies, and the assertion that the LORD hears the godly. It commands awe without sinning, self-examination and stillness, righteous sacrifices, and trust in the LORD. It asks for God’s favor, contrasts inner gladness with material increase, and ends with peaceful sleep in safety.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records David’s morning prayer to the LORD, asking to be heard. It contrasts God’s rejection of wickedness, deceit, and bloodshed with the psalmist’s worship toward God’s holy temple. David requests guidance in righteousness because of enemies, describes their lies and corruption, asks God to judge and cast them out, and affirms joy and protection for those who trust God, ending with blessing for the righteous.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for the LORD’s mercy, asking not to be rebuked in anger, requesting healing, deliverance, and salvation. It describes intense grief, tears, and weariness, and notes enemies. The psalmist states the LORD hears weeping and supplication, and commands evildoers to depart, ending with a request that enemies be ashamed and troubled.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a psalmist appealing to the LORD for rescue from persecutors, asserting innocence, and inviting judgment according to righteousness. It calls for God to rise in anger, judge the people, and end wickedness while establishing the just. It describes God as a righteous judge who prepares judgment on the unrepentant, and it states that the wicked fall into their own traps. It ends with praise to the LORD Most High.

This chapter contains 9 verses and describes praise to the LORD whose name is excellent in all the earth and whose glory is above the heavens. It records strength ordained from children to still enemies, reflection on the heavens, moon, and stars, and God’s mindfulness of humanity. It states humans are made slightly lower than angels, crowned with glory, and given dominion over animals, birds, and fish.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records David praising the LORD wholeheartedly for His works, rejoicing in His name, and affirming that God turns back enemies and judges righteously from His throne. It describes the LORD rebuking nations, destroying wickedness and cities, and being a refuge for the oppressed. It calls for praise in Zion, notes God remembers the humble and avenges blood, petitions for mercy and deliverance, and states the wicked are ensnared and nations forget God.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a prayer asking why the LORD seems distant in trouble, describes the wicked’s pride, boasting, deceit, and violence against the poor and innocent, and notes their belief that God will not see or require it. It petitions God to arise, defend the humble and fatherless, break the power of the wicked, and judge oppressors, affirming the LORD as everlasting King.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records the psalmist’s trust in the LORD despite counsel to flee from threats. It describes the wicked preparing to attack the upright and asks what the righteous can do if foundations are destroyed. It states the LORD is in his holy temple with a heavenly throne, observing and testing people. It contrasts the LORD’s regard for the righteous with judgment on the wicked and violent.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a plea for the LORD’s help amid disappearing godly and faithful people, widespread deceitful and flattering speech, and proud claims of self-rule. It states the LORD will cut off flattering lips and arise because of oppression of the poor and needy, setting them in safety. It affirms the purity and preserving power of the LORD’s words and notes wickedness spreading when vile people are exalted.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records David asking the LORD how long he will be forgotten and why God’s face is hidden, describing daily sorrow and an enemy’s exaltation. He petitions God to consider him and “lighten” his eyes to avoid death and prevent enemies from claiming victory. He affirms trust in God’s mercy, rejoices in salvation, and resolves to sing because the LORD deals bountifully with him.

This chapter contains 7 verses and describes the fool denying God and people acting corruptly, with none doing good. The LORD looks from heaven for anyone who understands and seeks God. It records condemnation of workers of iniquity who oppress God’s people and do not call on the LORD, fear among them, and God’s presence with the righteous. It ends with a request for Israel’s salvation from Zion and joy at restored captivity.

This chapter contains 5 verses and describes a question about who may dwell in the LORD’s tabernacle and holy hill, then lists required conduct: walking uprightly, doing righteousness, speaking truth, avoiding slander and harm to neighbors, rejecting vile persons, honoring those who fear the LORD, keeping oaths despite loss, not lending at usury, and refusing bribes against the innocent.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a prayer for God’s preservation and trust in the LORD. The psalmist affirms loyalty to the LORD, delights in the saints, and rejects pursuing other gods and their blood offerings. He calls the LORD his inheritance and secure portion, blesses Him for counsel, and keeps Him always before him. He expresses joy, hope, deliverance from the grave, and guidance in the path of life.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records a plea for the LORD to hear a sincere prayer, judge justly, and examine the speaker’s heart and conduct. The speaker asks for guidance to stay on God’s paths and for protection like the “apple of the eye” from wicked oppressors. Enemies are described as proud and predatory. The speaker requests deliverance and anticipates beholding God’s face in righteousness.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records David’s declaration of love for the LORD as his rock and deliverer. David recounts calling for help in distress and describes the LORD’s dramatic intervention to rescue him from death and enemies. He states he is rewarded for righteousness and keeping God’s statutes. The psalm notes God saves the afflicted, gives strength for battle, grants victory and rule over nations, and ends with thanksgiving and mercy to the king and David’s descendants.

This chapter contains 14 verses and describes the heavens and firmament declaring God’s glory, with the sun’s course spanning the sky. It records statements about the LORD’s law, testimony, statutes, commandment, fear, and judgments as perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, true, and desirable, warning and rewarding the servant. It includes prayers for cleansing from hidden faults, restraint from presumptuous sins, and acceptable words and meditation before the LORD.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a prayer for the LORD to hear and defend in trouble, send help from the sanctuary and Zion, remember offerings, and grant petitions. It states confidence that the LORD saves his anointed and hears from heaven. It contrasts trusting in chariots and horses with trusting the LORD, and ends with a plea for salvation and for the king to hear when called.

This chapter contains 13 verses and describes the king rejoicing in the LORD’s strength and salvation, receiving his desire, blessings, a crown, and length of days. It records that the king trusts in the LORD and is not moved. It covers the LORD finding and judging enemies, destroying their offspring, thwarting evil plans, and driving them back with arrows, ending with praise for the LORD’s power.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records a lament in which the psalmist feels forsaken, cries day and night, recalls Israel’s ancestors being delivered, and describes humiliation, mockery, and enemies likened to bulls, dogs, and a lion. The psalmist pleads for rescue amid physical anguish, pierced hands and feet, and garments divided by lot. It then shifts to praise in the congregation, vows fulfilled, and worldwide worship of the LORD across generations.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes the LORD as a shepherd who provides, leads to green pastures and still waters, restores the soul, and guides in righteous paths. It records confidence in God’s presence and protection in the valley of the shadow of death. It covers God preparing a table before enemies, anointing with oil, overflowing cup, and dwelling in the LORD’s house forever.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records that the earth and its inhabitants belong to the LORD, who founded it on seas and floods. It asks who may ascend the LORD’s hill and stand in his holy place, answering: one with clean hands, a pure heart, and truthful speech. It states such receive blessing and righteousness. It calls gates and everlasting doors to open for the King of glory, identified as the LORD strong in battle and the LORD of hosts.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a psalmist lifting his soul to the LORD, asking not to be ashamed before enemies. He requests instruction in God’s ways, truth, and paths, and asks God to remember mercy and not youthful sins. It states that the LORD teaches sinners and guides the meek, and that mercy and truth attend covenant keepers. The psalmist seeks pardon, deliverance from distress and enemies, preservation in integrity, and redemption for Israel.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for the LORD’s judgment and testing based on integrity and trust. He states he avoids vain people, dissemblers, evildoers, and the wicked, and desires innocence as he approaches the LORD’s altar with thanksgiving. He expresses love for the LORD’s house, asks not to be gathered with sinners or violent, bribery-filled men, and seeks redemption, mercy, and public blessing.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records David’s confidence in the LORD as light, salvation, and strength amid enemies, war, and false witnesses. He desires to dwell in the LORD’s house and seek Him in the temple, expecting protection and exaltation. He prays for mercy, guidance, and deliverance, affirms the LORD will receive him if forsaken, and exhorts waiting on the LORD with courage.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a psalmist crying to the LORD for help and for his voice not to be silent, with hands lifted toward the holy oracle. He asks not to be counted with the wicked and requests judgment on evildoers according to their deeds. He states the LORD hears his supplications, is his strength and shield, and receives praise. He petitions salvation and blessing for God’s people and inheritance.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a call for the mighty to give the LORD glory and worship. It describes the LORD’s voice over waters and thunder, its power and majesty, breaking cedars of Lebanon, making Lebanon and Sirion leap, dividing flames of fire, and shaking the wilderness of Kadesh. It notes temple proclamation of his glory, the LORD reigning over the flood forever, giving strength and peace to his people.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a psalm of praise to the LORD for deliverance from enemies, healing, and preservation from the grave and the pit. The psalmist calls the saints to sing and give thanks, notes that divine anger is brief and favor brings life, and contrasts weeping with morning joy. He recounts trouble when God hides his face, prays for mercy, and describes mourning turned to gladness.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a psalmist’s prayer for deliverance, protection, and guidance, calling the LORD rock and fortress. It describes distress, grief, reproach, slander, and enemies plotting, and includes committing one’s spirit to God and requesting mercy and salvation. It contrasts trust in the LORD with lying vanities, asks that the wicked be shamed, affirms God’s goodness to those who fear Him, and exhorts saints to love the LORD, be courageous, and hope in Him.

This chapter contains 11 verses and describes the blessedness of having sin forgiven and not imputed. It records the psalmist’s distress while concealing sin and relief after confessing to the LORD. It calls the godly to pray in a time of finding, describes God as a hiding place and deliverer, promises instruction and guidance, warns against stubbornness, contrasts sorrows of the wicked with mercy for those trusting the LORD, and exhorts the righteous to rejoice.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes a call for the righteous to rejoice and praise the LORD with song and instruments. It affirms the LORD’s righteous word and works, his creation of heavens and seas, and urges all the earth to fear him. It contrasts human power with divine counsel, notes God’s watch over all people, and trusts his mercy to deliver from death and famine.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records continual praise of the LORD, a call to magnify him, and testimony of being heard and delivered from fears and troubles. It mentions the angel of the LORD protecting those who fear him and urges trust in the LORD. It teaches ethical commands: guard speech, depart from evil, do good, seek peace. It contrasts the LORD’s care for the righteous with judgment on evildoers, and affirms redemption of his servants.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records a plea for the LORD to contend against the psalmist’s adversaries, protect him, and bring shame and downfall on persecutors. It describes enemies laying nets, using false witnesses, repaying evil for good, mocking, and rejoicing at his trouble. The psalmist recalls fasting and mourning for them, asks God to judge righteously, and vows public thanksgiving and continual praise.

This chapter contains 12 verses and describes the wicked person’s lack of fear of God, self-flattery, deceitful speech, and planned mischief. It records praise of the LORD’s mercy, faithfulness, righteousness, judgments, and preservation of man and beast. It covers trusting under God’s protection, satisfaction in his house, and the fountain of life. It includes a prayer for continued lovingkindness, protection from pride and the wicked, and the downfall of evildoers.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records exhortations not to fret over evildoers but to trust in the LORD, do good, commit one’s way to him, and wait patiently. It contrasts the temporary prosperity and ultimate cutting off of the wicked with the preservation, provision, and inheritance of the righteous and meek. It addresses anger, mercy, justice, wisdom, and God’s deliverance of the righteous from plots and violence.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a psalmist’s plea that the LORD not rebuke in wrath, describing affliction, weakness, and wounds attributed to sin. He states that friends and kin stand afar off while enemies set snares and speak deceit. He remains silent before them, declares his iniquity, and expresses sorrow. He hopes the LORD will hear, asks not to be forsaken, and requests swift help and salvation.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a psalmist resolving to guard his speech before the wicked, then praying to the LORD to know the measure of his days and his frailty. It states human life and riches are vanity and uncertain. He places hope in God, asks deliverance from transgressions, and accepts God’s chastening. He petitions for removal of affliction, for God to hear his tears, and to spare him before death.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the psalmist waiting for the LORD, being delivered from distress, and offering praise and testimony in the congregation. It states trust in the LORD over the proud and recounts God’s works. It contrasts sacrifices with doing God’s will and keeping His law in the heart. The psalmist asks for mercy, confesses iniquities, seeks deliverance from enemies, and calls seekers to rejoice.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a blessing on those who consider the poor, with the LORD’s promised deliverance, preservation, and strength in sickness. The psalmist asks for mercy and healing, confessing sin, and reports enemies who slander, conspire, and predict his death. A trusted friend betrays him. The psalmist prays to be raised up, notes the enemy does not triumph, affirms divine upholding, and ends with praise to the LORD God of Israel.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a psalmist thirsting for God amid sorrow and tears, recalling past worship with the multitude at the house of God. The speaker questions a downcast soul, urges hope and future praise, remembers God from the Jordan, Hermon, and Mizar, and describes overwhelming troubles. The psalm includes prayer to God as rock, mentions enemy oppression and taunts, and repeats resolve to praise God.

This chapter contains 5 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for God to judge his cause, deliver him from deceitful, unjust enemies, and explain perceived abandonment amid oppression. He asks for God’s light and truth to lead him to God’s holy hill, tabernacles, and altar, promising praise with a harp. He exhorts his soul to hope in God and anticipate future praise.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Israel recalling God’s past acts in driving out nations and giving the land, confessing trust in God rather than weapons. It laments current defeat, humiliation, scattering among nations, and reproach. The people claim they have not forgotten God or broken the covenant. It asks God to awake, remember their affliction, and rise to help and redeem them.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a poetic song for a king, praising his beauty, speech, warfare, righteousness, and enduring throne, and describing anointing, royal garments, and ivory palaces. It portrays a queen at the king’s right hand in gold of Ophir, calls the bride to leave her father’s house, notes gifts from Tyre, describes her procession into the palace, promises offspring as princes, and lasting remembrance and praise.

This chapter contains 11 verses and describes God as refuge and strength amid earthquakes and roaring seas, and the city of God sustained by a life-giving river and God’s presence. It records nations raging and kingdoms shaken as the LORD speaks. It calls readers to observe the LORD’s works and desolations, states he ends wars worldwide by destroying weapons, commands “Be still,” and repeats that the LORD of hosts, the God of Jacob, is with his people.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a call for all peoples to clap, shout, and sing praises to the LORD as King over all the earth. It states God subdues nations, chooses an inheritance for Jacob, and ascends with a shout and trumpet sound. It affirms God reigns over the nations on a holy throne and that princes gather as the people of Abraham.

This chapter contains 14 verses and describes praise to the LORD in the city of God on mount Zion, where God is known as a refuge. It records assembled kings seeing Zion, being troubled, and fleeing in fear. It mentions ships of Tarshish broken by an east wind, affirms God will establish the city forever, and reflects on lovingkindness in the temple. It commands rejoicing in Judah, surveying Zion’s towers and bulwarks, and declares God as guide unto death.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records a psalm addressed to all people, rich and poor, offering wisdom through a parable. It states that those who trust in wealth cannot redeem another or ransom a soul from death, and that all people die and leave riches behind. It warns against fearing the wealthy, notes the grave’s power, and affirms God redeems the psalmist’s soul. It repeats that honored people without understanding perish like beasts.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records God calling earth from Zion, coming in judgment, and summoning covenant saints. God testifies against Israel, saying he does not need their animals because all creation is his, and commands thanksgiving, vow-keeping, and calling on him for deliverance. He rebukes the wicked for hypocrisy, rejecting instruction, theft, adultery, deceit, and slander, warning of judgment and promising salvation to the upright.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a psalm of confession and petition for mercy, cleansing, and forgiveness of sin. The speaker acknowledges transgressions, asks for a clean heart and renewed spirit, and pleads not to be cast from God’s presence. It mentions teaching sinners, deliverance from bloodguiltiness, and praising God. It contrasts sacrifices with a broken, contrite heart, and prays for Zion and Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a rebuke of a “mighty man” who boasts in mischief, uses deceitful speech, and loves evil and lies. It states that God destroys and removes him from his dwelling and the land of the living. The righteous observe, fear, and mock his misplaced trust in riches. The psalmist trusts God’s mercy, likens himself to an olive tree in God’s house, and vows continual praise and waiting on God’s name.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records a psalm stating that the fool denies God and people act corruptly, with none doing good. God looks from heaven for anyone who understands or seeks Him and finds all turned aside. It mentions workers of iniquity who oppress God’s people and do not call on God, their sudden fear and shame, and a plea for Israel’s salvation from Zion and restoration from captivity.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records a prayer asking God to save and judge the psalmist by His name and strength. The psalmist reports strangers and oppressors seeking his life and not setting God before them. He affirms God as helper and asks that enemies be repaid and cut off. He vows to offer sacrifice and praise God’s name, citing deliverance from trouble and seeing enemies overcome.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for God to hear amid oppression, fear, and threats of death.
