He desires escape, describes violence, strife, deceit, and wickedness in the city, and laments betrayal by a close companion who once worshiped with him. He calls on God for deliverance, prays continually, urges casting burdens on the LORD, and expects judgment on deceitful, violent men.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a plea for God’s mercy amid daily oppression by many enemies. The psalmist declares trust in God when afraid and refuses fear of what humans can do. It describes enemies twisting words, plotting, hiding, and tracking his steps. He asks God to cast down the wicked, notes God’s record of his wanderings and tears, and vows to offer praise for deliverance from death and keeping from falling.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a plea for God’s mercy and refuge during calamities, with trust in God Most High to send help from heaven and deliver from reproach. The psalmist describes enemies as lions with weapon-like teeth and tongues, and mentions nets and pits laid for him. It includes repeated calls for God’s exaltation, and vows to sing, awaken instruments, and praise God among peoples and nations for mercy and truth.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a psalm questioning unjust rulers, accusing them of wickedness, violence, and lying from birth, and comparing them to venomous serpents that refuse correction. It petitions God to destroy their power and make them swiftly vanish. It states the righteous rejoice at vengeance and concludes that God judges the earth and rewards the righteous.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a plea for deliverance from enemies who lie in wait and surround the city, described as returning at evening like dogs. The psalmist asks God of hosts to visit the nations, defend him, and judge wicked transgressors for violent plots, cursing, and lying. He asks that they be scattered and brought down, and concludes with vows to sing of God’s power, mercy, defense, and refuge.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a communal lament asking God to restore and heal the nation after defeat and distress. It mentions a banner for those who fear God and requests deliverance by God’s right hand. God’s proclamation assigns territories: Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, Judah, and speaks of Moab, Edom, and Philistia. It asks who will lead into Edom’s strong city, rejects human help, and affirms victory through God.

This chapter contains 8 verses and describes a psalmist crying to God for help when overwhelmed, asking to be led to a higher rock and recalling God as shelter and strong tower from enemies. The speaker vows to abide in God’s tabernacle and trust under His wings, notes God has heard vows, asks for prolonged life and preservation of the king by mercy and truth, and promises continual praise and daily fulfillment of vows.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a psalm urging the soul to wait for God as rock, salvation, defense, and refuge. It addresses enemies who plot, lie, and seek to cast down a man. It commands the people to trust God and pour out their hearts to him. It warns against trusting in oppression, robbery, or increasing riches, and states God has power and mercy and repays each person according to works.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the psalmist seeking God early, thirsting for him in a dry land, and recalling God’s power seen in the sanctuary. The speaker praises and blesses God with lifted hands, meditates at night, and rejoices in God’s help and protection. Enemies who seek the speaker’s life face death by sword, while the king rejoices in God and liars are silenced.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records a prayer asking God to preserve the speaker from enemies, hidden plots, and slanderous speech. It describes the wicked conspiring, laying secret snares, and searching out iniquities. It states that God strikes them suddenly so their own tongues cause their downfall. It notes people fearing, declaring God’s work, and the righteous rejoicing, trusting in the LORD.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records praise and vow fulfillment to God in Zion, affirming that God hears prayer and all flesh comes to him. It mentions prevailing iniquities and God purging transgressions, and blessing the one chosen to dwell in God’s courts and temple. It describes God’s righteous answers, power over mountains, seas, and peoples, and provision through watering the earth, enriching crops, and filling pastures, valleys, and hills with abundance.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records a call for all lands to praise God and acknowledge his mighty works, including turning the sea into dry land. It affirms God’s rule over nations and urges the rebellious not to exalt themselves. The psalm recounts being tried and afflicted, passing through “fire and water,” and being brought into a prosperous place. The speaker vows to enter God’s house with burnt offerings and to pay vows, then testifies that God hears prayer when iniquity is not cherished.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records a prayer for God’s mercy, blessing, and favor so his way is known on earth among all nations. It calls for all peoples to praise God and for nations to rejoice because he judges righteously and governs the earth. It states the earth yields increase and God blesses his people, leading all ends of the earth to fear him.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records a call for God to scatter enemies and for the righteous to rejoice and sing. It recalls God leading Israel through the wilderness and Sinai, providing rain and help for the poor. It describes fleeing kings, God choosing a dwelling hill, and divine chariots and angels. It mentions ascending and receiving gifts, deliverance from death, defeat of enemies, sanctuary procession, tribes, Jerusalem temple tribute, and nations praising God.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for deliverance from overwhelming trouble, unjust hatred, and reproach, confessing sin and social alienation. He describes fasting, sackcloth, and public mocking, and asks God to hear, redeem, and save him. He calls for judgment on persecutors, including desolation and removal from the book of the living. He vows praise and thanksgiving, and ends with God saving Zion and building Judah’s cities for his servants’ descendants.

This chapter contains 5 verses and records a psalmist’s urgent plea for God to deliver and help quickly. It asks that enemies who seek his life be shamed, confounded, and turned back, including those who mock him. It calls for those who seek God to rejoice, love his salvation, and continually magnify God. The speaker describes being poor and needy and asks the LORD not to delay.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for the LORD’s deliverance and refuge from wicked enemies. The speaker recalls trusting God from youth and from the womb, asks not to be forsaken in old age, and requests that adversaries be confounded. He commits to continual hope and public praise of God’s righteousness and salvation, including praise with psaltery and harp.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records a prayer for the king to receive God’s righteousness to judge the people, defend the poor and needy, and break the oppressor. It describes lasting fear of the LORD, peace, and flourishing righteousness. It covers the king’s dominion from sea to sea, nations and kings bringing gifts (Tarshish, Sheba, Seba), and universal service. It ends with praise to the LORD and a note that David’s prayers are ended.

This chapter contains 28 verses and describes a psalmist who nearly stumbles while envying the prosperity, pride, and violence of the wicked and questioning God’s knowledge. He laments his own chastening, refrains from offending God’s people, and gains understanding in God’s sanctuary about the wicked’s sudden destruction. He confesses ignorance, affirms God’s continual guidance and strength, and resolves to draw near, trust, and declare God’s works.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records a communal lament asking God why he has rejected his people and to remember Zion, the covenant, and the congregation. It describes enemy destruction and desecration of the sanctuary and assemblies, loss of prophetic guidance, and ongoing reproach of God’s name. It recalls God’s past acts of power in creation and deliverance, and petitions for God to arise, defend his cause, and deliver the poor and oppressed.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records thanksgiving to God, declaring his name near and his wondrous works. God states he will judge uprightly when he receives the congregation and that he upholds the earth. The psalm warns fools and the wicked not to exalt themselves, noting promotion does not come from any direction but from God who raises and brings down. It describes God’s cup of judgment for the wicked, vows praise to the God of Jacob, and declares the wicked’s power cut off and the righteous exalted.

This chapter contains 12 verses and describes God being known in Judah and Israel, with his tabernacle in Salem and dwelling in Zion. It records God breaking weapons and defeating stouthearted warriors, horses, and chariots at his rebuke. It covers God’s fearsome anger and heavenly judgment that stills the earth and saves the meek. It commands making and paying vows and bringing presents, and notes God humbling princes and kings.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records a psalmist crying to God in trouble, sleepless and uncomforted, questioning whether God’s mercy and promises have ceased. The speaker resolves to remember and meditate on the LORD’s past works and wonders, describing God’s greatness in the sanctuary and redemption of Jacob and Joseph. It recounts God’s power over waters, storms, thunder, and sea, and leading Israel like a flock by Moses and Aaron.

This chapter contains 72 verses and records a call to teach God’s law and deeds to future generations, recounting Israel’s repeated rebellion and unbelief. It reviews God’s wonders in Egypt and at the sea, guidance by cloud and fire, provision of water, manna, and quail, and judgments in the wilderness. It recounts plagues on Egypt, settlement in Canaan, idolatry, Shiloh’s forsaking, conflict, God’s choice of Judah and Zion, and David’s appointment to shepherd Israel.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a communal lament over heathen invading God’s inheritance, defiling the temple, and destroying Jerusalem with unburied dead. The people report reproach from neighbors and ask how long God’s anger lasts. They request God’s wrath on nations that do not call on his name, forgiveness of former iniquities, deliverance, and vengeance for shed blood. They ask preservation of prisoners and promise perpetual thanks and praise.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a communal plea to the Shepherd of Israel to hear, shine forth, and save, naming Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. It asks God to turn the people again and end anger, describing distress and mockery by enemies. It recalls Israel as a vine brought from Egypt and planted in the land, then laments its devastation, requesting God to visit and restore it and strengthen “the man of thy right hand.”

This chapter contains 16 verses and records a call to sing, use instruments, and blow the trumpet at the new moon and feast as a statute for Israel. It recalls deliverance from Egypt, relief from burdens, and testing at Meribah. God commands Israel to hear and reject strange gods, promising provision. It notes Israel’s refusal, being given to their own counsel, and states that obedience would bring subdued enemies and abundant food.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records God standing in an assembly to judge among rulers called “gods.” He rebukes unjust judgment and partiality toward the wicked, commands defending the poor, fatherless, afflicted, and needy, and delivering them from the wicked. It states the judges lack understanding and walk in darkness. God declares them children of the Most High yet says they will die like men, and calls God to judge the earth and inherit all nations.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a plea for God not to remain silent as enemies plot to destroy Israel. It lists a confederacy of nations (Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistines, Tyre, Assur) and asks God to defeat them as in past battles against Midian, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna. It requests their shame and scattering so God’s name is acknowledged.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a psalm longing for the LORD’s tabernacles and courts, comparing even birds finding nests near the altars. It states blessings on those who dwell in God’s house, draw strength from him, and journey through the valley of Baca to appear in Zion. It includes a prayer to the LORD of hosts, mentions God as shield and his anointed, prefers one day in God’s courts over wicked tents, and blesses those who trust and walk uprightly.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a prayer recalling God’s favor in restoring Jacob’s captivity, forgiving sin, and removing wrath. It petitions God to turn and revive the people, end anger, show mercy, and grant salvation. The psalmist listens for God’s word of peace, warns against returning to folly, and states salvation is near those who fear him, bringing glory to the land; it mentions mercy, truth, righteousness, peace, and promised increase.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records David’s prayer for God to hear, preserve, and show mercy to a poor and needy servant who trusts in him. It affirms God’s goodness, forgiveness, and uniqueness above other gods, and anticipates all nations worshiping him. The psalm asks for instruction to walk in God’s truth, offers praise, mentions deliverance from death, and seeks help against proud and violent enemies, requesting a confirming sign.

This chapter contains 7 verses and describes Zion, the city of God, founded on holy mountains and loved by the LORD above other dwellings of Jacob. It records that glorious things are spoken of Zion and lists Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia in connection with people said to be born there. It states the LORD establishes Zion and counts people by birthplace, and mentions singers and musicians with their springs in Zion.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a psalmist crying to the LORD for help amid severe trouble, feeling near death and the grave. He describes being placed in darkness, overwhelmed by wrath, and cut off from strength and community. He prays daily, questions whether the dead can praise God or know his wonders, and asks why God seems to reject him and hide his face.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records praise for the LORD’s mercy, faithfulness, power over creation, and rule in the assembly of the saints. It recounts God’s covenant and oath to David, promises to establish his seed and throne, protect him, and discipline disobedient children without breaking the covenant. It then laments the anointed king’s humiliation, enemies’ triumph, and asks how long God’s wrath will last, ending with a blessing.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a prayer addressing the LORD as an eternal dwelling place and God from everlasting. It contrasts God’s eternity with human mortality, describing life’s brevity, divine anger over iniquity, and years of labor and sorrow. It asks for wisdom to number days, for the LORD to return with mercy, for gladness after affliction, for God’s work and glory to appear, and for the work of their hands to be established.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes trust in the LORD as refuge and fortress, with promised protection from snares, pestilence, terror, and destruction. It states that the faithful need not fear, will witness the wicked’s reward, and will be kept from evil and plagues. It records angels being charged to guard and uphold them, victory over dangerous beasts, and God’s promises to deliver, answer prayer, be present in trouble, honor, and grant long life and salvation.

This chapter contains 15 verses and describes giving thanks and singing praises to the LORD Most High, declaring his lovingkindness and faithfulness with musical instruments. It records joy in God’s works, contrasts the fool’s ignorance with God’s greatness, and states the wicked flourish briefly but perish. It covers the exaltation and anointing of the speaker, the scattering of enemies, and the flourishing of the righteous in God’s house, showing the LORD’s uprightness and rocklike reliability.

This chapter contains 5 verses and describes the LORD reigning in majesty and strength, establishing the world and an everlasting throne. It records imagery of floods and sea waves rising, and states the LORD on high is mightier than many waters. It affirms the LORD’s testimonies are sure and that holiness befits his house forever.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records a plea for the LORD, judge of the earth, to avenge oppression by the wicked who afflict God’s people and murder the vulnerable. It states God hears, sees, and knows human thoughts, and corrects and teaches through his law. It affirms the LORD will not forsake his inheritance, supports the psalmist in distress, and will cut off evildoers by returning their iniquity on them.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a call to sing, give thanks, and worship the LORD as creator and king over earth and sea. It identifies Israel as his people and sheep, urges hearing his voice, and warns against hardening the heart like the wilderness provocation. It recalls forty years of grief and God’s oath that the disobedient generation will not enter his rest.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a call for all the earth to sing a new song to the LORD, bless his name, and declare his salvation, glory, and wonders among the nations. It contrasts idols with the LORD as Creator, urges giving him glory with offerings and worship in his courts, proclaims his reign, and anticipates his righteous judgment of the world.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records the LORD reigning over the earth, with clouds, fire, lightning, and trembling creation displaying his righteousness and judgment. It calls idolaters to be confounded and all gods to worship him. Zion and Judah rejoice at his judgments. The psalm states his exaltation above all gods, commands those who love the LORD to hate evil, and notes his deliverance of saints, light for the righteous, and thanksgiving for his holiness.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a call to sing a new song to the LORD for his victory, salvation, and righteousness shown openly, and for his mercy and truth toward Israel seen by all the earth. It commands all the earth to rejoice and praise with song, harp, trumpets, and cornet, and summons sea, world, floods, and hills to join. It states the LORD comes to judge the earth in righteousness and equity.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a call to fear, exalt, and worship the LORD who reigns between the cherubims and is great in Zion. It states his name is holy and that he establishes equity, judgment, and righteousness in Jacob. It mentions Moses, Aaron, and Samuel calling on the LORD and being answered, receiving testimonies and ordinances in the cloudy pillar, with forgiveness and vengeance.

This chapter contains 5 verses and records a call for all lands to make a joyful noise to the LORD, serve him with gladness, and come before him with singing. It states that the LORD is God who made his people, described as sheep of his pasture. It commands entering his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise, being thankful and blessing his name, and affirms his goodness, everlasting mercy, and enduring truth.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a psalmist’s resolve to sing to the LORD of mercy and judgment, to live wisely with integrity at home, and to reject wickedness. It states refusal to tolerate slander, pride, deceit, and lying, while favoring the faithful and upright to dwell and serve. It declares intent to cut off the wicked from the land and from the city of the LORD.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for the LORD to hear amid trouble, loneliness, physical wasting, and enemies’ reproach. It contrasts the psalmist’s frailty with the LORD’s enduring remembrance, asks for mercy on Zion, and anticipates the LORD building Zion and being praised in Jerusalem by gathered peoples. It notes God hears prisoners and the destitute, affirms God as Creator, and states his unchanging years and servants’ descendants continuing.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a psalm calling the soul to bless the LORD and remember his benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, and mercy. It states God executes righteousness for the oppressed, reveals his ways to Moses and Israel, and is merciful and slow to anger. It contrasts human frailty with everlasting mercy to covenant keepers, affirms God’s heavenly throne, and summons angels, hosts, and all works to bless him.

This chapter contains 35 verses and describes a psalm blessing the LORD for creation and providence: light, heavens, clouds, angels, earth’s foundations, and waters’ boundaries. It covers springs, plants, food, trees (cedars of Lebanon), animals and birds, seasons by moon and sun, day and night activity, the sea with ships and leviathan, and God giving life and breath. It records vows to sing, and a request that sinners and the wicked be removed.

This chapter contains 45 verses and records a call to thank, sing to, and seek the LORD, and to remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob promising Canaan. It recounts Israel’s travels, divine protection, the famine and Joseph’s rise in Egypt, Israel’s growth and oppression, Moses and Aaron, the plagues, and the exodus with provision of cloud, fire, quail, manna, and water. It ends with Israel receiving nations’ lands to keep God’s statutes and laws.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records a call to praise and thanksgiving, confession of Israel’s sin, and a review of rebellions from Egypt onward: provoking at the Red Sea, craving in the wilderness, envy of Moses and Aaron (Dathan and Abiram), the golden calf at Horeb, despising the land, Baal-peor and the plague stopped by Phinehas, and strife waters affecting Moses. It covers idolatry in Canaan, oppression, repeated deliverance, covenant mercy, and a plea for gathering from nations.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records a call to thank the LORD and for the redeemed to testify of deliverance and gathering from many lands. It recounts four trouble-and-rescue scenes: wanderers led to a city, prisoners freed, the sick healed by his word, and sailors saved from storms. It urges thanksgiving sacrifices and public praise, describes God changing lands and humbling princes, exalting the poor, and ends by urging wise observation of his lovingkindness.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a psalm of praise and resolve to sing to the LORD among peoples and nations, exalting God’s mercy and truth. It petitions God to save and answer, that the beloved are delivered. It cites God’s declaration of possession over Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, and dominion over Moab, Edom, and Philistia, asking for leadership in battle and help against enemies.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for God to answer enemies who speak lies and repay good with evil. He asks judgment on an adversary, including condemnation, loss of office, shortened days, and calamity on his household. He describes his own poverty, fasting, weakness, and reproach, and prays for deliverance, vindication, and shame on adversaries, promising public praise to the LORD who helps the poor.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records the LORD addressing “my Lord” to sit at His right hand until enemies become a footstool. It covers strength sent from Zion to rule among enemies, willing people in the day of power, and an oath appointing a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. It also describes striking kings, judging nations, and lifting up the head after drinking from a brook.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records a call to praise the LORD in the congregation, recounting his great works, enduring righteousness, grace, and compassion. It mentions provision for those who fear him, remembrance of his covenant, and giving Israel a heritage. It affirms the truth and permanence of God’s works and commandments, notes redemption sent to his people, and states that fearing the LORD begins wisdom.

This chapter contains 10 verses and describes the blessings and stability of the man who fears the LORD and delights in his commandments, including blessed descendants, enduring righteousness, and provision. It records his compassion, lending, generosity to the poor, and steadfast trust without fear of evil reports. It contrasts this with the wicked, who grieve, gnash their teeth, melt away, and whose desires perish.

This chapter contains 9 verses and describes calls for the LORD’s servants to praise the LORD’s name continually and worldwide. It states the LORD is exalted above nations and the heavens, yet looks on heaven and earth. It records actions attributed to the LORD: raising the poor and needy from low estate to sit with princes, and giving the barren woman a household and children.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Israel’s exodus from Egypt, with Judah called the Lord’s sanctuary and Israel his dominion. It describes the sea fleeing, the Jordan turning back, and mountains and hills skipping. It asks why these events occur and commands the earth to tremble at the presence of the Lord, who turns rock and flint into waters.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a call to give glory to the LORD for mercy and truth, answers taunts about God by affirming his heavenly sovereignty, and contrasts him with powerless human-made idols. It urges Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD to trust him as help and shield. It states God will remember and bless them, increase their descendants, and notes the dead do not praise the LORD, but the living will bless him forever.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a psalmist’s love for the LORD for hearing prayer and delivering him from death, trouble, tears, and falling. He calls on the LORD for rescue, affirms God’s mercy and preservation of the lowly, and resolves to walk before the LORD. He asks what to render, takes the cup of salvation, offers thanksgiving, and pays vows publicly in Jerusalem’s courts, noting the LORD’s regard for the death of his saints.

This chapter contains 2 verses and records a call for all nations and peoples to praise the LORD. It gives reasons for praise: the LORD’s merciful kindness is great toward the speaker’s community, and the LORD’s truth endures forever, concluding with “Praise ye the LORD.”

This chapter contains 29 verses and records a call for Israel, Aaron’s house, and those who fear the LORD to give thanks for enduring mercy. The psalmist recounts deliverance from distress and surrounding nations, urges trust in the LORD over man or princes, and praises divine strength and chastening. It mentions gates of righteousness, the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, petitions for salvation and prosperity, blessing one coming in the LORD’s name, and sacrifice at the altar.

This chapter contains 176 verses and records an extended prayer and meditation on the LORD’s law, word, statutes, commandments, and judgments. The psalmist declares blessing for obedience, commits to keep God’s precepts, and asks for teaching, understanding, and strength. It mentions affliction, reproach, oppression, and persecution by the proud and wicked, and requests deliverance, mercy, and salvation while continuing praise and meditation.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records a psalmist crying to the LORD in distress and being heard, asking deliverance from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. It declares judgment imagery against the false tongue with sharp arrows and coals of juniper, laments dwelling among hostile peoples in Meshech and the tents of Kedar, and contrasts the speaker’s desire for peace with others’ preference for war.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a speaker lifting eyes to the hills and stating help comes from the LORD, maker of heaven and earth. It says the LORD keeps the worshiper and Israel, does not slumber or sleep, and prevents the foot from being moved. It describes the LORD as shade and protection from sun and moon, preserving from evil, guarding the soul, and keeping going out and coming in forever.

This chapter contains 9 verses and describes rejoicing at going to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, standing within its gates, and noting Jerusalem’s unified structure. It records tribes going up to give thanks, mentions thrones of judgment of the house of David, commands prayer for Jerusalem’s peace, and seeks peace and prosperity within its walls for companions’ sake and for the LORD’s house.

This chapter contains 4 verses and records a psalmist lifting eyes to the LORD in heaven, comparing Israel’s watchfulness to servants looking to masters for direction, and pleading repeatedly for mercy. It states the speaker’s soul is filled with contempt and scorn from those at ease and from the proud.

This chapter contains 8 verses and describes Israel acknowledging the LORD’s aid if enemies had risen against them, using images of being swallowed, overwhelmed by waters, and taken as prey. It blesses the LORD for not giving them to their foes, compares deliverance to a bird escaping a broken snare, and concludes that help is in the LORD who made heaven and earth.

This chapter contains 5 verses and records assurances that those who trust in the LORD are secure like Mount Zion, with the LORD surrounding his people as mountains surround Jerusalem. It states the wicked will not permanently rule over the righteous. It asks the LORD to do good to the upright, and declares that those who turn to crooked ways are led away with evildoers, while peace rests on Israel.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes Zion’s restored captivity bringing laughter and singing, with surrounding nations acknowledging the LORD’s deeds. It records Israel’s gladness and a prayer for further restoration like streams in the south. It states that those who sow in tears reap in joy, and one who weeps while bearing seed returns rejoicing with sheaves.

This chapter contains 5 verses and describes reliance on the LORD for building a house and guarding a city, stating human labor and vigilance are vain without him. It notes the futility of anxious toil and says he gives sleep to his beloved. It calls children a heritage and reward from the LORD, compares them to arrows, and mentions a full “quiver” brings confidence when facing enemies in the gate.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes blessings promised to those who fear the LORD and walk in his ways: enjoying the labor of their hands, a fruitful wife, and children like olive plants around the table. It records blessing from Zion, seeing Jerusalem’s good all one’s days, seeing grandchildren, and peace upon Israel.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Israel recounting repeated affliction from youth and survival despite oppression. It states the LORD is righteous and cuts the cords of the wicked. It calls for those who hate Zion to be confounded and turned back, compared to withering rooftop grass. It says such enemies gain no harvest or blessing from passersby.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records a psalmist crying to the LORD from “the depths,” asking God to hear his supplications. It states that if God marked iniquities none could stand, but forgiveness is with the LORD. The speaker waits for the LORD and hopes in his word. Israel is urged to hope in the LORD for mercy, redemption, and deliverance from iniquities.

This chapter contains 3 verses and describes the psalmist denying pride and lofty ambitions, stating he quiets his soul like a weaned child with its mother, and exhorting Israel to hope in the LORD from now and forever.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a prayer for the LORD to remember David’s afflictions and vow to find a dwelling place for God and the ark. It mentions hearing of it at Ephratah and going to worship at God’s footstool. It asks for righteous priests and joyful saints. It recounts God’s oath to David about his descendants’ throne if they keep the covenant. It states the LORD chooses Zion as his resting place, promises provision, salvation for priests, strength for David’s anointed, and shame for enemies.

This chapter contains 3 verses and describes brethren dwelling together in unity, comparing it to precious anointing oil flowing from Aaron’s head and beard to his garments and to the dew of Hermon descending on the mountains of Zion, and stating that the LORD commands blessing and life for evermore there.

This chapter contains 3 verses and records an exhortation to the LORD’s servants who stand by night in the house of the LORD to bless the LORD, lift up their hands in the sanctuary, and bless him. It states that the LORD, maker of heaven and earth, blesses the worshipers out of Zion.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes calls for the LORD’s servants to praise him in his house, citing his choosing of Jacob and supremacy over other gods. It records his power over creation and weather, his smiting Egypt’s firstborn, and judgments on Pharaoh. It lists defeats of Sihon and Og and the gift of Canaan to Israel. It contrasts lifeless idols with the LORD, and calls Israel, Aaron, Levi, and Zion/Jerusalem to bless him.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records repeated calls to give thanks to the LORD, the God of gods and Lord of lords, for enduring mercy. It recounts his works in creation (heavens, earth, lights) and redemption history: Egypt’s firstborn struck, Israel delivered, the Red Sea divided, Pharaoh overthrown, wilderness leading, kings Sihon and Og defeated, land given to Israel, remembrance in low estate, deliverance from enemies, and provision of food.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records the exiles’ weeping by Babylon’s rivers as they remember Zion, hanging their harps and refusing captors’ demands to sing. It vows never to forget Jerusalem, invoking loss of skill and speech if they do. It asks the LORD to remember Edom’s role in Jerusalem’s fall, and it pronounces judgment on Babylon, calling for repayment and violence against its children.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records David praising the LORD with his whole heart, worshiping toward the holy temple, and thanking God for lovingkindness, truth, and answering prayer with strength. It states that kings of the earth praise the LORD upon hearing his words. It notes God regards the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance, delivers in trouble, opposes enemies, and completes what concerns the psalmist.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records David stating that the LORD fully knows his actions, thoughts, words, and ways, and that no place—heaven, Sheol, sea, or darkness—hides him from God’s presence. It covers God’s role in forming him in the womb and knowing his days. David asks God to judge the wicked, separates from violent men, and prays for God to search his heart and lead him in the everlasting way.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a prayer asking the LORD to deliver and preserve the speaker from evil, violent, and proud men who plot war, use deceitful speech, and set snares and nets. The speaker asks God to hear supplications, deny the wicked their desires, and let their words bring judgment by fire and pits. It affirms the LORD defends the afflicted and poor, and that the righteous give thanks and dwell in God’s presence.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records David crying to the LORD for swift attention, comparing prayer to incense and uplifted hands to evening sacrifice. He asks for restraint over his speech and protection from evil desires and association with evildoers. He accepts rebuke from the righteous, describes hardship and danger, trusts God for deliverance from snares, and asks that the wicked fall into their own nets while he escapes.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records a psalmist crying to the LORD with supplication, pouring out complaint and trouble. He says his spirit is overwhelmed, enemies set a snare, and no one offers refuge or care. He declares the LORD as his refuge and portion, asks God to attend his cry, and seeks deliverance from stronger persecutors. He asks to be brought out of prison to praise, expecting the righteous to surround him.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a psalmist’s plea for the LORD to hear his prayer, show faithfulness and righteousness, and not enter judgment. He describes persecution by enemies, despair, and dwelling in darkness, then recalls God’s past works. He asks for quick deliverance, guidance in the right way, teaching to do God’s will, leading into uprightness, reviving from trouble, and cutting off his enemies.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records David blessing the LORD as strength for battle, fortress, and deliverer, and noting human frailty. He petitions God to come down, use lightning and arrows, and rescue him from “strange children” who speak vanity and falsehood. He vows to sing a new song with instruments, mentions God giving salvation to kings, and prays for national prosperity, security, strong families, abundant stores, and peace, calling blessed the people whose God is the LORD.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records David’s continual praise of the LORD as king, urging daily blessing of his name and declaring his unsearchable greatness. It recounts God’s mighty acts, goodness, righteousness, mercy, and compassion. It covers proclamation of God’s everlasting kingdom, his help for the fallen, provision of food, and satisfaction of living creatures. It states God hears those who call in truth, saves those who fear him, preserves those who love him, and destroys the wicked.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records a call to praise the LORD continually. It warns against trusting princes or mortals whose life and plans end at death. It states that those who hope in the God of Jacob are helped by the Creator. It lists the LORD’s acts: keeping truth, judging for the oppressed, feeding the hungry, freeing prisoners, giving sight, raising the bowed down, loving the righteous, preserving strangers, aiding widows and orphans, and overthrowing the wicked, and affirms his eternal reign in Zion.

This chapter contains 20 verses and describes calls to praise the LORD for rebuilding Jerusalem, gathering Israel’s outcasts, and healing the brokenhearted. It records God’s power in numbering stars, lifting the meek, and casting down the wicked. It covers providence in clouds, rain, grass, and feeding animals. It notes blessing Zion with security, peace, and wheat, and God’s swift word governing snow, frost, ice, wind, and waters, plus statutes given to Jacob and Israel.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records a call for all creation to praise the LORD: beings in heaven (angels, hosts, sun, moon, stars, highest heavens, waters above) and on earth (sea creatures, deeps, weather, mountains, trees, animals, rulers, and all people). It states God creates and establishes these by command and decree, and exalts the horn of his people, the children of Israel.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a call for the congregation of saints, Israel, and Zion to praise the LORD with a new song, rejoicing in their Maker and King, using dance, timbrel, and harp. It states the LORD delights in his people and grants salvation to the meek. It describes saints praising while armed with a two-edged sword to execute vengeance and written judgment on nations, binding kings and nobles.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records a call to praise the LORD in his sanctuary and in the firmament, for his mighty acts and greatness. It lists instruments for praise, including trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, dance, stringed instruments, organs, and loud and high-sounding cymbals. It commands everything with breath to praise the LORD.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Solomon’s proverbs’ purpose: gaining wisdom, instruction, justice, and understanding, with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge. It commands a son to heed parents and refuse sinners who entice to violence and greedy gain. Wisdom publicly calls in streets and gates, urges repentance, warns that rejecters face calamity and unanswered cries, while hearers dwell safely.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a father’s exhortation to seek wisdom and understanding diligently, promising knowledge of the LORD and discernment of righteousness. It states that the LORD gives wisdom and protects the upright. Wisdom and discretion deliver from evil men who choose darkness and from the strange woman who flatters and leads to death. The chapter contrasts outcomes: upright remain in the land; wicked are cut off.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records a father’s counsel to keep commandments, show mercy and truth, trust and fear the LORD, honor him with firstfruits, and accept his correction. It praises wisdom and understanding as superior to riches and linked with life and peace, and notes God’s creation by wisdom. It urges discretion, freedom from fear, doing good promptly, avoiding harm, strife, envy, and contrasts outcomes for righteous, wicked, lowly, scorners, wise, and fools.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records a father’s instruction to seek wisdom and understanding, retain commandments, and hold fast to discipline for life and health. It warns against entering the path of the wicked, describing their violence and darkness, and contrasts it with the growing light of the just. It commands guarding the heart, rejecting perverse speech, keeping focused eyes, weighing one’s steps, and turning away from evil.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records a father’s warning to heed wisdom and avoid the “strange woman,” whose end leads to bitterness, loss, and death. It urges staying far from her house to prevent giving honor, years, and wealth to others and later mourning. It counsels marital faithfulness, rejoicing with one’s wife, and avoiding adultery, noting the LORD observes all paths and sin ensnares the wicked.

This chapter contains 35 verses and covers warnings against becoming surety and urges urgent release from such pledges; rebukes sloth using the ant as an example and warns poverty follows laziness; describes traits and fate of a wicked man and lists seven things the LORD hates. It commands keeping parents’ instruction and warns against the immoral woman, lust, and adultery, describing severe consequences and jealous retaliation.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records a father urging his son to keep commandments and cling to wisdom and understanding to avoid the “strange woman.” He observes a naive youth going near her house at night, and a seductive woman flatters, kisses, and invites him to her perfumed bed, saying her husband is away. The youth yields and follows, facing ruin. The chapter warns not to turn aside to her paths; many fall, and her house leads to death.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Wisdom personified calling publicly for people to listen, value instruction above riches, and speak truth. Wisdom claims prudence, counsel, strength, and a role in kings and rulers administering justice. It promises lasting riches and righteousness to seekers. Wisdom describes being with the LORD before creation and present at forming the world. The chapter blesses those who keep Wisdom’s ways and warns that rejecting Wisdom brings harm and death.

This chapter contains 18 verses and describes Wisdom building a house, preparing a feast, and calling the simple to eat, forsake folly, and walk in understanding. It contrasts responses to reproof from scorners and wise people, states that fear of the LORD begins wisdom, and notes wisdom lengthens life. It also depicts a clamorous foolish woman enticing the simple with secret pleasures, leading to death.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Solomon’s proverbs contrasting the righteous and the wicked, and the wise and the foolish. It covers diligence versus sloth, honest labor and wealth, upright conduct, receiving instruction, and consequences of hatred, lying, slander, and excessive speech. It describes the righteous mouth as life-giving and wise, notes the LORD’s blessing, and contrasts lasting security and hope for the righteous with ruin for the wicked.

This chapter contains 31 verses and covers proverbs contrasting righteousness and wickedness, including honest weights, humility versus pride, integrity, and the limits of riches. It records counsel on speech and community life: avoiding hypocrisy, despising neighbors, tale-bearing, and withholding counsel. It addresses surety, mercy versus cruelty, generosity versus hoarding, seeking good, trusting riches, household conduct, and the recompense of righteous and sinners.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records proverbs contrasting the righteous and the wicked regarding teachability, divine favor, stability, marriage, speech, work, and outcomes. It addresses truth versus lying, wise counsel versus self-rightness, prudence versus wrath, diligence versus sloth, stewardship of animals, and the effects of words. It notes consequences for wicked plans and deceit, and states that righteousness leads to life.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records proverbs contrasting the wise and the foolish, righteous and wicked. It covers heeding parental instruction, guarding speech, diligence versus sloth, honesty, and pride causing contention. It addresses wealth and poverty, labor versus vanity, hope deferred, fearing commandments, and wise counsel. It notes effects of companions, faithful messengers, accepting reproof, inheritance, discipline of children, and provision for the righteous.

This chapter contains 35 verses and covers proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly in speech, anger, work, and decision-making. It addresses uprightness and fear of the LORD versus perversity, deceit, and pride; warns of ways that seem right but end in death; and notes hidden sorrow and personal joys. It treats true and false witnesses, mercy to the poor, justice, kings and subjects, riches and poverty, envy, and national righteousness.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records proverbs contrasting wise and foolish speech, including soft answers, truthful tongues, and timely words. It states the LORD sees all, rejects wicked sacrifices and thoughts, and hears the righteous. It commends receiving reproof, seeking counsel, diligence, humility, and fear of the LORD, contrasting pride, greed, wrath, sloth, and scorn. It notes contentment, love in the home, and joy versus sorrow.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records proverbs about the LORD’s sovereignty over plans, speech, steps, and lots; self-judgment versus God weighing spirits; committing works to the LORD; pride, humility, mercy, truth, and fearing the LORD. It addresses righteousness, honest weights, and the conduct of kings. It contrasts wisdom with riches, warns of seemingly right paths ending in death, and condemns strife, gossip, violence, and deceit; it commends patience and self-control.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records proverbs contrasting peace with strife, wisdom with folly, and truthful speech with lying tongues. It notes God tries hearts, condemns justifying the wicked, and warns against mocking the poor, rewarding evil for good, bribery, rebellion, and surety. It covers friendship and family themes, including children and grandchildren, foolish sons, mercy in covering transgression, timely reproof, and the value of restrained speech.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly, warning against isolation, sloth, talebearing, hasty answers, pride, and biased judgment. It describes the effects of speech, stating the tongue’s power over life and death. It notes the LORD as refuge, wealth as false security, gifts opening access, lots settling disputes, offended brothers and conflict, marriage as good, rich and poor responses, and friendship.

This chapter contains 29 verses and covers proverbs contrasting integrity with deceit, and wisdom with haste, anger, and folly. It addresses effects of wealth and poverty on friendships, and warns that false witnesses and liars face punishment. It notes kings’ wrath and favor, family troubles from a foolish son and contentious wife, and the value of a prudent wife. It commands keeping commandments, showing pity to the poor, disciplining children, receiving counsel, avoiding sloth, honoring parents, and warns of judgment for scorners and fools.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records proverbs warning against drunkenness, provoking rulers, strife, laziness, and deceit. It addresses drawing out counsel, integrity’s effect on children, and the limits of human purity. It condemns dishonest weights, gossip, and cursing parents, and warns about hasty inheritance, vows, and repaying evil. It notes God’s sovereignty over steps, kings’ justice, mercy and truth, youth and age, and discipline.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records proverbs about the LORD directing the king’s heart and weighing motives, and that justice is preferred over sacrifice. It contrasts diligence with haste, honesty with deceit, and wisdom with folly, warning against pride, sloth, greed, false witness, and refusing the poor. It addresses contentiousness in the home, guarding speech, and concludes that no counsel prevails against the LORD and safety comes from him.

This chapter contains 29 verses and covers proverbs on valuing a good name over riches, God as maker of rich and poor, prudence, humility, avoiding froward ways, child training and discipline, debt and oppression, generosity to the poor, removing scoffers, purity of speech, laziness, adultery temptation, heeding wise counsel, protecting the poor in court, avoiding angry companions, not guaranteeing debts, keeping ancient landmarks, and diligence rewarded before kings.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records counsel on self-control when dining with rulers, avoiding greed and unstable riches, and refusing food from the envious. It warns against speaking to fools, moving landmarks, and oppressing the fatherless. It urges instruction, correcting children, fearing the LORD, and avoiding envy. It cautions against drunkenness, gluttony, and sexual immorality, and describes the effects of wine addiction.

This chapter contains 34 verses and covers sayings warning against envy of evil men, valuing wisdom, counsel, and perseverance in adversity, and urging rescue of the endangered with accountability to God. It compares honey to wisdom’s reward, forbids ambushing the righteous, and warns against gloating over an enemy’s fall. It instructs fearing the LORD and the king, condemns partiality and оправдание of the wicked in judgment, urges truthful speech and planning work before building, forbids false witness and retaliation, and describes sloth leading to poverty.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records proverbs of Solomon copied by Hezekiah’s men, covering God concealing matters, kings searching them out, removing dross and wickedness, humility before rulers, avoiding hasty strife and gossip, wise speech and correction, faithful messengers, false boasting, patience and gentle words, moderation, respecting neighbors’ space, harms of false witness and unfaithful allies, kindness to enemies, curbing backbiting, domestic contention, good news from afar, compromise before the wicked, and self-control.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records proverbs about fools, warning that honor and responsibility do not fit them and that folly repeats. It gives paired counsel about answering a fool, and cautions against meddling in others’ strife. It describes the sluggard’s excuses and self-conceit. It addresses deception, “joking” harm, talebearing and contention, hidden hatred, lying and flattering speech, and consequences that return on wrongdoers.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records proverbs warning against boasting and self-praise, comparing wrath, anger, and envy, and commending open rebuke and faithful friendship. It contrasts hunger and satiety, advises staying in one’s place, valuing neighbors, and practicing prudence. It warns about surety, loud early blessings, contention, and insatiable desire. It notes sharpening influence, diligence, and teaches careful stewardship of flocks because riches fade.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records proverbs contrasting wicked and righteous conduct, including courage, justice, and leadership. It addresses keeping or forsaking the law, understanding judgment, confession of sin, and fearing God. It warns against oppression, usury, covetousness, partiality, flattery, pride, and self-trust, and commends uprightness, diligence, faithfulness, rebuke, and giving to the poor, noting outcomes for rulers and societies.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records proverbs on responding to reproof, effects of righteous or wicked rulers, loving wisdom versus immorality, just judgment versus bribery, dangers of flattery and snares of sin, care for the poor, scorners stirring trouble, handling fools and anger, restraint in speech, rulers listening to lies, discipline of children and servants, pride versus humility, partnership with thieves, fear of man versus trusting the LORD, and mutual abhorrence between just and unjust.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the words of Agur to Ithiel and Ucal, his humility and questions about the Creator, and statements about God’s pure words. Agur prays for honesty and moderated provision, warns against falsely accusing a servant, and lists corrupt generations. It gives numerical sayings on insatiable things, consequences for dishonoring parents, wonders in nature, adultery, social upheavals, small wise creatures, dignified movers, and ends warning against pride and wrath that produces strife.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records King Lemuel’s sayings taught by his mother: warnings against giving strength to women and against kings drinking wine or strong drink, with counsel to defend the afflicted and plead for the poor and needy. It also describes an exemplary virtuous woman—trustworthy wife, diligent worker and trader, provider for household and servants, generous to the needy, speaking wisely, managing her home—whose works and fear of the LORD earn praise.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, declaring all is vanity and questioning profit from labor under the sun. It observes cyclical patterns in generations, sun, wind, and rivers, and human dissatisfaction. It states there is nothing new and little remembrance of former things. The Preacher describes pursuing wisdom to examine all works, concluding vanity, limits, and that increased wisdom brings grief and sorrow.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the speaker testing pleasure, laughter, wine, and great projects, wealth, servants, and entertainment in Jerusalem, then judging them vanity and without profit. It compares wisdom and folly, noting both share death and are forgotten. It laments labor because its results pass to an unknown heir. It observes toil brings sorrow and unrest, and commends eating, drinking, and enjoying labor as from God, who gives wisdom and joy to the good and travail to sinners.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes times and seasons for various human actions, emotions, and events. It questions the profit of labor and notes that God gives people work, sets eternity in their heart, and makes his works enduring. It urges doing good and enjoying food and labor as God’s gift. It observes injustice in judgment, affirms God will judge, compares human mortality to beasts, and commends rejoicing in one’s work.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records observations about oppression under the sun and the lack of comfort for the oppressed, envy driving labor, and the futility of solitary wealth. It contrasts quietness with toil, states that companionship benefits work, help, warmth, and defense, and notes a poor wise youth surpassing an old foolish king. It describes shifting popularity and successors, concluding human acclaim is fleeting.

This chapter contains 20 verses and covers reverent conduct in the house of God, restraint in speech, and the duty to fulfill vows. It warns against many words, dreams, and excuses before God, and urges fearing God. It notes oppression and corrupted justice under rulers. It describes the futility of loving wealth, the anxiety of riches, loss of possessions, and dying with nothing, and commends enjoying one’s labor and portion as God’s gift.

This chapter contains 12 verses and describes observations about prosperity without the ability to enjoy it, where a stranger consumes one’s goods. It compares a long life with many children but no satisfaction or burial to an untimely birth, noting all go to one place. It states labor and desire remain unfilled, questions advantages of wisdom or poverty, urges accepting what is seen, and notes humans cannot contend with one mightier or know what is best or future outcomes.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records sayings on the value of a good name, mourning over feasting, patient endurance, accepting wise rebuke, avoiding anger and nostalgia, and the limits and benefits of wisdom and money. It urges considering God’s unchangeable work, balancing prosperity and adversity, and moderation in righteousness and wickedness. It notes universal sin, caution about overheard speech, searching out wisdom, warnings about snares, and concludes that God makes man upright but people seek inventions.

This chapter contains 17 verses and covers wisdom’s value, counsel to obey the king’s commandment, and the limits of human control over time, the future, and death. It records observations about rulers’ power, delayed punishment encouraging evil, and the burial and forgetting of the wicked. It states that fearing God fares well while the wicked do not, notes injustices where outcomes mismatch deeds, commends eating and mirth, and concludes that God’s work is unsearchable.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records that the righteous and wicked share the same fate of death, while the living have hope. It urges enjoying food, drink, clean garments, marriage, and diligent labor because the grave ends work and knowledge. It notes time and chance affect outcomes and people do not know their time. It recounts a besieged city saved by a poor wise man, then forgotten, and contrasts wisdom with strength and war.

This chapter contains 20 verses and covers proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly, warning that small folly harms reputation. It advises yielding to an angry ruler, notes misrule where fools are exalted and princes humbled, and describes hazards in labor and negligence. It addresses prudent speech versus babbling, the uncertainty of the future, and leadership marked by childish kings or drunken princes. It warns against laziness, mentions feasting, wine, and money, and forbids cursing rulers or the rich in secret.

This chapter contains 10 verses and covers counsel to act generously and diligently despite uncertainty, using images of casting bread on waters, giving portions, rain clouds, falling trees, and sowing seed. It notes human inability to know the spirit’s way or God’s works. It speaks of enjoying life and sunlight while remembering coming days of darkness and vanity, urging youth to rejoice yet remember judgment and remove sorrow and evil.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records an exhortation to remember the Creator in youth, using images of aging and death, and states that dust returns to earth and spirit to God. It repeats “all is vanity,” notes the preacher’s work teaching and arranging proverbs, warns against endless book-making and wearying study, and concludes to fear God, keep commandments, and expect judgment of every work, including secret things.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a love poem attributed to Solomon. A woman addresses her beloved and the daughters of Jerusalem, requesting kisses, praising his love, name, and ointments, and describing being darkened by the sun while keeping vineyards. She asks where he pastures his flock; she is told to follow the flock to shepherds’ tents. The speakers exchange compliments, compare her to horses in Pharaoh’s chariots, mention jewelry, myrrh, spikenard, and En-gedi, and describe a green bed and a house of cedar and fir.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records dialogue between lovers using nature imagery. The woman identifies herself as a rose of Sharon and lily, praises her beloved, describes being brought to a banqueting house, and charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love early. She hears her beloved approaching, he invites her to rise and come away as winter ends, mentions foxes spoiling vines, and she affirms mutual belonging until daybreak near the mountains of Bether.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a woman seeking her beloved at night, searching the city, questioning watchmen, finding him, and bringing him to her mother’s house. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love prematurely. It then describes a procession from the wilderness, Solomon’s guarded bed with armed men, Solomon’s Lebanon-wood chariot with silver, gold, and purple, and Solomon wearing a crown from his mother on his wedding day.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes the beloved praising his spouse’s beauty with comparisons to animals, plants, spices, and landmarks such as Gilead, Lebanon, Amana, Shenir, and Hermon. He invites her to come from Lebanon and calls her a sealed garden and fountain. She calls for north and south winds to blow on her garden and invites him to enter and enjoy its fruits.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records the beloved entering a garden and inviting friends to eat and drink. The woman hears him knocking but delays; when she opens, he has gone. She searches the city, is struck and wounded by watchmen, and loses her veil. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is lovesick, then describes his appearance in detailed comparisons.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records others asking where the beloved has gone; the woman says he is in his garden among spices and lilies and affirms mutual belonging. The man praises her beauty, comparing her to Tirzah and Jerusalem and describing her features. He notes many queens and concubines yet calls her unique and praised. He goes to gardens to observe fruitfulness, mentions chariots of Amminadib, and calls for the Shulamite to return.

This chapter contains 13 verses and describes a lover praising the prince’s daughter with detailed comparisons of her body and features to jewels, towers, pools, and fruit. The speaker expresses desire and plans to go into the fields and villages, rise early to inspect vineyards and orchards, and share love there. It mentions Heshbon, Bath-rabbim, Lebanon, Damascus, mandrakes, and stored fruits.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the beloved’s desire for public affection, bringing her lover into her mother’s house, and a charge to the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love early. It describes the couple coming from the wilderness, requests to be set as a seal, and statements about love’s strength. It mentions a “little sister,” Solomon’s vineyard at Baal-hamon with payments to keepers, and concludes with a plea to hear the beloved’s voice and for him to hasten like a roe.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Isaiah’s vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. It indicts Israel’s rebellion, moral corruption, and desolation, and rejects hypocritical sacrifices and assemblies. It commands repentance, justice for the oppressed, and care for the fatherless and widow. It contrasts promised cleansing and restoration of Zion with judgment on rebels and idolaters.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Isaiah’s word concerning Judah and Jerusalem, foretelling the LORD’s house established above the mountains as nations come to Zion for law and instruction, and describing judgment that ends warfare. It rebukes Jacob for soothsaying, wealth, horses, and idolatry. It warns of the day of the LORD humbling the proud, abolishing idols, driving people to hide in rocks, and commands ceasing from trusting man.

This chapter contains 26 verses and describes the LORD removing support and leadership from Jerusalem and Judah, bringing incompetent rulers and social oppression. It records Jerusalem’s ruin due to sinful speech and deeds, pronounces well-being for the righteous and woe for the wicked, and depicts the LORD judging elders and princes for exploiting the poor. It also lists the daughters of Zion’s ornaments and announces their humiliation, war losses, and desolation.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes seven women seeking one man’s name to remove reproach, then a future time when the LORD’s branch and the earth’s fruit benefit Israel’s survivors. It records that those left in Zion and Jerusalem are called holy and listed among the living. The Lord washes away Zion’s filth and purges Jerusalem’s blood, and creates protective cloud, smoke, and fire over Mount Zion, with a tabernacle as shelter and refuge.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the song of the LORD’s vineyard, identifying it as Israel and Judah, and announcing its hedges removed and land laid waste. It pronounces woes on greed, drunkenness, ignoring God’s works, drawing sin, moral inversion, self-wisdom, and corrupt judgment. It foretells captivity, famine, humiliation of the proud, desolation, and a foreign nation summoned to invade, bringing darkness and sorrow.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Isaiah’s vision of the Lord enthroned in the temple with seraphim proclaiming holiness, the temple shaking and filling with smoke, and Isaiah confessing unclean lips. A seraph touches his mouth with a live coal from the altar to purge sin. Isaiah accepts a commission to speak to a people who will not understand, until widespread desolation occurs; a remnant remains like a holy seed.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Isaiah meeting King Ahaz of Judah during the Syro-Ephraimite threat from Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel. The LORD promises their plan to replace Ahaz will fail and that Ephraim will be broken. Ahaz is told to ask a sign but refuses; Isaiah gives the sign of Immanuel. The chapter warns of Assyria’s coming devastation and resulting desolation of the land.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD commanding Isaiah to write the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, with Uriah and Zechariah as witnesses, and naming Isaiah’s son accordingly as a sign that Assyria will take Damascus and Samaria’s spoil. It warns Judah for rejecting Shiloah and trusting Rezin and Remaliah’s son, foretells Assyria overflowing Judah, instructs not to fear confederacies but to fear the LORD, seals the law among disciples, forbids consulting familiar spirits, and describes coming distress and darkness.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes relief from former affliction in Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee as light dawns on people in darkness. It records deliverance from oppression, the end of warfare, and a promised child who bears government on David’s throne with enduring justice and peace. It covers a word of judgment on Jacob/Israel: pride in Ephraim and Samaria, foreign attacks, failure to repent, corrupt leaders, social ruin, and internecine violence, while the LORD’s anger continues.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records woes against unjust rulers who oppress the poor, widows, and fatherless, warning coming judgment. It describes Assyria as an instrument sent against Israel/Judah, yet Assyria’s king boasts and is condemned for pride. The Lord promises to punish Assyria, preserve a returning remnant of Israel, and remove the Assyrian yoke. It lists Assyria’s advance through towns toward Jerusalem and foretells the Lord humbling the haughty like felled trees.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes a Branch from Jesse endowed with the LORD’s Spirit who judges righteously and strikes the wicked. It records peace in the holy mountain where animals and children dwell safely and the earth is full of the LORD’s knowledge. It covers an ensign drawing Gentiles, the second recovery of Israel’s remnant from many lands, reunion of Ephraim and Judah, victories over neighboring peoples, and a dried river and highway for return.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records a proclamation of praise to the LORD after his anger turns away and he gives comfort. It states trust without fear because God is salvation, strength, and song. It mentions drawing water with joy from the wells of salvation. It commands praising, calling on his name, declaring his deeds, singing, and shouting in Zion because the Holy One of Israel is present.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Isaiah’s oracle against Babylon. It calls for a banner and mustering of nations as the LORD gathers an army for the day of destruction. It describes terror, cosmic darkening, and punishment of the wicked and the proud. The Medes are stirred up to attack; slaughter and plunder follow. Babylon becomes desolate like Sodom, uninhabited, and occupied by wild creatures.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the LORD’s mercy on Jacob and Israel’s return to their land, with foreigners joining them and Israel ruling former oppressors. It gives a proverb against the king of Babylon, describing his downfall to the grave and judgment on his descendants, and Babylon’s desolation. It also declares the LORD’s fixed purpose, the breaking of the Assyrian, and an oracle against Philistia after Ahaz’s death, concluding with Zion’s founding and refuge for the poor.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records an oracle against Moab: Ar and Kir are destroyed at night. Moab weeps at Bajith and Dibon and howls over Nebo and Medeba, wearing sackcloth and mourning in streets and rooftops. Heshbon and Elealeh cry to Jahaz; fugitives flee toward Zoar via Luhith and Horonaim. Nimrim’s waters dry; people carry goods to the brook of willows. Crying reaches Eglaim and Beer-elim. Dimon’s waters fill with blood; lions strike survivors.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records an oracle concerning Moab: sending tribute from Sela, Moab’s daughters fleeing to the fords of Arnon, and counsel to shelter outcasts from the spoiler. It mentions a throne established in the tabernacle of David. It describes Moab’s pride, lamentation, and devastation of Kir-hareseth, Heshbon, Sibmah, Jazer, Elealeh, and vineyards. Moab prays at its sanctuary without prevailing; within three years its glory falls and only a small remnant remains.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records an oracle against Damascus: the city becomes a ruin and Aroer’s towns are forsaken. It says the fortress of Ephraim and the kingdom of Damascus cease, and Jacob’s glory diminishes like a harvested field, with only a small remnant left. People turn to their Maker and not to idols. Because God is forgotten, plantings fail and bring grief. Noisy invading nations are rebuked and scattered; evening trouble ends by morning.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records a woe to a land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia that sends ambassadors by sea to a scattered, oppressed nation. It calls all earth’s inhabitants to observe an ensign lifted on mountains and hear a trumpet. The LORD declares he will watch quietly, then cut down growth before harvest, leaving bodies for birds and beasts. A tribute is brought to the LORD at Mount Zion.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records an oracle against Egypt: the LORD comes, idols shake, and Egyptians fight each other under a cruel ruler. Waters and the Nile fail, harming reeds, crops, fishing, and linen work; leaders of Zoan and Noph give foolish counsel. Judah becomes a terror. Later, Egyptians worship the LORD, build an altar, receive deliverance and healing, and join Assyria and Israel in peace and blessing.

This chapter contains 6 verses and records Assyria’s capture of Ashdod by Tartan under Sargon. The LORD commands Isaiah to remove sackcloth and shoes, and he walks naked and barefoot. Isaiah’s action lasts three years as a sign concerning Egypt and Ethiopia. It predicts the Assyrian king leading Egyptians and Ethiopians away as naked captives, causing fear and shame, and prompting local inhabitants to question how they will escape Assyria.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records burdens concerning the desert of the sea, Dumah, and Arabia. A grievous vision commands Elam and Media to besiege, and a watchman reports chariots and announces Babylon’s fall and the breaking of its images. A watchman answers inquiries from Seir about the night. Dedan’s travelers lodge in Arabia as Tema gives aid to fugitives from war. The LORD declares Kedar’s glory and archers diminish within a year.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records an oracle against the “valley of vision,” describing Jerusalem’s turmoil, fleeing rulers, and siege preparations involving Elam and Kir. It recounts efforts to fortify walls and secure water while failing to look to the LORD, and it contrasts commanded mourning with feasting. It pronounces judgment on Shebna, announcing his removal and exile, and appoints Eliakim with authority over the house of David, later warning that the “nail” will be removed.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records an oracle against Tyre: ships of Tarshish and merchants of Zidon mourn its destruction, and the LORD purposes to abase its pride and destroy its strongholds. Tyre is driven to sojourn toward Tarshish and Chittim without rest. Tyre is forgotten seventy years, then returns to trade with kingdoms; its merchandise is designated for the LORD’s people for food and clothing.

This chapter contains 23 verses and describes the LORD emptying and devastating the earth, affecting all classes alike, because inhabitants transgress laws and break the covenant. It records mourning, collapse of city life, and scarcity, with only a remnant like gleanings remaining. It mentions songs glorifying the LORD from distant places amid treachery. It covers fear, pit, snare, cosmic shaking, punishment of heavenly powers and earthly kings, imprisonment, and the LORD reigning in Zion and Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records praise to the LORD for faithful purposes, the overthrow of a fortified city, and fear among strong nations. It describes God as refuge for the poor and needy and as one who humbles oppressors. On “this mountain” the LORD prepares a feast for all peoples, removes a covering over nations, swallows up death, and wipes away tears. It foretells salvation and the humiliation of Moab and fortified walls.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records a song for Judah about a strong city and gates opened to the righteous, exhorting trust in the LORD. It describes the LORD bringing down a lofty city and guiding the just. It contrasts the wicked’s refusal to learn, recalls past dominion by other lords, and notes national increase and prayer in trouble. It speaks of the dead rising, a call to hide during indignation, and the LORD punishing earth’s iniquity.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the LORD punishing Leviathan, a song of a protected vineyard, and Israel/Jacob taking root and bearing fruit. It contrasts measured discipline with devastation of a fortified city, calls for purging iniquity by removing idolatrous altars and images, and foretells Israel gathered from the river to Egypt, with exiles from Assyria and Egypt returning to worship in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records woes against Ephraim’s drunkards and corrupt priests and prophets, warning of coming judgment. It states the LORD becomes a crown to the remnant, speaks through “another tongue,” and rebukes Jerusalem’s rulers for trusting lies and a “covenant with death.” It announces a sure cornerstone in Zion, declares sweeping judgment, and uses plowing and threshing imagery to show measured discipline and divine counsel.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a woe against Ariel (Jerusalem), where David dwells, foretold distress and siege, and the sudden dispersal of attacking nations. It describes spiritual stupor over prophets and rulers and a “sealed book” vision. It condemns lip-service worship and secret counsel. It promises a coming work, reversal of oppressors, renewed hearing and sight, and Jacob’s children sanctifying God and gaining understanding.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records a woe against Judah for seeking counsel and military help from Egypt (Zoan, Hanes) instead of the LORD. It condemns rejecting prophets, warns of sudden collapse and flight, and calls for returning, rest, quietness, and confidence. It promises grace to Zion/Jerusalem, guidance, rejection of idols, agricultural abundance, and healing. It depicts the LORD judging nations and beating Assyria, with Tophet prepared for the king.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a woe against seeking Egypt’s horses and chariots instead of the LORD. It states the LORD rises against evildoers and that Egypt is human, not God. The LORD is described as defending Mount Zion and Jerusalem. Israel is called to return and cast away silver and gold idols. It foretells Assyria’s defeat and flight, with princes fearing the ensign in Zion.

This chapter contains 20 verses and describes a king reigning in righteousness and princes ruling with justice, bringing clarity to hearers and speakers and exposing vile and deceitful actions against the poor. It addresses complacent women, warning of failed harvests, lamentation, and desolation of fields, houses, palaces, and towers. It records restoration when the Spirit is poured out, producing righteousness, peace, secure dwellings, and agricultural prosperity.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a woe against a spoiler and treacherous oppressor, and a plea for the LORD’s grace and salvation. It describes nations scattering, spoil gathered, and Zion filled with judgment and righteousness. It depicts desolation in the land and the LORD rising to judge. It defines righteous conduct, promises protection and provision, and portrays Zion/Jerusalem as secure. It declares the LORD as judge, lawgiver, and king, and ends with healing and forgiveness for inhabitants.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a summons to all nations to hear of the LORD’s indignation and slaughter of their armies. It describes cosmic upheaval and the LORD’s sword coming in judgment on Idumea/Edom, with sacrifice at Bozrah. The land becomes burning pitch and perpetual desolation; nobles and princes vanish.
