It becomes inhabited by unclean birds and wild creatures. A command to read “the book of the LORD” affirms these outcomes.

This chapter contains 10 verses and describes the wilderness and desert rejoicing and blossoming, with references to Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon seeing the LORD’s glory. It commands strengthening the weak and encouraging the fearful, stating God comes with recompense to save. It records healings of blind, deaf, lame, and mute, and waters appearing in the desert. It describes a “way of holiness” for the redeemed, free from beasts, and the ransomed returning to Zion with joy.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Sennacherib of Assyria capturing fortified cities of Judah and sending Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem. Rabshakeh confronts Hezekiah’s officials at the upper pool, challenges Judah’s trust in Egypt and in the LORD, and urges surrender with promises of provisions and relocation. He speaks in Judean despite requests, and the officials remain silent by command, then report to Hezekiah with torn clothes.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Hezekiah mourning and seeking the LORD in the temple, sending Eliakim, Shebna, and priests to Isaiah. Isaiah delivers a message that Assyria will withdraw and Sennacherib will die in his land. Rabshakeh returns; Sennacherib sends a threatening letter citing conquered nations. Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD and prays. Isaiah prophesies Assyria’s defeat, Judah’s remnant, and a sign of future harvest. The angel of the LORD kills 185,000 Assyrians; Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and is slain by his sons; Esar-haddon reigns.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Hezekiah’s terminal illness, Isaiah’s message to set his house in order, and Hezekiah’s prayer and weeping. The LORD tells Isaiah Hezekiah will live fifteen more years and promises deliverance of Jerusalem from Assyria. A sign is given as the sun’s shadow on Ahaz’s sundial moves back ten degrees. The chapter includes Hezekiah’s writing about sickness, death, and praise. Isaiah prescribes a fig plaster, and Hezekiah asks for a sign to go to the LORD’s house.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records Merodach-baladan king of Babylon sending letters and a gift to Hezekiah after hearing of his recovery. Hezekiah shows the Babylonian envoys all his treasures and armory. Isaiah questions him and prophesies that Judah’s possessions will be carried to Babylon and some of Hezekiah’s sons taken as eunuchs in the Babylonian palace. Hezekiah accepts the message and notes peace in his days.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records a message of comfort to Jerusalem announcing pardon and completion of warfare, and a voice in the wilderness calling to prepare the LORD’s way. It contrasts human frailty with God’s enduring word, proclaims good tidings to Zion and Judah, and describes the LORD coming with power as a shepherd. It declares God’s incomparability to idols, sovereignty over nations and rulers, creation of the heavens, and strength given to those who wait on him.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records the LORD summoning the nations to judgment, citing one raised from the east and one from the north, and declaring himself first and last. Israel/Jacob is chosen as the LORD’s servant and told not to fear, with promises of help, victory over enemies, and transformation like a threshing instrument. The LORD promises water and trees in wilderness for the needy. Idols are challenged to predict events and declared worthless.

This chapter contains 25 verses and describes the LORD’s servant endowed with God’s Spirit to bring justice, serve as a covenant and light to the Gentiles, open blind eyes, and free prisoners. It declares God’s uniqueness and new things foretold, calls worldwide praise, portrays the LORD as a warrior who judges and transforms creation, shames idolaters, rebukes deaf and blind servants, magnifies the law, and explains Israel’s spoil and captivity as punishment for disobedience.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records the LORD’s assurance to Jacob/Israel of redemption, protection through waters and fire, and gathering of descendants from all directions. It names Israel as the LORD’s witnesses against the nations and declares the LORD as sole God and savior. It mentions sending to Babylon and past deliverance at the sea, promises a new way in wilderness and rivers in desert, rebukes Israel’s neglect of worship and sacrifices, offers forgiveness, calls for pleading, and cites ancestral and priestly sin leading to reproach.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records the LORD’s address to Jacob/Israel, promising help, outpoured Spirit and blessing, and calling them witnesses that there is no other God. It condemns idol-making by craftsmen and describes the futility of worshiping wood images. It calls Israel to remember, return, and notes forgiveness and redemption. It declares the LORD as Creator, frustrater of diviners, restorer of Jerusalem and Judah, drying rivers, and naming Cyrus to rebuild Jerusalem and lay the temple foundation.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the LORD addressing Cyrus, pledging to subdue nations, open gates, grant hidden treasures, and use him to rebuild the city and release captives. It declares the LORD as the only God, creator of light and darkness, and maker of heaven and earth. It pronounces woe on those who contend with their Maker, condemns idol makers, calls the nations to assemble and look to the LORD for salvation, and states every knee will bow; Israel is saved and justified.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Bel and Nebo’s idols stooping and being carried as burdens into captivity. The LORD addresses the house of Jacob and remnant of Israel, stating he has carried them from birth and will continue to bear and deliver them. It contrasts powerless man-made idols with God’s uniqueness, foreknowledge, and fixed counsel, calling a bird from the east to execute his purpose. It promises near righteousness and salvation in Zion.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records a proclamation of Babylon’s humiliation and downfall. The daughter of Babylon/Chaldeans is told to sit in dust and darkness, lose royal status, and be exposed. The LORD says he gave Israel into Babylon’s hand, but Babylon showed no mercy and boasted “I am.” Judgment comes suddenly as widowhood and loss of children; sorceries, enchantments, astrologers, and counselors cannot save her, and merchants scatter.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD addressing Jacob/Israel for swearing by His name without truth, recalling foretold events to prevent credit to idols, and stating He restrains anger and refines them in affliction for His name’s sake. It affirms His power as Creator and announces action against Babylon and the Chaldeans through one He calls. It urges obedience, commands leaving Babylon, recalls wilderness provision, and states there is no peace for the wicked.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the LORD calling his servant from the womb to restore Jacob/Israel and be a light to the Gentiles. It describes deliverance of prisoners, safe guidance and gathering from distant lands, and Zion’s complaint of being forgotten answered with assurance. It foretells returning children, Gentiles and rulers assisting, kings honoring Zion, and the LORD rescuing captives and judging oppressors.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the LORD stating Israel is not sold off but separated because of iniquities, affirming his power to redeem and to dry seas and darken heavens. It presents the LORD’s servant as taught and obedient, enduring beating and shame while trusting God’s help and vindication. It commands those who fear the LORD to trust him in darkness and warns self-reliant fire-kindlers of sorrow.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD calling those who seek righteousness to remember Abraham and Sarah, promising to comfort and restore Zion, and declaring enduring salvation and righteousness. It recalls God’s power in cutting Rahab and dividing the sea, promises the redeemed return to Zion with joy, and urges Jerusalem to awake after drinking the cup of fury. God removes this cup from Jerusalem and gives it to her afflicters.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records calls for Zion and Jerusalem to awake, rise from captivity, and put on holy garments. The LORD says his people are redeemed without money, recalls sojourn in Egypt and oppression by Assyria, and promises they will know his name. It describes messengers of peace, watchmen rejoicing, and the LORD comforting and redeeming Jerusalem. It commands departure from uncleanness, with the LORD leading. It introduces the LORD’s servant, marred yet exalted, affecting many nations and kings.

This chapter contains 12 verses and describes a servant who is unbelieved, grows without outward attractiveness, and is despised, rejected, and afflicted. He bears others’ griefs and iniquities, is wounded and silent under oppression, and is cut off and buried with the wicked and the rich though innocent. The LORD makes his life an offering for sin; he justifies many, bears their sins, intercedes for transgressors, and is allotted a portion with the great.

This chapter contains 17 verses and describes the LORD addressing the barren and desolate to sing and enlarge their tent, promising expansion, inheritance, and restored honor. It records covenant assurances of mercy like the oath of Noah, promises of peace and protection, and imagery of an rebuilt city with precious stones. It states children are taught by the LORD, oppression is removed, enemies fail, and weapons and accusations do not prevail.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records an invitation for the thirsty and poor to come and receive food and drink without price, urging hearers to listen and live under an everlasting covenant tied to David. It calls nations to come, commands seeking the LORD, repentance, and return for mercy and pardon. It contrasts God’s ways with human ways, compares God’s word to rain accomplishing its purpose, and promises joyful peace and renewed creation.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records the LORD commanding justice and Sabbath-keeping, promising blessing and inclusion for foreigners and eunuchs who keep the covenant. It states they receive a lasting name, are brought to God’s holy mountain, and have offerings accepted in a house of prayer for all people, as God gathers outcasts and others. It also denounces blind, greedy watchmen and shepherds and calls beasts to devour.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the death of the righteous and their entering peace, then condemns idol worship, adultery, child sacrifice, and falsehood. It contrasts reliance on idols and alliances with trusting the LORD, who promises land and holy mountain inheritance. It calls to remove stumblingblocks and describes God dwelling with the contrite, limiting wrath, healing the repentant, and declaring peace to near and far, while stating the wicked have no peace.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records a command to expose Jacob’s sins, criticizing fasting done with oppression, strife, and self-interest. It defines the chosen fast as loosening wickedness, freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, housing the poor, and clothing the naked. It promises answered prayer, guidance, restoration, and rebuilding. It commands honoring the sabbath and promises delight in the LORD and Jacob’s heritage.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes how Israel’s sins separate them from God and hinder answered prayer. It lists violence, lying, injustice, and lack of truth, and portrays the people seeking light, justice, and salvation but finding darkness. The LORD observes no intercessor, brings salvation by his own arm, and repays enemies. It records the Redeemer coming to Zion and a covenant of God’s Spirit and enduring words with Jacob’s repentant.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes Zion being told to arise as the LORD’s glory appears, drawing Gentiles and kings. It records return of sons and daughters, wealth arriving by camels, flocks, and ships of Tarshish from Midian, Ephah, Sheba, Kedar, and Nebaioth. Strangers build walls; gates stay open; resisting nations perish. Lebanon’s trees adorn the sanctuary; former oppressors bow. Peace and righteousness replace violence; the LORD is everlasting light; Zion’s people inherit the land and multiply.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the Lord’s anointed servant proclaiming good tidings, liberty to captives, comfort for mourners in Zion, and the acceptable year and day of vengeance. It covers restoration of desolations, foreigners serving, Israel being called priests, double portion and everlasting joy, the Lord’s love of justice and an everlasting covenant, recognition among nations, rejoicing in salvation and righteousness spreading worldwide.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records declarations for Zion and Jerusalem: righteousness and salvation shine forth; Gentiles and kings see her glory; she receives new names and is no longer called Forsaken or Desolate. Watchmen are set on Jerusalem’s walls to pray continually. The LORD swears enemies will not consume Israel’s grain and wine. The people are told to prepare the way and raise a standard; Zion is called holy, redeemed, sought out, and not forsaken.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a dialogue about one coming from Edom/Bozrah with bloodstained garments, treading the winepress alone in anger and executing vengeance while bringing salvation. It recounts the LORD’s past mercies to Israel, His saving presence, and Israel’s rebellion. It recalls the Exodus under Moses and the Spirit’s guidance, then petitions God to look from heaven, acknowledge them as Father and Redeemer, return to the tribes, and address the profaned sanctuary.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a plea for the LORD to rend the heavens and come down in power so nations tremble. It recalls past mighty acts and states that God prepares blessings for those who wait for him. The people confess sin and uncleanness, note God’s hidden face, and ask mercy as the potter over clay. It laments Zion, Jerusalem, and holy cities desolated and the temple burned.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the LORD’s response to a rebellious people practicing idolatry and defilement, promising recompense. It preserves a remnant from Jacob and Judah to inherit the mountains, with Sharon and Achor restored. It contrasts judgment on those who forsake the holy mountain with blessing on servants. It announces new heavens, a new earth, and renewed Jerusalem with peace, longevity, secure labor, answered prayer, and harmony among animals.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD’s rejection of hypocritical sacrifices, favoring the contrite, and promising recompense on enemies. It describes Zion and Jerusalem’s sudden birth and comfort, peace like a river, and rejoicing of servants. The LORD comes with fire and sword to judge idolaters. He gathers all nations, sends survivors to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, and Javan, brings exiles to Jerusalem, appoints priests and Levites, establishes new heavens and earth, universal worship, and punishment of transgressors.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Jeremiah’s identification as a priest from Anathoth and the timeframe of his ministry from Josiah to the exile. The LORD calls and appoints Jeremiah as a prophet, touches his mouth, and commissions him to speak. Two visions appear: an almond rod and a boiling pot from the north, foretelling invasion and judgment for idolatry. Jeremiah is commanded not to fear opposition.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records the LORD’s message through Jeremiah to Jerusalem, recalling Israel’s early devotion and accusing the nation of forsaking Him for idols. It indicts priests, rulers, and prophets, cites Baal worship, moral pollution, and bloodshed, and likens Judah to an unfaithful vine. It warns that reliance on Egypt or Assyria brings shame and judgment.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the LORD’s charge that Israel and Judah commit spiritual adultery through idolatry on high places, bringing drought and shame. It compares Israel’s “divorce” to Judah’s treachery and calls the backsliding nation to return, confess sin, and obey. It promises mercy, restoration to Zion, shepherds, Jerusalem as the LORD’s throne, reunified Judah and Israel, and a confession of guilt.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD calling Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem to return, remove abominations, and repent (“break up fallow ground,” “circumcise” the heart). It commands warnings by trumpet and flight to fortified cities as destruction comes from the north. It describes rulers and priests dismayed, invasion imagery from Dan and Ephraim, widespread desolation yet not a full end, and Zion lamenting like a woman in labor.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD’s search in Jerusalem for anyone who executes judgment and seeks truth, indicting Judah and Israel for false oaths, idolatry, adultery, and refusing correction. It announces judgment by a distant nation that devastates land and cities, yet not a full end. It links calamity to serving strange gods and condemns oppression, deceit, and false prophets and priests.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records a warning for Benjamin to flee Jerusalem as destruction comes from the north, with siege preparations against Zion. It lists Jerusalem’s oppression, violence, covetousness, and false prophets proclaiming “peace.” The LORD urges seeking the old paths and heeding watchmen, but the people refuse; sacrifices are rejected. A northern nation attacks, bringing fear and mourning; Judah is tested like metal and called rejected silver.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records the LORD’s message to Jeremiah to preach at the temple gate in Jerusalem, calling Judah to amend conduct, execute justice, and stop oppression, bloodshed, theft, adultery, false oaths, and idolatry. It warns that trusting in the temple will not prevent judgment, citing Shiloh. Jeremiah is told not to intercede. It condemns worship of the “queen of heaven,” temple defilement, and child sacrifice at Tophet in the valley of Hinnom, forecasting slaughter, exile, and desolation.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD warning that graves in Judah and Jerusalem are desecrated and survivors prefer death in exile. It rebukes Jerusalem for persistent backsliding, deceit, and refusal to repent, while priests and prophets speak falsely of peace. It announces loss of land and produce and an invading force from Dan, with serpents as judgment. Jeremiah laments Zion’s hurt and asks about balm in Gilead.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Jeremiah’s lament for the slain and Judah’s pervasive deceit, lying, and treachery. The LORD warns not to trust neighbors, declares he will test and punish the people, and foretells Jerusalem and Judah made desolate. Causes include forsaking God’s law and following Baalim. Judgments include wormwood and gall, scattering among nations, and the sword. Mourning women are summoned; death and unburied corpses are described. Boasting is forbidden except in knowing the LORD. The LORD promises to punish Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and others, citing uncircumcised hearts.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records the LORD warning Israel not to follow heathen customs or fear celestial signs, describing the making and helplessness of idols. It contrasts idols with the LORD as creator and everlasting king who controls nature and judges nations. It announces the scattering of Judah’s inhabitants, laments devastation and failed leaders, foretells invasion from the north, and includes prayers for correction and for wrath on nations that consume Jacob.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD commanding Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant to Judah and Jerusalem, warning of a curse for disobedience. It reports Judah and Israel breaking the covenant through idolatry, including altars to Baal, and announces unavoidable calamity and rejected prayers. Jeremiah learns of a plot against him. The LORD pronounces judgment on the men of Anathoth who seek Jeremiah’s life.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Jeremiah questioning why the wicked prosper and describing land devastation and loss of beasts and birds. The LORD warns Jeremiah about greater trials, betrayal by his own family, and cautions him not to trust them. The LORD declares he has forsaken his house, his heritage is desolated by shepherds and spoilers, and judgment comes by the sword. He announces uprooting Judah and neighboring nations, possible restoration if they learn Israel’s ways, and destruction if they refuse.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records the LORD commanding Jeremiah to wear a linen girdle, hide it by the Euphrates, and retrieve it ruined as a sign that Judah and Jerusalem’s pride will be marred. It warns that kings, priests, prophets, and Jerusalem will be filled with drunkenness and destroyed. Jeremiah urges humility before coming darkness, foretells captivity from the north, scattering, and public shame for idolatry and “adulteries.”

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a drought in Judah and Jerusalem, with mourning, empty water pits, and famine conditions affecting people and animals. Jeremiah voices confession and pleas for mercy, but the LORD says the people love to wander, rejects their fasting and offerings, and forbids Jeremiah to pray for their good. The LORD condemns lying prophets promising peace and declares sword, famine, and pestilence judgments, followed by renewed lament and covenant appeal.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the LORD’s declaration that Judah faces death, sword, famine, and captivity, with scattering among kingdoms for sins linked to Manasseh in Jerusalem. It describes judgment imagery of bereavement and spoil, and Jeremiah’s lament over opposition. Jeremiah prays for remembrance and vindication, recalls receiving God’s words, and questions his suffering. The LORD calls him to return, separate precious from vile, and promises protection and deliverance.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the LORD commanding Jeremiah not to marry or have children and not to join mourning or feasting, because death, sword, famine, and loss of joy come on the land. It gives reasons: Judah forsakes the LORD, worships other gods, and disobeys the law, so exile follows. It also foretells a future return from northern lands, pursuit by “fishers” and “hunters,” recompense for defilement, Gentiles acknowledging false gods, and the LORD making his power known.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Judah’s sin as ingrained and bringing loss of land, treasure, and exile. It contrasts curse on trusting humans with blessing on trusting the LORD, states the LORD searches hearts, and warns against unjust gain. Jeremiah prays for healing and deliverance from persecutors. The LORD commands Sabbath observance at Jerusalem’s gates, promising Davidic rulers and ongoing worship if obeyed, but unquenchable fire on the city if not.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Jeremiah going to a potter’s house, where a marred clay vessel is remade, and the LORD applies it to Israel’s fate. It states God may destroy or build nations based on their repentance or disobedience. Jeremiah warns Judah and Jerusalem to turn from evil; they refuse. God announces desolation and scattering. Opponents plot against Jeremiah; he prays for judgment on them.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records the LORD sending Jeremiah with elders to the valley of the son of Hinnom to proclaim judgment on Judah and Jerusalem for idolatry, child sacrifice, and innocent blood. The place is renamed the valley of slaughter; enemies bring sword, desolation, siege cannibalism, and defilement. Jeremiah breaks a potter’s bottle as a sign of irreversible ruin and repeats the warning in the temple court.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Pashur the priest striking Jeremiah and placing him in stocks by the Benjamin gate, then releasing him. Jeremiah renames Pashur “Magor-missabib” and prophesies Judah’s defeat, plunder, and captivity to Babylon, and Pashur’s death there. Jeremiah laments mockery and threats, struggles to remain silent, affirms the LORD’s support, calls for vengeance, praises deliverance, and curses his birth.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Zedekiah sending Pashhur and Zephaniah to Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD during Babylon’s siege. Jeremiah relays that the LORD turns Judah’s weapons back, fights against Jerusalem, and brings pestilence, famine, and sword. Zedekiah and survivors are delivered to Nebuchadrezzar. The people are set before life (surrender to Chaldeans) or death (remain). The house of David is commanded to execute judgment; Jerusalem is warned of punishment and fire.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD’s message at Judah’s royal house commanding justice, protection of the oppressed, and warning of desolation for disobedience and idolatry. It predicts Shallum’s exile and death away from Judah, condemns Jehoiakim’s oppression and foretells his dishonorable burial, laments Judah’s ruined allies and leaders, and declares Coniah’s removal, exile to Babylon under Nebuchadrezzar, and that none of his offspring prospers on David’s throne.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records the LORD’s woe against corrupt pastors who scatter the flock, with a promise to gather a remnant and appoint new shepherds. It foretells a righteous Branch from David who reigns in justice and brings safety to Judah and Israel. It denounces profane prophets and priests in Samaria and Jerusalem, condemns false visions and dreams, warns of coming judgment, and forbids using the phrase “burden of the LORD,” threatening punishment and exile.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records Jeremiah seeing two baskets of figs set before the LORD’s temple after Nebuchadrezzar carries Jeconiah and Judah’s leaders and craftsmen from Jerusalem to Babylon. The LORD identifies the good figs as the Judahite exiles, promises to watch over them, return them, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know Him. The bad figs represent Zedekiah, remaining Jerusalemites, and those in Egypt, who face dispersion, reproach, and sword, famine, and pestilence.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jeremiah’s message in Jehoiakim’s fourth year, recounting Judah’s refusal to heed prophets and commanding repentance and rejection of other gods. It announces Babylon under Nebuchadrezzar will devastate Judah and surrounding nations, bringing seventy years of servitude. Afterward Babylon is punished. Jeremiah is told to make many nations drink a cup of wrath, listing Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, Arabia, Elam, Medes, and all kingdoms, with widespread sword and desolation.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD sending Jeremiah to preach in the temple court during Jehoiakim’s reign, warning Judah to obey or the temple becomes like Shiloh and Jerusalem a curse. Priests and prophets seek Jeremiah’s death, and princes hear the case at the new gate. Jeremiah defends his message; elders cite Micah under Hezekiah. Urijah is extradited from Egypt and executed. Ahikam protects Jeremiah.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD commanding Jeremiah to wear bonds and yokes and send them to Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon via envoys at Jerusalem to Zedekiah. It declares God gives the lands to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and warns nations to submit or face sword, famine, and pestilence. Jeremiah urges Zedekiah, priests, and people to reject false prophets about temple vessels; remaining vessels will go to Babylon until later restoration.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Hananiah of Gibeon prophesying in the temple that Babylon’s yoke is broken and that within two years the temple vessels, Jeconiah, and Judah’s captives return. Jeremiah responds about testing prophets, then Hananiah breaks Jeremiah’s yoke. The LORD sends Jeremiah to declare iron yokes of Babylonian service, accuse Hananiah of lying, and announce his death; Hananiah dies that year.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Jeremiah’s letter from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon, sent by Elasah and Gemariah. It commands them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, increase, and seek Babylon’s peace, rejecting false prophets. It promises return after seventy years. It warns those remaining in Jerusalem of sword, famine, and pestilence. It condemns Ahab and Zedekiah for false prophecy and immorality, and Shemaiah for opposing Jeremiah, pronouncing punishment on him and his descendants.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records the LORD commanding Jeremiah to write his words, promising to restore the captives of Israel and Judah to their land. It describes fear and “Jacob’s trouble,” the breaking of the yoke, and Israel serving the LORD and “David their king.” It states Judah’s wounds come from sin, yet oppressors are judged. It promises healing, rebuilding of Jerusalem, growth and thanksgiving, native rulers, covenant renewal, and a whirlwind of judgment on the wicked.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records the LORD’s promise to be God to Israel, gather the remnant from exile, restore Ephraim and Judah, and bring rejoicing in Zion. It mentions Rachel weeping in Ramah, calls Israel to return with waymarks, and declares individual responsibility for sin. It announces a new covenant with Israel and Judah, with the law written in hearts and sins forgiven. It also foretells Jerusalem rebuilt with defined boundaries and made holy.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Jeremiah imprisoned during Babylon’s siege of Jerusalem in Zedekiah’s reign, with prophecy of the city’s fall and Zedekiah’s capture. The LORD commands Jeremiah to buy Hanameel’s field in Anathoth, seal the deed, and store it with Baruch. Jeremiah prays recounting Israel’s history and Judah’s disobedience. The LORD announces Jerusalem’s burning for idolatry, then promises regathering, an everlasting covenant, safety, and future land purchases in Judah.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the LORD’s word to Jeremiah while imprisoned, describing Jerusalem’s destruction by the Chaldeans and promising healing, restoration, return from captivity, cleansing from sin, and renewed joy in Judah and Jerusalem. It mentions shepherds and flocks returning, foretells a righteous Branch from David bringing safety, and reaffirms enduring covenants with David and the Levite priests, likened to day and night, addressing claims that God cast off Israel and Judah.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Jeremiah’s message during Nebuchadnezzar’s siege: Jerusalem is given to Babylon; Zedekiah is captured, meets the king of Babylon, and goes to Babylon but dies in peace. It notes Babylon’s attacks on Jerusalem, Lachish, and Azekah. It covers Zedekiah’s covenant to free Hebrew slaves, the people’s later reversal, and judgment for breaking the covenant: sword, famine, pestilence, exile, and Judah’s desolation.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records Jeremiah, in Jehoiakim’s days, bringing the Rechabites into a temple chamber and offering them wine, which they refuse due to Jonadab’s command to abstain, live in tents, and not farm. The LORD uses their obedience to rebuke Judah for ignoring prophetic calls to repent, announces coming judgment on Jerusalem, and promises Jonadab’s line endures before him.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Jeremiah directing Baruch to write and read a scroll of the LORD’s words against Israel, Judah, and the nations during Jehoiakim’s reign. Baruch reads it at the temple on a fast day; officials report it to the king. Jehoiakim burns the scroll and orders Jeremiah and Baruch seized, but they are hidden. Jeremiah dictates a replacement scroll with added words and judgment on Jehoiakim.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Zedekiah’s reign in Judah and the people’s refusal to heed the LORD through Jeremiah. Zedekiah sends Jehucal and Zephaniah to request Jeremiah’s prayer. The LORD declares Pharaoh’s army will return to Egypt and the Chaldeans will resume the siege, capture, and burn Jerusalem. Jeremiah is arrested at Benjamin gate, beaten, and imprisoned; Zedekiah questions him secretly, then keeps him in the court with daily bread.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records princes accusing Jeremiah of weakening the city and persuading Zedekiah to allow his imprisonment in a miry dungeon. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian petitions the king and rescues Jeremiah, who remains in the prison court. Zedekiah secretly questions Jeremiah, who warns surrender to Babylon brings life and refusal brings burning, captivity, and loss of family. Zedekiah orders secrecy; Jeremiah gives a cover story to princes and stays confined until Jerusalem falls.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Babylon’s siege and capture of Jerusalem, the Babylonian princes at the Middle Gate, Zedekiah’s flight and capture near Jericho, judgment at Riblah, and the killing of his sons and Judah’s nobles, with Zedekiah blinded and taken to Babylon. It covers the burning of houses and walls, deportations under Nebuzar-adan, the poor left with fields, Jeremiah released to Gedaliah, and a promise of deliverance to Ebed-melech.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Jeremiah’s release from chains at Ramah by Nebuzar-adan, who offers him travel to Babylon or freedom in Judah. Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah, Babylon’s appointed governor. Captains and their men come to Gedaliah, who urges serving the Chaldeans and gathering provisions. Dispersed Jews return to Judah. Johanan warns Gedaliah of Ishmael’s plot from Baalis, but Gedaliah rejects it.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Ishmael son of Nethaniah killing Gedaliah at Mizpah, then killing Jews and Chaldeans there. He deceives and slays pilgrims from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, sparing ten for promised stores, and throws bodies into a pit. Ishmael takes captives, including the king’s daughters, toward Ammon. Johanan pursues at Gibeon, frees captives, and Ishmael escapes. The remnant gathers near Bethlehem planning flight to Egypt, fearing Chaldeans.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Judah’s remnant, led by Johanan, asking Jeremiah to pray for guidance and pledging obedience. After ten days Jeremiah delivers the LORD’s word: remain in the land and God will build and plant them, show mercy, and protect them from the king of Babylon. If they go to Egypt, sword, famine, and pestilence will overtake them; they are warned not to go and are accused of dissembling.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Azariah, Johanan, and others accusing Jeremiah of lying and blaming Baruch, then leading Judah’s remnant, including women, children, king’s daughters, Jeremiah, and Baruch, into Egypt to Tahpanhes. There the LORD commands Jeremiah to hide stones at Pharaoh’s house entrance, prophesying Nebuchadnezzar’s throne there, Egypt’s defeat, and the burning of Egyptian temples and images, including at Beth-shemesh.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records the LORD’s word through Jeremiah to Jews living in Egypt at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros. It recalls Judah’s desolation for idolatry and warns the Egyptian remnant of judgment by sword, famine, and pestilence. The people refuse and vow offerings to the “queen of heaven.” Jeremiah rebukes them; only a few escape to Judah. A sign is given: Pharaoh-hophra is delivered to enemies.

This chapter contains 5 verses and records the LORD’s word to Baruch son of Neriah after he writes Jeremiah’s words in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Baruch laments his grief and lack of rest. The LORD declares He will break down what He has built and pluck up what He has planted in the whole land, and commands Baruch not to seek great things for himself, promising him his life as spoil wherever he goes.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Jeremiah’s prophecy against Egypt: Pharaoh-necho’s army at Carchemish by the Euphrates is struck by Nebuchadrezzar, and Egypt’s allies and mercenaries flee. It announces Babylon’s coming invasion, calls cities like Migdol, Noph, and Tahpanhes to prepare, and predicts captivity and desolation. The LORD declares punishment on No, Pharaoh, Egypt’s gods and kings, yet promises Jacob/Israel preservation and eventual return.

This chapter contains 7 verses and records the LORD’s word to Jeremiah against the Philistines before Pharaoh smites Gaza. It describes waters rising from the north as an overflowing flood, with horse and chariot sounds causing panic. It announces spoiling of Philistia and loss of help from Tyre and Sidon, mentions Caphtor’s remnant, and names Gaza and Ashkelon as judged. The LORD’s sword is charged against the seashore.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records an oracle against Moab: cities including Nebo, Heshbon, Dibon, Kiriathaim, and Kerioth are spoiled; Moab is urged to flee; the spoiler reaches every city. Moab’s pride, reliance on treasures, and exalting itself against the LORD are cited; Chemosh and its priests go into captivity. Lamentation, desolation of fields and vineyards, and cessation of high-place offerings are described. Judgment comes as fear, pit, and snare, yet a latter-days restoration is promised.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records oracles of judgment and restoration against surrounding nations. It addresses Ammon’s seizure of Gad, announcing war on Rabbah, captivity, and later return. It proclaims Edom’s desolation (Teman, Bozrah) and downfall. It foretells Damascus’s weakening, slaughter, and fire on its walls. It predicts Nebuchadrezzar’s plunder of Kedar and Hazor. It declares Elam’s bow broken, scattering, king removed, and eventual restoration.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Jeremiah’s oracle against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans: Babylon is proclaimed taken, idols broken, and a northern coalition attacks, making the land desolate. Israel and Judah return together, seeking the LORD and Zion in a perpetual covenant. The chapter commands departure from Babylon, announces punishment on its king and people, battle and siege, and desolation like Sodom, with captives redeemed and Babylon’s power overthrown.

This chapter contains 64 verses and records the LORD’s announced judgment on Babylon: nations, including the Medes and kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz, attack and make it desolate. Israel is told to flee Babylon. Babylon’s idols and walls fall, its land becomes uninhabited, and Bel is punished. Jeremiah commands Seraiah to read the written prophecy in Babylon and cast it, weighted with a stone, into the Euphrates as a sign of Babylon sinking.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Zedekiah’s reign in Jerusalem, his rebellion, and Nebuchadnezzar’s siege, famine, breach, and capture near Jericho. Zedekiah is judged at Riblah; his sons and princes are killed, he is blinded and imprisoned in Babylon. Nebuzar-adan burns the temple and city, breaks walls, takes temple vessels, deports people, and executes leaders. Captivity totals are listed. Jehoiachin is released and honored by Evil-merodach.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes Jerusalem/Zion sitting desolate and grieving after Judah’s captivity. It records abandonment by allies, enemies surrounding and prospering, and the cessation of feasts as gates, priests, and people mourn. The city recounts sin and rebellion as cause of affliction, sanctuary profanation, hunger, and death. It appeals to the LORD to see distress, acknowledges his righteousness, and requests judgment on adversaries.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records the LORD’s anger against Zion/Jerusalem: habitations, palaces, walls, gates, and strongholds are destroyed; tabernacle, altar, sanctuary, feasts, and sabbaths cease; king and princes go among the nations, and prophets receive no vision. Elders and virgins mourn while children faint from hunger. Passersby and enemies mock. The people are urged to weep and pray. Cannibalism and slaughter in streets and sanctuary leave none escaping.

This chapter contains 66 verses and records a first-person lament of affliction, darkness, and mocked suffering, followed by remembrance of the LORD’s mercies and hope. It urges quiet waiting, bearing the yoke, self-examination, repentance, and prayer. It describes national ruin and tears for the people, the speaker pursued and cast into a dungeon, then calling on the LORD and being heard, and ends with petitions for judgment and recompense on enemies.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes Zion’s ruin: sanctuary stones scattered, children starving, and former nobles reduced to misery. It records famine, sword deaths, and women boiling their children. It attributes Jerusalem’s fall to sins of prophets and priests, with bloodshed and exile. It notes vain hope for foreign help, pursuit by enemies, and capture of “the anointed.” It announces judgment for Edom and an end to Zion’s captivity.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records a communal plea to the LORD to remember Judah’s reproach after devastation. It lists losses of inheritance and homes, orphanhood, scarcity of water and wood, forced labor and subjection to foreign powers, and danger and famine. It describes abuses in Zion and Judah, executions, and social collapse. It laments sin and Zion’s desolation, affirms God’s enduring throne, and asks for restoration and renewal amid fear of rejection.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi, among exiles by the river Chebar in Chaldea receiving the LORD’s word and seeing an opened-heaven vision. He describes a northern storm with fire and brightness, four living creatures with four faces and wings, and wheels within wheels full of eyes moving with the creatures. A firmament and throne appear above, with a manlike figure and surrounding glory; Ezekiel falls and hears a voice.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records the LORD addressing Ezekiel as “son of man,” raising him by the spirit, and commissioning him to speak to rebellious Israel. Ezekiel is commanded to deliver “Thus saith the Lord GOD” whether they listen or refuse, and not to fear their threats or looks. He is told not to be rebellious but to eat what is given. Ezekiel sees a hand holding a scroll written on both sides with lamentations, mourning, and woe.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Ezekiel being commanded to eat a scroll and speak God’s words to the house of Israel, who will not listen. The Spirit transports him to the exiles at Tel-abib by the river Chebar, where he sits astonished seven days. God appoints him watchman, requiring warning to wicked and righteous. Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory in the plain and is commanded to shut in his house, bound and made mute until God opens his mouth.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Ezekiel acting out Jerusalem’s siege by drawing the city on a tile, building siege works, and setting an iron pan as a barrier. He lies on his left side 390 days for Israel’s iniquity and on his right side 40 days for Judah. He eats measured bread made from mixed grains and drinks limited water; the bread is baked with dung (changed to cow dung). God announces severe rationing and famine in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Ezekiel shaving his head and beard, dividing the hair into thirds to burn, strike, and scatter, with a few strands bound and then burned as a sign. It identifies Jerusalem among the nations, charges it with rejecting God’s statutes and defiling the sanctuary, and announces unprecedented judgments: famine, pestilence, sword, scattering, cannibalism, desolation, and reproach.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the LORD commanding Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s mountains, hills, valleys, and rivers. It announces judgment by sword, famine, and pestilence, with cities ruined, high places destroyed, altars desolated, and idols and images broken, and slain lying before idols. It states a remnant escapes and is scattered among nations, remembers the LORD, loathes its abominations, and acknowledges Him. The land becomes desolate toward Diblath.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records the LORD’s message to Ezekiel announcing the imminent end for the land of Israel. It describes divine judgment without pity for abominations, with wrath, sword, famine, and pestilence. It notes mourning and flight to the mountains, helplessness, and discarded silver and gold. It states strangers seize and defile holy places, violence fills the land, leaders mourn, and guidance from prophet, priest, and elders fails.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Ezekiel, while sitting with Judah’s elders, being taken in a vision to Jerusalem’s temple. He sees the image of jealousy at the north gate, secret idol images worshipped by seventy elders including Jaazaniah, women weeping for Tammuz, and about twenty-five men in the inner court worshipping the sun. God denounces these abominations and violence and declares judgment without pity.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a vision of six men with destroying weapons coming to Jerusalem from the north gate, with a seventh clothed in linen carrying an inkhorn. The glory of the God of Israel moves to the temple threshold. The linen-clothed man marks those grieving over abominations, and the others kill the unmarked, beginning at the sanctuary. Ezekiel pleads; the LORD cites Judah and Israel’s iniquity. The man reports completing the marking.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Ezekiel’s vision of cherubim and wheels beneath a sapphire-like throne. A man clothed in linen takes coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatters them over the city. The cloud and brightness fill the temple as the LORD’s glory moves from the cherub to the threshold, then departs to stand over the cherubim at the east gate. The chapter details the wheels, eyes, four faces, wings, and coordinated movement.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Ezekiel’s vision at the east gate of the LORD’s house, where 25 leaders including Jaazaniah and Pelatiah are condemned for wicked counsel and violence. Ezekiel prophesies judgment: sword, exile, and judgment at Israel’s border; Pelatiah dies. The LORD promises to be a sanctuary for exiles, gather them back, remove abominations, and give one heart and a new spirit. The glory departs Jerusalem eastward; Ezekiel reports the vision in Chaldea.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records the LORD commanding Ezekiel to act out exile by preparing baggage, digging through a wall, and departing at twilight as a sign to Israel. Ezekiel explains it concerns the prince in Jerusalem and the people’s coming captivity, scattering, and a remnant spared. He also eats and drinks with trembling to signify Jerusalem’s desolation, and rebukes proverbs delaying judgment, declaring the visions will occur soon.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD’s word to Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s false prophets who speak from their own hearts, claim visions, and promise peace. God declares judgment: they are excluded from the assembly and register of Israel, and their “wall” daubed with untempered mortar collapses in storm and hail. Ezekiel also condemns prophetess women using pillows and kerchiefs to “hunt souls”; God tears these away and delivers his people.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records elders coming to Ezekiel, and the LORD condemning idolatry in the heart and commanding Israel and sojourners to repent. It states God answers idolaters and cuts off those who seek prophets while clinging to idols, and that deceived prophets share punishment. It lists four judgments—famine, beasts, sword, pestilence—and says Noah, Daniel, and Job would save only themselves. A remnant from Jerusalem remains.

This chapter contains 8 verses and records the LORD’s word to Ezekiel comparing a vine’s wood to other trees, stating it is useless for work and fit only for fire. The LORD applies the image to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, declaring judgment: He sets His face against them, they escape one fire but are consumed by another, and the land becomes desolate because of their trespass.

This chapter contains 63 verses and records the LORD’s allegory of Jerusalem as an abandoned infant raised and covenant-married, then becoming unfaithful through idolatry, alliances, and child sacrifice. It lists “whoredoms” with Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldea, and announces judgment by former lovers: stripping, stoning, sword, and burning. It compares Jerusalem with Samaria and Sodom, cites Sodom’s sins, and promises remembrance and establishment of an everlasting covenant bringing shame.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records a riddle of two eagles and a vine, then explains it as Babylon taking Judah’s king and princes, installing a king under covenant, and that king rebelling by seeking Egypt’s horses and help. It declares judgment for breaking the oath: capture, exile to Babylon, death, and scattering of fugitives. It also promises God planting a tender cedar on Israel’s high mountain to grow and shelter birds.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the LORD rejecting the proverb about fathers’ sour grapes in Israel, stating each person is accountable for his own sin. It contrasts a righteous man’s obedience with a violent, idolatrous son’s death, and a grandson who refuses his father’s sins. It declares that the son and father do not bear each other’s iniquity, calls Israel to repent, and states God judges each by his ways.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records a lamentation for Israel’s princes, using imagery of a lioness raising two young lions who devour men; nations capture the first and take him in chains to Egypt, and capture the second and bring him to the king of Babylon. It also portrays Israel as a fruitful vine by waters, then uprooted, dried by an east wind, burned, replanted in a wilderness, and left without a ruling scepter.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records elders of Israel seeking inquiry as Ezekiel recounts Israel’s rebellions in Egypt, the wilderness, and the land, including idolatry, polluted Sabbaths, high places, and child sacrifice. It declares refusal to be inquired of, foretells scattering and later gathering, covenant purging of rebels, restored worship on God’s holy mountain, and a fire prophecy against the southern forest.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records the LORD’s prophecy of a drawn sword against Jerusalem, the holy places, and the land of Israel, cutting off righteous and wicked. Ezekiel is told to sigh as a sign of coming terror and slaughter. The king of Babylon chooses by divination a route toward Jerusalem and Rabbath. A wicked prince of Israel is judged, the crown removed, and rule overturned. Judgment is also pronounced on Ammon.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD’s charges against Jerusalem as a “bloody city” guilty of bloodshed, idolatry, dishonoring parents, oppressing strangers, widows, and the poor, profaning holy things and Sabbaths, sexual sins, bribery, usury, and extortion. It announces scattering among nations and uses a furnace/dross metaphor for judgment. It indicts corrupt prophets, priests, princes, and people, and states no intercessor is found, so wrath is poured out.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records an allegory of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), who commit harlotry with Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon and defile themselves with idols. It recounts Samaria’s judgment by Assyria and declares Jerusalem’s greater corruption. The LORD announces punishment by Babylon and allied peoples, including stripping, slaughter, fire, and desolation, for adultery, bloodshed, child sacrifice, profaning the sanctuary, and breaking sabbaths.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records the date Babylon begins the siege of Jerusalem, then gives a parable of a boiling pot condemning the “bloody city” and declaring judgment. It reports Ezekiel’s wife dies and he is commanded not to mourn as a sign to Israel. It foretells the sanctuary’s profanation, children falling by the sword, and Ezekiel’s speech returning when a survivor brings news.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Ezekiel’s prophecies of judgment against Ammon, Moab/Seir, Edom, and Philistia for rejoicing over Israel’s desolation and Judah’s captivity, and for taking vengeance. It predicts these lands are given to “men of the east,” Rabbah becomes pasture, Moab’s frontier cities (Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim) are opened, Edom is made desolate from Teman to Dedan, and the Cherethites and coastal remnant are cut off.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records a prophecy against Tyre for rejoicing over Jerusalem’s fall. God declares opposition to Tyre, bringing many nations and Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to besiege it, break walls and towers, kill outlying towns, and plunder wealth. Tyre becomes scraped bare, submerged, and uninhabited, a place for spreading nets. Sea princes and isles lament and tremble at its destruction.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records a lamentation over Tyrus (Tyre), portrayed as a merchant city at the sea’s entry. It lists materials and craftsmen for its ships and adornment, its mariners and soldiers, and its trading partners and goods from many regions. It then describes Tyre’s wreck by an east wind, loss of riches and crews, widespread mourning by seafarers, and astonishment among isles and kings at its ruin.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records prophecies against the prince and king of Tyre for pride, wealth, and claiming divinity, foretelling invasion by foreigners, death, and a lament describing former splendor in Eden and expulsion for iniquity and violent trade. It also prophesies judgment on Zidon by pestilence and sword, and promises Israel’s gathering, secure dwelling in Jacob’s land, and safety from surrounding enemies.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records an oracle against Pharaoh and Egypt, portraying Pharaoh as a river dragon and warning of judgment, desolation from Syene to Ethiopia, and forty years of uninhabited land with Egyptians scattered among nations. It states Egypt later returns to Pathros as a diminished kingdom and no longer supports Israel. It also assigns Egypt to Nebuchadrezzar as wages for Babylon’s service against Tyre and mentions Israel’s horn budding and Ezekiel speaking.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Ezekiel’s prophecy of the near “day of the LORD” bringing sword and desolation on Egypt and its allies (Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, Chub). It names Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon as the agent who destroys Egypt, dries rivers, ends idols and princes, and judges cities such as Noph, No, Zoan, Sin, Pathros, Tehaphnehes, Aven, and Pi-beseth. Pharaoh’s arms are broken, Egypt is scattered among nations.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records a prophecy to Pharaoh king of Egypt comparing Assyria to a towering cedar in Lebanon nourished by waters and sheltering nations. Because of pride, God delivers it to a mighty foreign ruler; strangers cut it down and peoples depart. Its fall brings mourning, nations tremble, and it descends to the pit with the slain. Pharaoh and his multitude are likewise brought down among the uncircumcised.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records two dated lamentations over Pharaoh and Egypt. It portrays Pharaoh as a sea creature taken in God’s net, cast on land, and Egypt made desolate by the sword of the king of Babylon. It describes cosmic darkening and nations’ kings fearing Egypt’s fall. It then depicts Egypt’s multitude descending to the pit among the uncircumcised slain, alongside Asshur, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, northern princes, and Zidonians.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records the LORD appointing Ezekiel as watchman to warn Israel, explaining accountability for warning the wicked. It covers calls for repentance, stating that the wicked who turn and do right live, and the righteous who sin die, and that each is judged by his ways. It reports a fugitive announcing Jerusalem’s fall, Ezekiel’s speech returning, judgment on idolatrous land-claimers, and hearers who listen but do not obey.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records the LORD’s indictment of Israel’s shepherds for exploiting and neglecting the flock, resulting in scattering and prey to beasts. The LORD declares judgment on the shepherds, personally seeks and gathers the scattered sheep, and restores them to the mountains of Israel. He judges between rams and goats, promises one shepherd “David,” a covenant of peace, safety, and land blessings.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records the LORD’s word to Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir (Edom/Idumea). It announces judgment for perpetual hatred, bloodshed against Israel, and claiming Israel’s lands. The LORD declares cities will be laid waste, the land made perpetually desolate, and the mountains filled with slain. It condemns boasting and blasphemies against Israel and states Edom will be desolated as it rejoiced over Israel’s desolation.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Ezekiel prophesying to Israel’s mountains and land against surrounding nations and Edom, promising restored fruitfulness, rebuilding, and repopulated cities. It recounts Israel’s defilement, bloodshed, and idolatry, leading to scattering among nations and profaning God’s name. God promises to act for his name’s sake: gather Israel back, cleanse them, give a new heart and spirit, ensure obedience, end famine, and fill cities with people like flocks.

This chapter contains 28 verses and describes Ezekiel’s vision of a valley of dry bones revived by prophecy and breath, explained as Israel restored and returned to its land. It records the sign of two sticks for Judah and Joseph joined as one, symbolizing reunification. The LORD promises gathering from nations, one king “David,” cleansing from idols, obedience to statutes, an everlasting covenant of peace, and a permanent sanctuary among them.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD commanding Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. Gog gathers allies (Persia, Ethiopia, Libya, Gomer, Togarmah) to invade restored Israel’s mountains and unwalled villages for spoil. Sheba, Dedan, and Tarshish question the invasion. God promises fury, earthquake, confusion, sword, pestilence, and hail, fire, and brimstone to destroy Gog and magnify God among nations.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records prophecy against Gog of Magog: he comes from the north to Israel’s mountains, is defeated, and his forces become food for birds and beasts. Israel burns captured weapons for seven years and buries the dead for seven months in the Valley of Hamon-gog, cleansing the land. God’s judgment is shown to nations, Israel’s captivity is explained, and Jacob is restored with God’s Spirit.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records Ezekiel’s vision in Israel of a temple complex measured by a man with a measuring reed. It details the outer wall, the east, north, and south gates, their chambers, steps, windows, arches, and palm-tree carvings, and the outer court with thirty chambers and pavement. It measures distances between gates and the inner court, describes tables and chambers for washing and slaughtering offerings, identifies chambers for singers and priests (sons of Zadok), and measures the inner court, altar area, and porch.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records the man guiding Ezekiel measuring the temple: doorways, posts, inner sanctuary, and the most holy place. It details wall thickness, three levels of side chambers with winding ascent, surrounding spaces, and a west building and separate place with dimensions. It describes porches, galleries, narrow windows, and wood paneling. Cherubim and palm-tree carvings cover walls and doors. A wooden altar/table stands before the LORD.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Ezekiel being shown temple chambers in the outer court on the north and south, with their dimensions, galleries, walks, doors, and entrances. The guide identifies these as holy chambers where priests eat most holy things and store offerings and priestly garments. After measuring the inner house, he measures the surrounding area on all four sides, 500 reeds each, with a wall separating sanctuary from profane.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Ezekiel being brought to the east gate as the glory of the God of Israel enters the temple and fills it. The LORD declares the house as his dwelling and commands Israel to stop defiling his name. Ezekiel is told to show Israel the temple pattern and ordinances. Measurements and laws of the altar are given, including seven-day cleansing and consecration sacrifices by Zadokite priests.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records regulations for the temple: the east outer gate remains shut because the LORD enters by it, and only the prince uses its porch to eat before the LORD. Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory fill the house. Foreigners uncircumcised in heart or flesh are barred. Wayward Levites serve as gatekeepers and slaughter sacrifices but are restricted from priestly access. Sons of Zadok minister at the altar with linen garments, purity and marriage rules, teaching and judging duties, sabbath observance, defilement limits, offerings, and priestly portions.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records instructions for dividing the land, setting apart a holy oblation with measured portions for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, the city, and the prince. It commands princes to stop oppression and use just weights and measures. It specifies required offerings of grain, oil, and lambs supplied by the people for the prince. It assigns the prince festival sacrifices and gives rites for cleansing the sanctuary and for Passover and the seventh-month feast.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records temple regulations for opening the east inner gate on Sabbaths and new moons, the prince’s entry and required burnt, peace, and meal offerings, and people’s movement through north and south gates at feasts. It commands a daily morning lamb offering with flour and oil, sets inheritance rules for the prince, and describes priestly kitchens and corner courts for boiling and baking offerings.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Ezekiel’s vision of waters flowing east from the temple threshold, measured in stages into an impassable river with trees on both banks. The river goes to the sea and heals it, bringing abundant fish; marshes remain salty; trees yield continual fruit and medicinal leaves. It also defines Israel’s land borders and inheritance by tribes, including portions for Joseph and resident foreigners.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records the allotment of land to Israel’s tribes from north to south, naming borders and portions for Dan through Gad. It defines the central holy oblation with areas for the sanctuary, priests of the sons of Zadok, and Levites, forbidding its sale. It gives measurements for the city and suburbs, assigns remaining land to the prince, lists the city’s twelve tribal gates, and names the city “The LORD is there.”

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar’s siege of Jerusalem, Jehoiakim’s capture, and temple vessels taken to Shinar. It covers Ashpenaz selecting royal Judean youths, including Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, renaming them and training them in Chaldean language and learning. Daniel requests a diet of pulse and water; after a ten-day test they appear healthier. God gives them knowledge; Daniel understands visions and dreams, and they serve before the king until Cyrus’s first year.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar’s troubling dream and his demand that Babylon’s wise men recount and interpret it, threatening death when they cannot. Daniel seeks time, prays with Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, receives the secret in a night vision, and blesses God. Daniel tells the dream of a multi-metal statue shattered by a stone and interprets successive kingdoms. Nebuchadnezzar honors Daniel, promotes him, and appoints Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego over Babylon’s affairs.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar setting up a golden image on the plain of Dura and commanding all officials to worship it at musical signals, with death in a fiery furnace for refusal. Chaldeans accuse Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who refuse to worship. They are cast into an overheated furnace; the guards die, and the three are seen unharmed with a fourth figure. Nebuchadnezzar summons them out, issues a decree against speaking against their God, and promotes them.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Nebuchadnezzar’s proclamation about signs shown to him, his troubling dream of a great tree cut down by a heavenly watcher, and the failure of Babylon’s wise men to interpret it. Daniel interprets the tree as Nebuchadnezzar and predicts his removal, beast-like living for seven times, and later restoration. After twelve months the judgment occurs; his reason returns, his kingdom is restored, and he praises the God of heaven.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Belshazzar’s feast in Babylon using vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple and praising idol gods. A hand writes on the palace wall; the king summons wise men, who cannot interpret it. The queen recommends Daniel, who recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation and rebukes Belshazzar. Daniel reads “MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN,” declaring the kingdom numbered, weighed, and divided to Medes and Persians. Belshazzar honors Daniel, then is slain; Darius the Median takes the kingdom.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Darius appointing princes and presidents, with Daniel promoted. Officials obtain a Medo-Persian decree banning petitions to any god or man except the king for thirty days. Daniel prays toward Jerusalem and is accused; Darius, unable to change the law, casts him into a lions’ den and seals it. Daniel is preserved, the accusers and their families are executed, and Darius issues a decree honoring Daniel’s God; Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Daniel’s dream in Belshazzar’s first year: four beasts rise from the sea, and a fourth has ten horns and a little horn. Daniel sees the Ancient of days convene judgment, books opened, and the beast destroyed. One like the Son of man receives everlasting dominion. An attendant interprets the beasts as four kings and the horns as kings; the little horn wars against the saints until judgment grants them the kingdom.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Daniel’s vision in Belshazzar’s third year at Shushan by the Ulai: a two-horned ram conquers until a goat with a great horn breaks the ram, then the horn breaks into four and a little horn rises, stops daily sacrifice, and profanes the sanctuary. A time of 2,300 days is given. Gabriel identifies the ram as Media-Persia and the goat as Greece, with a later fierce king. Daniel becomes sick, then returns to the king’s business.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Daniel, in Darius’s first year, studying Jeremiah’s seventy years and praying with fasting, confession, and petitions for Jerusalem and the desolate sanctuary. He cites Israel’s disobedience to the law and prophets and asks for mercy. Gabriel appears, gives understanding, and announces “seventy weeks,” timelines for rebuilding Jerusalem, events concerning Messiah, and future desolation and cessation of sacrifice.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Daniel mourning and fasting three weeks by the river Hiddekel, where he sees a radiant man in linen. Daniel’s companions flee, and Daniel collapses until touched and strengthened. The messenger says Daniel’s prayers are heard but delayed by the prince of Persia until Michael helps. He comes to explain future events for Daniel’s people and mentions conflict with Persia and Grecia.

This chapter contains 45 verses and records an angelic prophecy given in the first year of Darius the Mede. It covers successive Persian kings, a mighty Greek king whose kingdom divides four ways, and prolonged conflicts between kings of the south and north, including alliances, invasions, taxes, and deceit. It describes persecution against the holy covenant, removal of daily sacrifice, the abomination of desolation, and an end-time northern king’s campaigns in the glorious land, Egypt, and surrounding nations, ending in his downfall.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Michael standing for Daniel’s people during an unparalleled time of trouble and deliverance for those written in the book. It describes many awakening from the dust to everlasting life or contempt, and the wise shining. Daniel is told to seal the words until the end. Two figures question a man in linen about timing; durations and 1290/1335 days are given, and Daniel is told to rest and stand in his lot.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records the LORD’s word to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, and Jeroboam. Hosea marries Gomer and has three children named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-ammi. The LORD announces judgment on Jehu’s house, the end of Israel’s kingdom, and defeat in Jezreel, while showing mercy to Judah. It also foretells Israel’s future increase and Judah and Israel being gathered under one head.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD’s charge against an unfaithful “mother,” threatening exposure, deprivation, and removal of grain, wine, wool, and feast days for pursuing Baal. It describes hedging her path, ending her mirth, and destroying vines and fig trees. It then records restoration promises: alluring her into the wilderness, giving vineyards and the valley of Achor, removing Baal’s names, making a covenant of peace, betrothing her, and declaring “not my people” as “my people.”

This chapter contains 5 verses and records the LORD commanding Hosea to love and redeem an adulterous woman, whom he buys for silver and barley and instructs to remain faithful for many days. It covers Israel abiding many days without king, prince, sacrifice, image, ephod, or teraphim, and later returning to seek the LORD and David their king.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records the LORD’s charge against Israel for lacking truth, mercy, and knowledge of God, listing sins such as swearing, lying, murder, theft, adultery, and idolatry. It announces judgment on land, people, priests, and prophets, rejection of priests for forgetting the law, and punishment for corrupt worship on hills and mountains. It warns Judah to avoid Gilgal and Beth-aven, declares Ephraim joined to idols, and foretells shame for their sacrifices.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records a warning of judgment to priests, Israel, and the king’s house for ensnaring others and committing whoredom and treachery. Ephraim and Israel are exposed, and Judah also falls. They seek the LORD with sacrifices but do not find him. Alarm sounds at Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth-aven; Ephraim becomes desolate. Judah’s princes violate boundaries. Ephraim turns to Assyria and King Jareb but is not healed. The LORD withdraws, tears like a lion, and waits until they acknowledge guilt and seek him.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records a call to return to the LORD for healing and revival, with promises of being raised up and knowing the LORD. It rebukes Ephraim and Judah for fleeting goodness and covenant transgression. The LORD states he desires mercy and knowledge of God over sacrifices. It condemns Gilead’s bloodshed, priests’ robbery and murder, Ephraim’s whoredom, Israel’s defilement, and announces a harvest judgment for Judah.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes the LORD exposing Ephraim and Samaria’s iniquity, falsehood, theft, adultery, and corruption of kings and princes. It records internal plots and the fall of rulers, Israel’s unnoticed weakening by strangers, and refusal to return to the LORD. Ephraim seeks help from Egypt and Assyria; the LORD promises to net and chastise them. It covers unrepentant cries for grain and wine, rebellion, and princes falling by the sword.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records judgment against Israel for breaking the covenant and rejecting good, with an enemy coming like an eagle. It covers unauthorized kings and princes, idolatry with Samaria’s calf, and the promise it will be broken. Israel “sows the wind,” is swallowed among nations, and seeks Assyria. Ephraim multiplies sinful altars, ignores the law, offers unacceptable sacrifices, and is told they will return to Egypt. Judah’s fortified cities face fire.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records warnings to Israel/Ephraim against rejoicing amid unfaithfulness, announcing failed harvests, exile to Egypt and Assyria, and inability to offer acceptable sacrifices. It describes coming visitation and recompense, corrupt prophets, and remembered sins like Gibeah and Baal-peor. It covers bereavement and barrenness, judgment from Gilgal, princes’ revolt, loss of fruitfulness, and being cast away to wander among nations.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Hosea’s indictment of Israel’s idolatry and divided heart, predicting the breaking of altars and images. Samaria fears for the calves of Beth-aven; the idol is carried to Assyria to king Jareb, bringing Ephraim shame, and Samaria’s king is cut off. High places are destroyed. Israel is chastised, recalled to seek the LORD and sow righteousness, and warned of coming spoil of fortresses and Beth-el’s role, ending with the king’s sudden removal.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records the LORD recalling love for Israel from childhood and the exodus, Israel’s turn to Baal and idols, and continued backsliding. It announces Assyria as king and sword in Israel’s cities. The LORD hesitates to give up Ephraim, restrains anger, and promises future return as the people follow Him. It ends noting Ephraim’s lies, Israel’s deceit, and Judah’s faithfulness.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the LORD’s charges against Ephraim and Judah for deceit, oppression, and foreign alliances with Assyria and Egypt. It recalls Jacob’s struggles and encounters with God at Beth-el and his service in Syria. The people are commanded to return to God, keep mercy and judgment, and wait continually. It mentions prophetic revelation, condemns sacrifices in Gilead and Gilgal, recalls the exodus by a prophet, and announces coming recompense and reproach for Ephraim.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records condemnation of Ephraim/Israel for increasing sin and idolatry with molten images, recalling the LORD’s deliverance from Egypt and care in the wilderness. It warns that prosperity leads to forgetting God and announces violent judgment likened to lion, leopard, and bear. It mentions Israel’s self-destruction, the giving and removal of kings, bound-up iniquity, coming travail, and a declared ransom from death. It foretells an east wind drying springs and Samaria’s desolation by war.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a call for Israel to return to the LORD with repentant words, rejecting Assyria, reliance on horses, and idols. The LORD promises to heal Israel’s backsliding, turn away anger, and bless them with growth and restoration described as dew, lily, Lebanon roots, olive branches, grain, vine, and wine scent. Ephraim renounces idols, and the chapter ends urging the wise to understand the LORD’s right ways.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records the word of the LORD to Joel son of Pethuel, calling elders and inhabitants to hear of an unprecedented locust devastation. It describes crops, vines, fig trees, and offerings to the LORD cut off, with priests mourning. Joel commands lamentation, sackcloth, a sanctified fast, and a solemn assembly at the LORD’s house, warning of the day of the LORD. It reports drought, fire, ruined barns, and suffering livestock.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records an alarm in Zion about the day of the LORD and a great invading army bringing darkness and devastation. It commands repentance with fasting, assembly, and priestly intercession. The LORD promises pity, removal of the northern army, restoration of crops and rains, and renewal after locust loss. It foretells the Spirit poured on all flesh, cosmic signs, and deliverance for those calling on the LORD in Zion and Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the LORD restoring Judah and Jerusalem, gathering the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat for judgment over scattering Israel and dividing the land. It names Tyre, Zidon, and Philistia for plundering and selling captives, and announces retaliation. It calls nations to war, depicts cosmic signs, and the LORD speaking from Zion. It promises Jerusalem’s holiness, abundant waters, Egypt and Edom desolated, and Judah enduring.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Amos of Tekoa prophesying about Israel during Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II, before the earthquake. The LORD roars from Zion and announces judgments for repeated transgressions against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon. It specifies crimes against Gilead and captive-taking, and declares fire, destruction of rulers and strongholds, and captivity for Syria and Ammon’s king and princes.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records the LORD’s judgments on Moab, Judah, and Israel. Moab is punished for burning Edom’s king’s bones; fire consumes Kerioth and rulers are cut off. Judah is punished for despising the law; fire consumes Jerusalem’s palaces. Israel is charged with selling the righteous and oppressing the poor, sexual sin, and profaning pledges and wine; the LORD recalls deliverance from Egypt, defeat of the Amorites, and raising prophets and Nazarites, then declares no escape in coming judgment.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records the LORD’s word against Israel, stating Israel’s special relationship and coming punishment for iniquities. It uses rhetorical examples (walking, lion, snare, trumpet) to affirm that judgment is announced through prophets. Witnesses are summoned from Ashdod and Egypt to observe violence in Samaria. An adversary surrounds the land, spoils palaces, leaves few survivors, and judgment falls on Bethel’s altars and Israel’s houses.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the LORD’s warning to the “kine of Bashan” in Samaria for oppressing the poor, foretelling exile with hooks. It references worship at Beth-el and Gilgal with sacrifices and tithes. It lists chastisements—famine, withheld rain, drought, blight and mildew, locusts, pestilence, sword, and overthrow like Sodom—repeating Israel’s failure to return, and commands Israel to prepare to meet God.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records a lamentation over Israel’s fall and coming depletion. It commands Israel to seek the LORD to live and not to seek Beth-el, Gilgal, or Beer-sheba.
