It condemns injustice, oppression of the poor, bribery, and rejecting upright rebuke. It announces widespread wailing and that the day of the LORD is darkness. It rejects feasts, sacrifices, and songs without justice, recalls wilderness idolatry (Moloch, Chiun), and foretells captivity beyond Damascus.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records a woe against those at ease in Zion and secure in Samaria, citing Calneh, Hamath, and Gath. It lists luxury, feasting, music, and indifference to Israel’s affliction, and foretells captivity. The LORD swears to abhor Jacob’s pride, deliver the city, and bring widespread death and destruction, raising a nation to afflict Israel from Hemath to the wilderness river.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Amos’s visions of locusts and consuming fire, both averted after his pleas, and a plumb line set in Israel with judgment announced on shrines and Jeroboam’s house. Amaziah of Bethel accuses Amos and orders him to leave. Amos states his calling and prophesies punishment on Amaziah and Israel’s captivity.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Amos’s vision of a basket of summer fruit, signaling the end for Israel. It condemns merchants who exploit the poor through dishonest measures and selling the needy. The LORD swears he will remember their deeds and announces mourning, many deaths, land trembling, and daytime darkness. It foretells a famine of hearing the LORD’s words, fruitless searching, and the fall of idol-swearers in Samaria, Dan, and Beer-sheba.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Amos seeing the Lord at the altar declaring unavoidable judgment on sinners, with none able to escape by flight, hiding, sea, or captivity. It describes God’s power over land and seas and his dealings with Israel and other nations. It foretells destruction of the sinful kingdom yet not total extinction of Jacob, a sifting among nations, and sinners dying by the sword. It promises restoration of David’s fallen tabernacle, possession of Edom and nations, agricultural abundance, return from captivity, rebuilding cities, planting vineyards, and permanent settlement in the land.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Obadiah’s vision pronouncing judgment on Edom for pride and violence against Jacob, including aiding foreigners during Jerusalem’s calamity, looting, and cutting off fugitives. It announces Edom’s humiliation, betrayal by allies, and destruction of its wisdom and warriors. It declares the day of the LORD on the nations, deliverance on Mount Zion, Israel’s restored possessions and territorial expansions, and Zion leaders judging Esau.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the LORD commanding Jonah to go to Nineveh, Jonah fleeing toward Tarshish from Joppa, and a divinely sent storm threatening the ship. Mariners cast lots identifying Jonah, question him, and learn he is a Hebrew who fears the LORD. Jonah says he is the cause and asks to be thrown overboard; the sea calms. The sailors pray, sacrifice, and vow to the LORD. A great fish swallows Jonah for three days and nights.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records Jonah praying to the LORD from inside the fish, recounting being cast into the deep and surrounded by waters, and remembering the LORD and looking toward his holy temple. Jonah states that those who follow lying vanities forsake mercy, vows thanksgiving and sacrifice, and affirms salvation is of the LORD. The LORD commands the fish to vomit Jonah onto dry land.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records the LORD commanding Jonah a second time to preach in Nineveh. Jonah goes to the great city and proclaims that in forty days Nineveh will be overthrown. The people believe God, fast, and wear sackcloth. The king decrees fasting for people and animals and calls for turning from evil and violence. God sees their repentance and does not bring the announced destruction.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records Jonah’s anger over Nineveh’s sparing and his prayer, including recalling his flight toward Tarshish and asking to die. The LORD questions Jonah’s anger. Jonah waits east of the city. God provides a gourd for shade, then a worm to wither it and an east wind that causes Jonah to faint. God contrasts Jonah’s pity for the gourd with God’s concern for Nineveh’s people and cattle.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records the word of the LORD to Micah during Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. It summons all peoples to witness the LORD’s coming in judgment for Israel and Judah’s sins, foretelling Samaria’s ruin and idols destroyed. Micah laments, warns Judah as harm reaches Jerusalem, names towns affected, and ends with mourning and captivity.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records a woe against those who plan evil, covet fields, seize houses, and oppress families. The LORD announces judgment, lamentation over lost land, and exclusion from allotment in the congregation. The people reject prophecy and commit violence, dispossessing women and children. A command to depart is given. False prophets are noted. The LORD promises to assemble Jacob’s remnant, lead them out, and go before them with their king.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Micah rebuking the heads and princes of Jacob/Israel for perverting judgment, oppressing the people, and building Zion and Jerusalem through bloodshed and iniquity. It condemns prophets who mislead for gain, proclaiming peace for payment and threatening others. It announces that God will not answer them, visions will cease, and seers will be ashamed. Micah declares power to expose sin and foretells Zion plowed and Jerusalem ruined.

This chapter contains 13 verses and describes the LORD establishing Zion as an elevated center where many nations come to learn his law from Jerusalem, resulting in judgment among nations and the end of warfare. It records peace and security, the gathering of the afflicted remnant, and the LORD reigning in Mount Zion. It also covers Zion’s labor pains, exile to Babylon and redemption, hostile nations gathered, and Zion commanded to thresh them and consecrate their gain to the LORD.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Jerusalem under siege and Israel’s judge struck. It names Beth-lehem Ephratah as the birthplace of a ruler in Israel, followed by a return of a remnant. It describes deliverance from the Assyrian and the remnant of Jacob among many peoples. The LORD promises to cut off horses, chariots, cities, strongholds, witchcraft, soothsayers, idols, groves, and to execute vengeance on the heathen.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records the LORD’s controversy with Israel before the mountains, recalling deliverance from Egypt and leaders Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, and the events of Balak and Balaam from Shittim to Gilgal. It contrasts proposed sacrifices with the requirement to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly. It condemns wicked wealth, false measures, violence, and deceit, announces punishment with hunger and loss, and cites statutes of Omri and Ahab leading to desolation and reproach.

This chapter contains 20 verses and describes lament over the absence of upright people, corruption among rulers, and distrust within families. The speaker waits for the LORD, accepts indignation for sin, and expects vindication and enemy shame. It records promises of restored walls, returning peoples from Assyria and other regions, and land desolation for wrongdoing. It asks God to shepherd Israel and recalls Egypt. It concludes with God pardoning iniquity, showing mercy, and keeping promises to Jacob and Abraham.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Nahum’s vision concerning Nineveh, describing the LORD’s jealousy, vengeance, and power over seas, rivers, mountains, and storms, while being a refuge for those who trust him. It foretells Nineveh’s utter end, the cutting down of its multitude, and the defeat of a wicked counselor. It announces breaking a yoke from Judah, destroying idols, ending Nineveh’s name, and calling Judah to keep feasts and vows.

This chapter contains 13 verses and describes the assault and collapse of Nineveh: a destroyer approaches, defenses are urged, and the attackers’ shields, chariots, and rush through streets are depicted. River gates open and the palace dissolves; Huzzab is taken captive. Nineveh’s people flee, silver and gold are plundered, and the city is left desolate. The LORD declares opposition, burning chariots, ending prey, and silencing messengers.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a woe against Nineveh for violence, deceit, robbery, and harlotry and witchcraft. It depicts attacking armies, slaughter, and public shame pronounced by the LORD of hosts. It compares Nineveh to No (Thebes) with Egypt, Ethiopia, Put, and Lubim, yet carried into captivity. It foretells Nineveh’s fortresses falling, gates burned, siege preparations failing, merchants and leaders fleeing, Assyria’s king left with scattered people, and no healing.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Habakkuk’s burden and complaint to the LORD about violence, injustice, and corrupted judgment in the land. The LORD answers that He raises the Chaldeans to march and conquer, taking captives and deriding rulers. Habakkuk responds that the LORD ordains them for judgment yet questions why a purer God allows the wicked to devour the more righteous, likening the Chaldeans to fishermen who capture nations and honor their nets.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Habakkuk watching for God’s reply; the LORD commands him to write the vision and wait for its appointed time. It contrasts the proud with the righteous living by faith. It pronounces five woes on an oppressor for plunder, covetousness, bloodshed, exploitation and making others drunk, and for idolatry. It declares coming retribution, the earth filled with the LORD’s glory, and the LORD in his holy temple.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records a prayer of Habakkuk asking the LORD to revive his work and remember mercy. It describes God’s coming from Teman and Mount Paran with glory, power, pestilence, and judgment over nations, mountains, rivers, and the sea. It mentions Cushan and Midian trembling, the sun and moon standing still, and salvation for God’s people and anointed. Habakkuk fears yet rejoices, declaring the LORD his strength.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the LORD’s word to Zephaniah in Josiah’s reign, announcing sweeping judgment on the land. It targets Judah and Jerusalem for idolatry and apostasy, including Baal, heavenly host worship, and those who do not seek the LORD. It warns of the day of the LORD, punishing princes, merchants, and complacent sinners, bringing cries, desolation, war alarm, blindness, and futile silver and gold.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records a call for the nation to gather and seek the LORD, righteousness, and meekness before the day of the LORD’s anger. It pronounces judgments on Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron) and the sea coast, later given to Judah’s remnant. It condemns Moab and Ammon for reproach, foretells their desolation, mentions Ethiopia’s slaying, and predicts Assyria and Nineveh’s ruin and abandonment.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records a woe against the polluted, oppressive city for disobedience and corrupt leaders, prophets, and priests. The LORD declares judgment on nations and calls people to wait for his gathering of kingdoms for indignation. He promises purified speech, dispersed worshipers returning with offerings, removal of the proud, and a humble remnant. Zion is told to rejoice; enemies are cast out, the LORD is present, and exiles are gathered and restored.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records the LORD’s word through Haggai in Darius’s second year to Zerubbabel and Joshua, rebuking the people for living in paneled houses while the temple lies waste. It commands them to consider their ways, gather wood, and rebuild, citing poor harvests and drought as judgment. The leaders and remnant obey, fear the LORD, receive “I am with you,” and begin temple work.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD’s messages through Haggai to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people about rebuilding the temple, urging strength and work without fear. It promises future shaking of heaven and nations, greater glory and peace for the latter house, and affirms God’s ownership of silver and gold. It uses priestly rulings on holiness and uncleanness to declare the people’s offerings unclean, recalls crop shortages and plagues, promises blessing from the temple’s foundation day, foretells overthrow of kingdoms, and chooses Zerubbabel as a signet.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the word of the LORD to Zechariah in Darius’s second year, calling the people to return to the LORD and not repeat their fathers’ disobedience. Zechariah sees a night vision of a rider among myrtle trees with horses reporting the earth at rest, and the angel asks mercy for Jerusalem after seventy years. The LORD declares jealousy for Jerusalem, displeasure with the nations, and that the temple and city will be rebuilt and prosper. Zechariah then sees four horns that scattered Judah and four craftsmen sent to cast them out.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Zechariah’s vision of a man with a measuring line sent to measure Jerusalem. Angels announce Jerusalem will be inhabited without walls, with the LORD as a surrounding wall of fire and glory within. The LORD calls exiles to flee from the north and Babylon, promises judgment on nations that spoiled Zion, and declares he will dwell in Zion as many nations join him. Judah and Jerusalem are chosen; all flesh is told to be silent.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records a vision of Joshua the high priest before the angel of the LORD with Satan opposing him, and the LORD rebuking Satan. Joshua’s filthy garments are removed and he is clothed with clean raiment and a fair mitre, with iniquity said to pass from him. The angel charges Joshua to walk in God’s ways and keep his charge, and promises governance in God’s house. It mentions the BRANCH, a stone with seven eyes, removal of iniquity in one day, and peaceful neighborly dwelling.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records an angel awakening Zechariah and showing a vision of a gold lampstand with seven lamps, a bowl, and two olive trees supplying oil. The angel explains the message to Zerubbabel: the work proceeds by the LORD’s Spirit; obstacles become level; Zerubbabel finishes the temple and sets the headstone. It mentions the LORD’s seven eyes and identifies the two anointed ones.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records Zechariah’s visions of a flying scroll measuring twenty by ten cubits, identified as a curse going over the whole earth against thieves and false swearers, entering their houses to consume them. It also covers an ephah with a woman called wickedness sealed with a lead weight and carried by two winged women to Shinar to be set in a house.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Zechariah’s vision of four chariots with colored horses coming between two bronze mountains, explained as four spirits sent by the Lord to patrol the earth, with missions to the north and south. It then commands taking silver and gold from exiles from Babylon to make crowns for Joshua the high priest, speaks of “the Branch” who builds the LORD’s temple, and sets the crowns as a temple memorial with a call to obey.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the LORD’s word to Zechariah in Darius’s fourth year after Sherezer and Regem-melech ask priests and prophets whether to continue fifth-month mourning. The LORD questions past fasting motives, recalls warnings by former prophets, and commands true judgment, mercy, and no oppression of widows, orphans, strangers, or poor. It notes Israel’s refusal to listen, resulting wrath, unanswered cries, scattering among nations, and a desolated land.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records the LORD of hosts declaring zeal for Zion, return to dwell in Jerusalem, and future peace with elders and children in its streets. It promises gathering from east and west, prosperity, and Judah and Israel becoming a blessing. It commands truth, just judgments, no evil plotting, and no false oaths. It says certain fasts become joyful feasts, and nations come to seek the LORD in Jerusalem.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records an oracle against Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon, foretelling Tyre’s overthrow and Philistine cities’ decline. It states the LORD encamps around his house to stop oppressors. Zion is told to rejoice as a king comes humble on a donkey, cutting war weapons and proclaiming peace with wide dominion. By covenant blood prisoners are freed, Judah and Ephraim oppose Greece, and the LORD defends and saves his people with future prosperity.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records a call to ask the LORD for rain, contrasting idols and diviners with the LORD’s care. The LORD expresses anger at false shepherds, visits Judah, and makes them strong in battle. He promises to strengthen and save Judah, Joseph, and Ephraim, gather and increase them, and restore exiles from Egypt and Assyria to Gilead and Lebanon, humbling Assyria and Egypt.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records a lament over Lebanon, Bashan, and Jordan, then the LORD commands feeding “the flock of slaughter.” The shepherd takes two staffs (Beauty and Bands), cuts off three shepherds, and withdraws care, breaking a covenant. He receives thirty pieces of silver and casts them to the potter in the house of the LORD. Bands is broken, ending brotherhood between Judah and Israel, and judgment is pronounced on a foolish, idol shepherd.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records an oracle for Israel: Jerusalem becomes a destabilizing object to surrounding nations during siege, and the LORD strikes attackers’ horses and riders while strengthening Judah and Jerusalem. The LORD saves Judah first, defends Jerusalem, and seeks to destroy nations that come against it. He pours a spirit of grace and supplication; the house of David and Jerusalem mourn for one pierced, with nationwide mourning by families.

This chapter contains 9 verses and records a fountain opened for the house of David and Jerusalem for sin and uncleanness, the cutting off of idols, prophets, and an unclean spirit from the land, and punishment of false prophecy. It mentions prophets denying their role and explaining wounds. The LORD calls for the shepherd to be struck and the sheep scattered; two-thirds die, and a remnant is refined and acknowledged as God’s people.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes the day of the LORD when nations gather against Jerusalem, the city is taken, and captives are led away. The LORD fights, stands on the Mount of Olives, and it splits to form a valley for flight. Living waters flow from Jerusalem; the LORD reigns over all earth. Enemies are struck with plague and panic, Judah gathers spoil, survivors keep Tabernacles or receive no rain, and holiness marks Jerusalem and temple vessels.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the LORD’s message to Israel through Malachi, affirming love for Jacob over Esau and announcing judgment on Edom. It rebukes priests for despising the LORD’s name by offering polluted, blind, lame, sick, and torn sacrifices and calling the altar contemptible. The LORD refuses such offerings, declares his name great among the nations, and pronounces a curse on deceptive worshipers.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the LORD’s commandment to the priests, warning of curses for dishonoring his name and corrupting the covenant with Levi, and describing the ideal priestly role. It indicts Judah for treachery, profaning the covenant, and marrying foreign worshipers, and warns of being cut off. It rebukes divorce and faithlessness to one’s wife, and condemns words questioning God’s justice.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records the LORD’s promise to send a messenger and come to his temple to purify the sons of Levi and judge sinners. It calls Israel to return and stop robbing God in tithes and offerings, promising blessings, protection of crops, and honor among nations. It rebukes complaints that serving God is vain, notes a book of remembrance for those who fear the LORD, and foretells distinction between righteous and wicked.

This chapter contains 6 verses and describes the coming day of the LORD that burns the proud and wicked like stubble, leaving them without root or branch. It records promises of healing and prosperity for those who fear God’s name and their victory over the wicked. It commands remembrance of Moses’ law given at Horeb. It foretells Elijah’s sending to turn fathers’ and children’s hearts and avert a curse.
